You're going to hurt each other.
Let me say that again, because nobody else will tell you this truth:
In every relationship that matters, you will wound the person you love most.
Not maybe.
Not if you're "toxic."
Not if you're doing it wrong.
Guaranteed.
You will say the thing that lands like a knife in their most tender place.
They will do the thing that makes your nervous system scream "DANGER" even though they're just loading the dishwasher.
You will misread their tone and respond to a threat that doesn't exist.
They will withdraw exactly when you need them most.
This is not a bug in the relationship software.
This is the feature.
Here's what nobody tells you about love:
The person who can hurt you most is the person who knows you best.
The same intimacy that creates your deepest connection also creates your greatest vulnerability.
The closer you get, the more precisely you can wound each other.
Your partner knows exactly which button to push to make you crumble—not because they're cruel, but because they've seen your blueprint.
And here's the part that will blow your mind:
The couples who last aren't the ones who never hurt each other.
They're the ones who've mastered the art of repair.
Most people think a good relationship means no conflict.
Wrong.
A good relationship means you know how to come back from conflict.
You know how to find each other after you've both turned into monsters.
You know how to say "I see how I hurt you" without defending why you had to do it.
The skill nobody teaches you:
How to repair a rupture in real time.
Not tomorrow when you've cooled off.
Not next week when you've talked to your therapist.
Right now. In the moment. While it's still bleeding.
Here's what repair actually looks like:
Not: "I'm sorry you feel that way."
But: "I can see that I hurt you. Help me understand how."
Not: "You're being too sensitive."
But: "Your pain makes sense. I want to get this."
Not: "I didn't mean to..."
But: "Impact matters more than intention. I hurt you."
The couples who make it learn to catch the wound before it becomes the scar.
They've practiced the conversation that goes:
"Something just happened between us."
"Yeah, I felt it too."
"Can we pause and figure this out?"
"Yes. Right now. Before it gets bigger."
This is the skill they don't teach in school:
How to stay curious about your partner's pain instead of defensive about your innocence.
How to move toward the hurt instead of away from it.
How to let your heart break a little when you realize you've wounded someone you adore.
Because here's the secret:
Every rupture is also an opportunity.
Every moment of "I hurt you" is also a moment of "I see you."
Every repair is a deposit in the trust account.
Every time you choose connection over being right, you're building something unbreakable.
The people in the strongest relationships aren't the ones who never fight.
They're the ones who fight well.
They know how to go to war with the problem, not each other.
They know the difference between being heard and being right.
They know that sometimes love looks like saying "I was wrong" even when you're only 51% wrong.
This is why your relationship keeps struggling:
Nobody taught you that hurting each other is inevitable.
Nobody taught you that repair is a skill.
Nobody taught you that the strongest couples are forged in the fire of learning how to find each other after they've lost each other.
You keep thinking you're doing it wrong when you hurt each other.
You're not.
You're just human.
The question isn't whether you'll wound each other.
The question is: Can you find your way back?
Can you sit in the discomfort of "I caused you pain"?
Can you resist the urge to explain away their hurt?
Can you choose repair over being right?
Because this is where love lives.
Not in the easy moments when everything's perfect.
But in the hard moments when everything's broken and you choose each other anyway.
In the moment when you look at the person whose heart you just stepped on and say:
"I see you. I hear you. I hurt you. How do we fix this?"
That's the skill that changes everything.
That's the skill that saves relationships.
That's the skill nobody teaches you but everyone needs.
Master repair, and you can love anyone.
Stay in rupture, and you'll lose everyone.
The choice is yours. See less

We pick romantic partners as the closest thing that makes sense to the drama of our childhood.
A neural pathway gets set in the brain on a daily basis of how the Universe works. Not how your parents work. Not how you work. But how the whole Universe works.
If your mom was distant, the Universe is distant.
If your dad yelled out you, that's what it takes to get you back in line.
This sets up how you fall in love with somebody.
Not because you want to, not because you don't want to.
But because it is that way for all of us.
Until.
You learn.
Usually by getting hurt.
The harsher the childhood, the more sophisticated the healing process.
We barely have choice in understanding why we pick the negative.
It fits PERFECTLY into what we've experienced.
Humans try to learn mindset work and ask each other "do you believe you deserve to be treated like that?" - but this stays in the intellect.
There is a neural pathway that is programmed in childhood of EXACTLY what makes sense on a daily basis.
We pick a partner in the hopes of resolving that.
I will say that again.
You choose a person because of high hopes of resolving the childhood unfairness.
At first, you don't choose a partner that simply makes you feel better.
You choose a partner that perfectly abandons or criticizes you in the hopes that one day they will not do it again.
Your brain attempts to get them to understand if they just don't hurt you again this way, then you would feel resolution.
Notice that you don't choose a partner in the first place that gives you resolution.
You choose a partner that holds the promise of resolving the familiar.
Resolving what happened on a daily basis in childhood.
"Falling in love" could sometimes be changed to "Falling in desperate need to make my experience different inside my soul."
The more unpredictable the childhood, the more sophisticated your protections to stay put.
This is why I have worked with clients for 10 to 12 years to get out of a relationship.
They must eventually learn to sit with the discomfort, with the knowing of how to stop chasing the dream of getting mom and dad to be nicer.
They have to face the opposite direction.
They have to feel the discomfort, the agonizing newness of how to feel the yumminess and sexiness of somebody treating them with care. See less

The Avoidant Partner Survival Guide
(For the partner who has to love someone who keeps disappearing on the inside.)
Loving an avoidant partner is its own kind of emotional marathon.
Not the kind you trained for.
The kind where the map keeps changing, the signs point in different directions, and half the time you’re running alone.
Avoidants aren’t bad people.
They’re scared people who learned a long time ago that closeness hurts.
So when you get close, even with good intentions, their nervous system flares like a silent alarm and they retreat.
And that retreat feels personal.
It feels like rejection.
It feels like you’re being punished for wanting connection.
But what’s actually happening is this:
Your avoidant partner is gasping for emotional air in a room you didn’t know was suffocating them.
Most days you’re trying to decode behaviors that don’t make sense:
They want you but don’t move toward you.
They love you but act indifferent.
They say you matter but don’t follow through.
They soften one moment and shut down the next.
You’re constantly guessing which version of them you’ll get, and your body pays the price.
Not because they’re cruel, but because they were never taught how to stay present when emotions rise in the room.
This survival guide is for you, the person trying to hold steady while someone you love keeps emotionally disappearing.
1. Learn the most painful truth:
Avoidants don’t retreat because of you.
They retreat because their entire system collapses under emotional intensity.
Your needs didn’t cause it.
Your heart didn’t cause it.
Your longing didn’t cause it.
They were shutting down long before they met you.
2. Stop taking their distance as a verdict.
Avoidants don’t distance to hurt you.
They distance because closeness activates panic.
Your story says, “I’m being rejected.”
Their story says, “I’m overwhelmed and don’t know how to stay.”
Two different wars.
Two different wounds.
3. Their silence isn’t clarity.
It’s survival.
And survival looks flat, cold, withdrawn.
That doesn’t mean they don’t care.
It means they don’t know how to show care without feeling swallowed.
4. Don’t chase.
Every time you chase, their alarm spikes.
Their body reads pursuit as pressure, even if your intention is love.
You can want closeness without suffocating them.
That balance is fragile but possible.
5. Don’t punish.
Anger will feel justified.
Coldness will feel tempting.
Pulling away will feel fair.
But punishment sends an avoidant back into the childhood they’ve been trying to escape.
You can be firm without being cruel.
6. Your softness is not weakness.
Your vulnerability doesn’t make you clingy.
Your desire for connection isn’t a flaw.
If anything, your willingness to stay open is the emotional leadership they’ve never had.
7. You can’t fix their childhood.
You can understand it.
You can support them.
You can stay regulated.
But you can’t be the parent they never had.
The moment you try to become their emotional oxygen, you both lose yourselves.
8. Your avoidant partner’s love is subtle, not absent.
They show it differently:
They run errands.
They fix things around the house.
They remember your food order.
They stay physically close even when emotionally quiet.
These are not small.
These are the languages they know.
9. But love without presence will break you over time.
You deserve contact, not just coexistence.
You deserve partnership, not emotional ghosting.
You deserve someone who learns what closeness feels like in real time.
10. Healing with an avoidant partner is slow, but not impossible.
It requires:
Your patience.
Their willingness.
Your vulnerability.
Their nervous system learning that closeness isn’t danger.
Your steadiness.
Their risk to show up even when it scares them.
Both of you have to do the work.
Not one.
Both.
Mirror Meditation: For the person loving an avoidant
(Look in the mirror, breathe slow, and say these one line at a time. Make eye contact with yourself.)
1. I can want closeness without losing myself.
2. Their distance doesn’t define my worth.
3. I can stay present even when they pull back.
4. I’m allowed to tell the truth about what hurts.
5. I deserve emotional contact, not just physical presence.
6. I’m not responsible for managing their fear.
7. I can walk toward connection without chasing.
8. My needs matter as much as theirs.
9. I’m allowed to set limits on withdrawal.
10. I can choose love without abandoning myself. See less

This is how a secure relationship actually works.
Not because you never hurt each other.
Not because you never misunderstand each other.
Not because triggers magically vanish once you “do the work.”
You still get hit with that same familiar moment.
You walk into the kitchen, or climb into bed, or open your mouth to bring something up, and your body tightens before a single word is spoken. Your chest braces. Your jaw sets just a little. Your mind whispers, “Please don’t let this turn into that again.”
That moment happens in every relationship, even the healthy ones.
The difference in a secure relationship isn’t that this moment disappears.
The difference is what you both do with it.
In distressed relationships, that moment is the starting gun.
You feel that tiny internal flinch, and before you know it you’re off to the races.
Defensiveness. Sarcasm. Blame. Silence. Withdrawal. Raised voices.
Maybe you shut down. Maybe you attack.
Maybe one of you walks away and the other chases.
By the time it’s over, both of you feel a little more alone than you did an hour ago.
In secure relationships, that same moment is treated like an alarm, not a weapon.
One or both of you notice the shift.
You notice the tightening in your body.
You notice their eyes change.
You notice the tone that just landed wrong.
And instead of speeding up, you slow down.
You might say,
“I’m starting to get tense. I don’t want us to go where we usually go.”
or
“I just felt my stomach drop. Something hurt. Can we take a second?”
That pause is everything.
Because repair doesn’t begin with the perfect sentence.
It begins with the courage to name that something’s happening inside you.
Secure couples don’t avoid conflict.
They just refuse to abandon themselves or each other inside it.
They learn how to say what actually hurts instead of firing off what the other is doing wrong.
They learn that, “You never listen,” is really, “I feel invisible and I’m scared that means I don’t matter to you.”
They learn that, “You’re so cold,” is really, “When you go quiet, I feel completely alone and my nervous system panics.”
They still mess it up.
They still overreact.
They still say things they wish they could take back.
But they circle back.
They come back to the moment and say things like,
“I know my voice got sharp. Underneath that, I was scared,”
or
“When you walked away, I felt dropped. I need you to know how fast that feeling shows up for me.”
They stop treating conflict like a courtroom and start treating it like a hospital room.
The goal isn’t to win the argument.
The goal is to stop the bleeding.
And when that happens, when real repair lands even once, something shifts in a place deeper than words.
Your brain quietly records it.
Your nervous system files it away.
Your heart takes a snapshot:
“I broke down and they didn’t leave.”
“I messed up and they stayed present.”
“I said the scary thing and the connection didn’t shatter.”
That experience sinks into your system in a way no communication technique can touch.
It doesn’t show up as a thought right away.
It shows up as a feeling the next time you hit that same vulnerable spot.
You walk into a familiar trigger and something is different.
Yes, your body still flinches.
Yes, old fear still shows up.
But right next to the fear is a new memory:
The memory of being met instead of dismissed.
The memory of being understood instead of analyzed.
The memory of both of you sitting in the discomfort and not abandoning each other.
That’s where something like forgiveness begins to grow.
Not the kind where you force yourself to “move on” because it’s the “right” thing to do.
Not the version where you swallow your hurt and call it healing.
A deeper kind.
The kind where you know, in your bones, that your partner isn’t your enemy, even when they’re clumsy.
The kind where your system already expects that, if things go sideways, you’ll eventually return to each other and work through it.
That’s what I call future forgiveness.
Future forgiveness is what happens when you’ve repaired the same type of injury enough times that your body relaxes a little earlier in the process.
You start to walk into a hard conversation and some quiet part of you goes,
“We’ve been here before. We know how to come back from this.”
You still speak up.
You still set boundaries.
You still name what hurts.
But you’re no longer talking to your partner as if they’re the monster in the story.
You’re talking to someone who has already shown you that they’re willing to face hard things with you.
And on the other side, your partner is changing too.
They know your history with this wound.
They know how quickly your nervous system ignites.
They know what your eyes look like when you’re about to shut down or explode.
So they start to do their version of future forgiveness.
They remember the times you’ve come back and owned your part.
They remember the conversations where you went past blame and into real emotion.
They remember the nights you cried and they finally understood what their behavior meant to you.
So when you slip, they hold more context.
They’re less likely to label you as “dramatic” or “cold” or “too much.”
They’re more likely to think, “We’re in the spot that scares us. Let’s slow this down.”
That is what secure love actually is.
It isn’t the end of triggers.
It isn’t the end of conflict.
It isn’t a permanent state of calm.
It’s a living, breathing pattern where you:
Notice the moment your nervous systems collide.
Name what’s happening inside, even clumsily.
Reveal a little more of the real feeling instead of launching another criticism.
Stay just a bit longer in the room, even when your instinct is to run or shut down.
Come back for repair when you miss each other.
Over time, those choices reshape the relationship.
You start trusting that when you say, “I’m scared,” you won’t be mocked or dismissed.
You start trusting that when you say, “I’m angry,” you’ll be seen as hurting, not as the enemy.
You start trusting that when you say, “That landed hard,” someone will care enough to lean closer, not further away.
And eventually, something subtle and astonishing happens:
You don’t just believe your partner loves you.
You feel loved while you’re hurting.
You don’t just believe your partner wants the relationship.
You feel them fighting for the connection in real time when it shakes.
You don’t just say the words, “I forgive you.”
Your nervous system slowly stops bracing for the blow that never comes.
That’s the quiet miracle of secure love.
Two people who still trigger each other.
Two nervous systems that still get scared.
Two histories that still ache sometimes.
But every time they fall apart, they know how to come back together.

3. Your breathing stays steadier instead of going shallow and rapid.
4. Your shoulders don’t lock up like armor; they stay a little softer.
5. Your voice doesn’t immediately rise into defense; it searches for clarity instead.
6. Your eyes stay open and connected instead of looking away or shutting down.
7. Your face shows more sadness than rage, because sadness finally feels safe enough to reveal.
8. Your mind stays curious about what your partner is experiencing instead of sprinting to assumptions.
9. Your nervous system allows you to listen instead of preparing your next argument.
10. Your body remembers that closeness is possible again, so it doesn’t treat conflict like abandonment.
11. Your stomach doesn’t drop into that “I am alone again” feeling as quickly, because it has evidence you won’t stay there.
12. Your nervous system makes room for compassion without you forcing it, because compassion now feels safer than attack.
13. Your muscles release a little sooner instead of staying braced for emotional impact.
14. Your thoughts slow down enough to say something real instead of something protective.
15. Your system lets you feel guilt or accountability without drowning in shame, because being wrong no longer equals being unloved.
16. Your nervous system expects reunion, not permanent rupture.
17. Your heart allows vulnerability faster, because vulnerability has stopped being punished in this relationship.
18. Your system can tolerate discomfort longer, because it trusts that safety is coming.
19. Your body stops treating your partner like a threat and remembers they are someone you love.
20. Your entire nervous system reorganizes toward connection instead of self-protection, because it has experienced again and again that repair is real and reachable.

Here are 20 things your nervous system automatically does when there is no real repair, and your body is preparing for emotional war instead of emotional safety:
1. Your chest tightens before you even know why, because your body expects pain.
2. Your breathing gets shallow as your system prepares to defend instead of connect.
3. Your jaw locks and your muscles brace like armor.
4. Your eyes harden or glaze over because you’re not really present anymore; you’re protecting yourself.
5. Your voice becomes sharper, louder, colder, or completely silent, depending on your survival style.
6. Your heart rate spikes the second a familiar tone or look appears on your partner’s face.
7. Your mind starts racing ahead, building arguments, defenses, and counterattacks instead of listening.
8. Your nervous system rewrites the story in real time, and everything becomes proof you aren’t safe here.
9. Your stomach knots because your body doesn’t expect kindness; it expects damage.
10. Your nervous system starts shutting doors emotionally so you don’t feel the full extent of the hurt.
11. Your shoulders rise toward your ears like shields.
12. Your body goes into fight mode (attack), flight mode (escape), freeze mode (go numb), or fawn mode (appease), often without your permission.
13. Your nervous system prepares for loneliness, even while you’re standing right in front of the person you love.
14. Your thoughts become all-or-nothing, because nuance feels dangerous when you’re trying to survive.
15. Your nervous system stores the moment as evidence: “See? This is what happens. Don’t trust. Don’t open.”
16. Your system stops believing repair is even possible and starts planning emotional exit strategies.
17. Your body gets tired, heavy, drained, as if it’s saying, “I can’t keep doing this.”
18. Your tone becomes more sarcastic, dismissive, or distant, because staying tender feels too risky.
19. Your face stops showing the real emotion underneath (fear, grief, longing) and replaces it with anger or detachment.
20. Your nervous system slowly stops reaching for your partner at all, not because you don’t care, but because it no longer believes you’ll be held if you do.

Here are 20 things your nervous system does when it’s desperately pretending it’s fine, even though real repair has never happened, the masked, functional, slowly-collapsing nervous system:
1. You smile in conversations while something inside you is quietly tightening.
2. You say “it’s fine” so often your mouth knows the shape of the lie better than the truth.
3. You stay calm on the outside while your body quietly stores the ache as tension.
4. You become “reasonable,” “understanding,” and “logical” while your nervous system is grieving that you weren’t met.
5. You talk about the situation like it’s a story, not like it’s your life that’s hurting.
6. You lower your expectations to avoid being disappointed again.
7. You convince yourself that what happened was “not that bad” because the alternative is facing how deeply it hurt.
8. You become accommodating, flexible, or emotionally “mature,” but it’s not peace, it’s self-protection disguised as wisdom.
9. You keep moving forward, but the part of you that needed comfort never actually moves with you.
10. You say “I understand why they did it” instead of “this shattered something inside me.”
11. You distract yourself with productivity, kindness, caretaking, or competence, so you don’t have to feel the wound.
12. You stop asking for reassurance because you don’t want to look “needy,” even though your nervous system is starving for it.
13. You laugh and make light of things that actually scared you to death emotionally.
14. You tell yourself you’re “strong” when in reality your system is just numb.
15. You stay polite and calm while your nervous system slowly loses its ability to trust closeness.
16. You avoid deep conversations, not because there’s peace, but because your system expects nothing good to come from them.
17. You mistake emotional shutdown for emotional maturity.
18. You stay loyal on the outside while your nervous system quietly pulls further away inside.
19. You look functional, stable, and composed while your capacity for vulnerability gets thinner and thinner.
20. You wake up one day feeling distant, detached, “over it,” or quietly done, not because you stopped caring, but becausse your nervous system simply could not keep pretending anymore.

My healing journey began December 2, 1990 at 7:30pm, when I attended my first codependents anonymous meeting at Pine Grove Hospital on Shoup Avenue in Los Angeles.
I had no problem with drugs nor alcohol.
I had an enormous problem with people.
15 minutes into the meeting, it was asked if somebody wanted to share.
I was overwhelmed and in so much pain, and it wasn't clear to me what it meant to have a speaker at a meeting that was the main person that would speak.
So when they asked if somebody wanted to share, I raised my hand.
I just talked and talked and then some buzzer went off.
I barely even realized I spoke for 15 minutes.
I barely even realized that I was the main event, the speaker, 15 minutes into my first meeting.
It was the most relief of my pain that I had ever experienced.
As I was talking to people at the end of the meeting, with all their praise and disbelief that I was 20 years old and that I spoke at my first meeting, a woman came up to me.
She said that "you have to have been in the program at least 30 days before you can speak, a rule at this meeting, please remember that the next time you decide to play by your own rules."
Separate from the fact that she was correct, I was pretty darn innocent, as I barely knew what was happening I was so immersed in my own depression and pain.
Apparently all these people go to Denny's after the meeting, so I went.
A very old soul was watching me while I was busy over-eating.
The level of shame in me, often still in my life today 33 years later, occurs when somebody is displeased with my actions.
His name was Robert.
Robert knew exactly the level of suffering I was in.
I had a hugely successful moment, then the wind got knocked out of me.
He sat down to talk to me.
He talked to me long enough, I think on purpose, until he got to see my fury, my rage, my judgment of the woman.
I think Robert was smart enough to know that I used my judgment as a way to protect myself from other's judgment.
But it doesn't work.
Robert changed my life, as he was getting the bill for his meal, and paying the waitress at the same time.
The waitresses name was Chloe.
That's how vivid this moment was for me.
When was the last time you remembered a waitresses name?
I will have to paraphrase Robert's words, because I was gasping for air, crying, and clenching my teeth in rage all at the same moment.
"Derek, that's your name, right?"
"Right"
"Every one of us human struggles when we are judged.
It hurts to the core.
While it makes sense to me how mad you are at the lady at the meeting, you are judging her back in retaliation.
It's not hurting her one bit.
But it's destroying you.
So I want to tell you what I do when I begin judging somebody.
I imagine their story.
I imagine my story.
I think of all the times I messed up and the people who forgave me. 
By the way, you'll get a chance to learn more about this when you do some of these silly 12 steps.
The moment when somebody says something mean or stupid to you is the moment that person has no contact with their own pain, so they can't possibly care about your pain.
As somebody criticizes me, I imagine their life filled with criticisms coming at them, because life is pretty damn difficult.
I hate to tell you this, but that moment when Joan judged you, that was not a custom-built moment for Derek.
That was a moment of Joan's pain, the culmination of an extremely unsuccessful life, coming out at you all at once.
Am I asking for you to forgive her?
No. She's pretty much a pain in my ass also.
But I saw something in you when you spoke tonight, and you have the gift.
You will be speaking at these meetings for as long as you want to, because I was enthralled by your stories.
So now I'm going to do something I've never done before.
I've never divulged details of somebody else's story in these 12-step rooms.
So here I am breaking the rules.
Joan would probably be upset."
"Okay thank you."
"When Joan was 8 years old, she accidentally fired a loaded gun that had one bullet accidentally left in the chamber.
She killed her 3 year old brother instantly.
For some reason, she didn't have enough information to know that she could dial 911, and her parents were down the street, somewhere she didn't know.
She spent 40 minutes alone with her brother, and his body.
Joan shared this one time about a year ago, and I've seen her in probably 60 meetings in the last year.
She has not shared once.
I cannot begin to imagine what she's going through, especially because she doesn't speak.
I have no idea how this affected her life, but she has not smiled once in my presence, and while she does eat the bagels and cream cheese in the meetings, she seems to derive no pleasure from it.
So do you think she's mad because you broke the rules, or do you think she's mad because she has to exist on this planet inside her own world of suffering?
Do you understand my point here, or do I have to spell it out for ya?"
"I got it."

With deep childhood trauma it’s almost impossible to name exactly what on the outside is hurting our inside. It just hurts.
Not in neat sentences.
Not in clean stories.
Not in ways that make logical sense to other people.
It hurts in the nervous system.
It hurts in the silence you don’t know how to explain.
It hurts in the moments when nothing “bad” is happening and yet your chest feels like it’s bracing for impact.
People ask, What triggered you?
Sometimes the honest answer is, Life.
A tone of voice can hurt.
A delayed text can hurt.
Being misunderstood can hurt.
Too much attention can hurt.
Not enough attention can hurt.
It’s not because you’re dramatic.
It’s not because you’re weak.
It’s because your body learned very early that safety wasn’t guaranteed, and now your nervous system still scans the world like everything could change in an instant.
Childhood trauma makes the world feel like a constant negotiation between:
holding on
letting go
not wanting to need
and desperately wanting to be held.
And when people say, “Just tell me what’s wrong,” how do you explain something that never started in words? How do you translate decades of stored-up emotion into a tidy explanation that makes everyone comfortable?
You don’t always know what’s wrong.
You just know your chest tightens.
Your heart drops.
Your voice disappears.
Your body remembers something your mind can’t fully explain.
So if this is you, please hear this:
You’re not broken for struggling to explain your pain.
You’re not failing because you don’t have perfect language for it.
Your feelings were once too big for the world to hold.
Now they’re too layered for simple sentences.
Healing doesn’t start with the perfect explanation.
Healing begins with someone who can sit with you in the I don’t know why it hurts, it just does.
Someone who doesn’t rush you.
Someone who doesn’t demand clarity before offering care.
Sometimes the bravest sentence you’ll ever say is simply:
“I’m hurting, and I don’t fully understand it yet.”
- Derek Hart See less

You already know the red flags.
But what heals relationships isn’t spotting danger, it’s recognizing safety.
Most of us can identify what hurts.
Far fewer of us know how to name what would actually help.
So let’s do this honestly.
Here are the red flags most people live with every day, and the green flags that actually change a nervous system, repair trust, and make love feel safe again.
---
Red Flag → Green Flag
 Blames you for their feelings → Takes self-responsibility
“I feel this way, and I’m working with it,” instead of, “You made me feel this.”
 Feels threatened by your growth → Supports your personal growth
They don’t shrink you to feel safer. They want more of you, not less.
 Runs themselves into the ground and collapses on the relationship → Practices self-care
They actually tend to their body, sleep, emotions, and energy, so they can show up.
 Never looks inward, always has a story about you → Self-reflective
They ask, “What’s happening in me?” instead of only asking what’s wrong with you.
 No real friendships, constant relational chaos → Long-standing friendships
People stay in their life because they’re safe to love, not because they perform.
 Dismissive, harsh, mocking, cold → Empathy
They might not always get it right, but they try to feel with you.
 Avoids closeness, hides, stays armored → Vulnerability
Not drama. Not oversharing. But real, steady reachable humanity.
 Disconnected from meaning, numb to inner life → Spirituality (in whatever form is true for them)
Something larger than ego shapes how they treat people.
 Emotionally or practically dependent, or expects you to carry everything → Self-sufficiency
They can stand on their own feet and still choose you, not lean on you like a crutch.
 Unhealthy obsessions, addictions, or no life outside the relationship → Healthy hobbies
They have interests that regulate their nervous system instead of destroying it.
 Talks “at” you, avoids hard conversations, shuts down or explodes → Communicates openly
They slow down, stay in the room emotionally, and try to reach you instead of winning.
 Violates boundaries, guilt trips, punishes, or controls → Honors boundaries
“No” doesn’t threaten the bond. “No” belongs in the relationship.
---
Green flags aren’t “nice traits.”
They’re attachment safety.
They’re what tell your nervous system,
“I can soften here.”
“I can be myself here.”
“I can stay.”
If you find someone with these…
don’t rush them.
don’t sabotage it.
don’t confuse safety for boredom.
This is the kind of love that doesn’t just feel good.
It heals. See less

The Disorganized Partner Survival Guide
(For the person loving someone who can’t decide whether to run toward you or run away.)
Loving a disorganized partner is one of the most confusing emotional experiences on earth.
They want closeness more than almost anyone you’ve ever met.
And at the exact same time, closeness terrifies them more than almost anyone you’ve ever met.
They didn’t choose this.
They didn’t design this.
They didn’t wake up someday and say, “Let me create the most painful relationship dynamic possible.”
This is a nervous system that learned early that the source of comfort and the source of fear were the same person.
So their body sends two signals at once:
Come closer.
Stay away.
Help me.
Don’t touch me.
Please hold me.
Please leave me alone.
Loving them means you live inside a storm that changes direction every five minutes.
And you’re not crazy for feeling tired.
You’re not cruel for feeling confused.
You’re not wrong for wondering if you’re too much, not enough, or both.
Let’s name the truth so you can breathe again.
1. They’re not indecisive. They’re terrified.
Every time they pull you close, they’re craving the connection they never consistently had.
Every time they push you away, they’re protecting themselves from being hurt the way they were.
This contradiction is the only thing their body knows.
2. Their panic is never about you, even when it hits you directly.
The fear you see on their face is older than you.
It’s older than your relationship.
It’s the ghost of every unsafe moment they never got to process.
You’re not the cause.
You’re the trigger.
3. They want to trust you but their body doesn’t let them.
They can love you deeply and still feel unsafe.
Love doesn’t override fear.
Safety rewires fear.
They need repetition.
Not perfection.
Not reassurance on demand.
Repetition of softness, slowness, and presence.
4. They’re not dramatic. Their nervous system swings between two survival strategies.
Hyperactivation.
Deactivation.
On.
Off.
Cling.
Disappear.
It’s not moodiness.
It’s fragmentation.
5. They’ll sometimes hurt you without meaning to.
Not because they don’t love you.
Because they’re in survival mode and survival mode makes no room for nuance.
You’re dealing with instinct, not intention.
6. If you shame their chaos, the chaos gets worse.
If you judge them, they retreat.
If you abandon them, they collapse.
If you get defensive, they panic.
But if you stay grounded, the storm weakens.
7. Their deepest desire is closeness.
Their deepest terror is closeness.
Imagine a body that wants something and fears it in the same breath.
That’s their daily reality.
8. They’re not broken. They’re unwitnessed.
Their pain wasn’t mirrored.
Their fear wasn’t held.
Their confusion wasn’t explained.
You might be the first person who ever sees the whole picture.
9. You can’t save them. But you can help them regulate.
Your job isn’t to fix their trauma.
Your job is to create openings where safety can begin to exist.
Safety is the soil where healing grows.
But they have to do the growing.
10. A disorganized partner in a regulated moment is extraordinary.
They love with intensity.
They see everything.
They read emotional landscapes most people overlook.
They have depth, intuition, and a heart that wants to attach with everything inside them.
When they trust you, their love is breathtaking.
Mirror Meditation: For the person loving a disorganized partner
(Stand in front of a mirror. Make eye contact with yourself. Go slow. Say these lines one at a time.)
1. I’m not responsible for the injuries that came before me.
2. I can offer steadiness without sacrificing myself.
3. Their fear isn’t a reflection of my worth.
4. I can stay grounded even when they can’t.
5. I’m allowed to rest.
6. I can love without rescuing.
7. I can say, “I’m here,” without promising the impossible.
8. I’m not weak for caring.
9. I’m not unlovable when they withdraw.
10. I deserve a relationship where safety grows in both directions. See less

Men are dying inside.
When a husband dies, his wife grieves but usually survives. Friends surround her. Kids call daily. She knows how to let people in.
When a wife dies, her husband often follows within two years. Not from grief alone. From isolation. Because she was his only connection to the human race.
60% of men say their wife is their best friend.
Only 30% of women say their husband is theirs.
Think about that for a second.
Men are putting all their emotional eggs in one basket. Women are building networks. Smart. Except it leaves men completely fucked when that one relationship struggles.
Here's what nobody talks about:
When you criticize a man in a relationship, his nervous system doesn't hear "you did something wrong." It hears "relationships are dangerous. You're not safe here either."
Most men learned before age 10 that feelings equal weakness. That needing someone makes you pathetic. That real men don't cry, don't ask for help, don't admit they're drowning.
So they stuff everything into their romantic relationship. All their vulnerability. All their need for connection. All their terror of being alone.
Then when she says "you never listen" or "why can't you open up," his body translates it as: "Even here, you're not good enough. Even the person who's supposed to love you thinks you're failing."
No wonder they shut down.
We've created a generation of men who are relationship-starved but relationship-terrified. Who need connection desperately but have no idea how to build it safely.
The loneliness is killing them. Literally. Men die younger partly because they don't know how to let anyone see their pain.
So maybe instead of demanding men "open up," we start by being gentle with how much courage it takes for them to try.
They're not robots. They're terrified humans who've been taught that needing love makes them weak.
And that's not their fault. That's what we did to them.
Time to stop criticizing them for being exactly what we trained them to be.

When a husband dies, his wife grieves but usually survives. Friends surround her. Kids call daily. She knows how to let people in.

When a wife dies, her husband often follows within two years. Not from grief alone. From isolation. Because she was his only connection to the human race.

60% of men say their wife is their best friend.

Only 30% of women say their husband is theirs.

Think about that for a second.

Men are putting all their emotional eggs in one basket. Women are building networks. Smart. Except it leaves men completely fucked when that one relationship struggles.

Here's what nobody talks about:

When you criticize a man in a relationship, his nervous system doesn't hear "you did something wrong." It hears "relationships are dangerous. You're not safe here either."

Most men learned before age 10 that feelings equal weakness. That needing someone makes you pathetic. That real men don't cry, don't ask for help, don't admit they're drowning.

So they stuff everything into their romantic relationship. All their vulnerability. All their need for connection. All their terror of being alone.

Then when she says "you never listen" or "why can't you open up," his body translates it as: "Even here, you're not good enough. Even the person who's supposed to love you thinks you're failing."

No wonder they shut down.

We've created a generation of men who are relationship-starved but relationship-terrified. Who need connection desperately but have no idea how to build it safely.

The loneliness is killing them. Literally. Men die younger partly because they don't know how to let anyone see their pain.

So maybe instead of demanding men "open up," we start by being gentle with how much courage it takes for them to try.

They're not robots. They're terrified humans who've been taught that needing love makes them weak.

And that's not their fault. That's what we did to them.

Time to stop criticizing them for being exactly what we trained them to be.

Quite possibly the most addictive emotional scenario for a man is what happens to him when the woman he loves is upset with him.
Not irritated.
Not mildly annoyed.
Not frustrated about something small.
I mean when she is **truly hurt**.
When her energy changes.
When her voice disappears.
When the warmth leaves the room and he can feel it.
In that moment, something massive happens inside him.
On the outside he may look defensive, distant, rational, irritable, or emotionally unavailable.
But inside?
He feels like the ground drops out from under him.
He feels like he is **deeply in trouble**.
Not “in trouble” like he forgot to take out the trash.
In trouble in the emotional way men almost never talk about.
He feels like:
“I failed her.”
“I disappointed someone I love.”
“I broke something precious.”
“I am the reason the person I care about is hurting.”
And for a lot of men, this does not start with the woman they are with now.
This feeling is old.
Many men have spent their entire lives being emotionally assigned responsibility for women’s feelings. They have been conditioned from childhood to believe:
“If she is upset, it is your fault.”
“If she is crying, you did something wrong.”
“If she is hurt, you better fix it.”
“If she is unhappy, you are failing.”
They watched their mothers hurt and felt helpless.
They watched their mothers cry and felt responsible.
They learned that a woman’s emotional world is something they must hold up, repair, regulate, stabilize, and protect… or they are a bad man.
And when you grow up with that wiring, every time a woman you love is hurt, it activates something enormous.
It is not just the moment.
It is the entire emotional lineage of expectation.
He has lived his life absorbing tears.
He has lived his life managing emotional temperature.
He has lived his life trying not to upset anyone.
So when the woman he loves is upset with him now…
It becomes overwhelming.
He feels *in trouble with love itself*.
In trouble with goodness.
In trouble with being “enough.”
In trouble with being lovable.
In trouble with his identity as a “good man.”
And the panic floods him.
His nervous system jumps into emergency mode. Shame. Fear. Helplessness. Tightness in his chest. A desperate, primal longing to make the feeling stop, not because he does not care…
But because he cares so much he does not know how to survive the feeling.
So he reaches for the only tools he was taught:
He argues.
He explains.
He defends.
He withdraws.
He shuts down.
He becomes logical.
He blames back.
He intellectualizes.
Not to hurt her.
Not to dismiss her.
But because the sensation of being “in trouble with a woman’s heart” feels unbearable.
He is not addicted to conflict.
He is addicted to escaping the terror of:
“I hurt a woman I love, and now I do not know if I am still good.”
He has spent years feeling responsible for women’s emotional weather. Now, when the woman he loves storms, he believes instinctively:
“This is my fault.”
“This is my punishment.”
“This is proof I failed.”
Which is heartbreaking.
Because that moment, the one that scares him the most…
Could be the most intimate doorway of his life.
If a man can allow himself to stay in that moment…
If he can remain present while feeling “in trouble”…
If he can tolerate the discomfort without self-destructing…
If he can breathe instead of defend…
If he can care instead of collapse…
Then something sacred happens.
He discovers that being accountable does not mean being destroyed.
He learns that feeling responsible does not mean losing himself.
He learns that love is not “fixing her emotions”…
Love is staying while they both feel.
He realizes that being “in trouble” does not mean he is unlovable.
And instead of living as a man terrified of failing women…
He becomes a man capable of meeting love courageously.
Men are not heartless.
Many are simply exhausted from a lifetime of emotional responsibility they never knew how to carry.
A mature man is not one who never upsets a woman.
A mature man is one who can stay kind, grounded, honest, accountable, and emotionally present…
Even in the moments where he feels most in trouble.
She will feel less alone if he reveals this.
If he does not, her flame for him will burn out. See less

The Gift of Hiding the Truth 
We like to tell ourselves that withholding honesty is kindness. That protecting someone from the truth is noble. That silence is compassion. That if we say nothing, everyone stays safe.
But the truth is harsher.
When you hide what is real, you’re not protecting the relationship.
You’re quietly killing it.
Real love tells the truth.
Not because it wants to hurt.
But because it refuses to abandon reality.
If you actually cared about the person in front of you, you'd give them the gift of your honest reaction. Even if it stings. Especially if it stings. Because that’s the only way they get to truly know who you are, who they are with you, and what is actually happening between you.
When you pretend, they feel it.
Even when you think you’re being subtle.
Their nervous system registers the mismatch.
The careful tone.
The polite smile.
The “it’s fine” energy that clearly is not fine.
Their body feels danger.
They may not have the words for it, but their nervous system whispers:
“Something is off. I am not safe. I cannot relax here.”
Now they are walking on eggshells around your “kindness.”
And here’s the twisted part:
Your protection creates the very thing you’re trying to avoid.
When you tiptoe around someone's feelings, what you're actually saying is,
“I don’t trust you with reality.”
“I don’t think you’re strong enough.”
“I have to manage your experience because you can’t handle life.”
That lands like a slap wrapped in velvet.
Because the niceness is actually violence.
Every time you swallow the truth to “keep the peace,” you don’t dissolve the conflict… you store it. It sits inside you, pressed down, tightening, fermenting, rotting into resentment. And when it finally explodes, it doesn’t come out as clarity…
It comes out as character assassination.
What could have been a conversation becomes a demolition.
Meanwhile, you tell yourself you were being kind.
No. Let’s be honest.
The protection was never really about them.
It was about you.
You weren’t afraid of hurting them.
You were afraid of what would happen next.
Afraid of conflict.
Afraid of confrontation.
Afraid of emotions that can’t be controlled with logic.
Your “kindness” was really self-protection dressed up as virtue.
And while you were busy protecting yourself from discomfort…
You stole something precious from them:
Their strength.
When you consistently shelter someone from difficult truth, you teach them they’re fragile. You teach them they can’t handle life. You teach them the world must bend around their feelings because they won’t survive otherwise.
Congratulations.
Your protection just helped weaken the very person you claim to love.
And here’s the worst part of all:
Delayed truth becomes weaponized truth.
By the time it comes out, it’s no longer about the moment. It’s stacked with every unspoken frustration, every swallowed irritation, every silent betrayal layered on top. Now it’s not feedback. It’s a verdict. It’s not about behavior. It’s about identity.
It didn’t have to be that way.
The real gift is honesty spoken with care.
Truth delivered with humanity.
Reality offered with presence, love, and courage.
That is what mature love does.
Not because truth is easy.
But because pretending is far more destructive.
Stop calling it kindness when it’s really fear.
Stop calling it protection when it’s really avoidance.
Stop calling it peace when it’s really slow emotional suffocation.
Real love risks discomfort.
Real love sits in the mess.
Real love believes the other person is strong enough to meet life with you.
Honesty isn’t cruelty.
Silence is.
And the bravest thing you can ever do in love is stop hiding behind niceness…
and finally tell the truth. See less

You are literally trying to make sense of your partner’s view of you all day long.
It follows you into every room.
It sits in the car with you.
It rides with you to work.
It crawls into your sleep.
When your relationship is distressed, you’re not “just having a hard time as a couple.”
You are living inside emotional hell… privately.
You wake up already scanning:
“Am I okay with them?”
“Are we okay?”
“Did yesterday destroy something?”
“Do they still love me the same way?”
“Am I failing?”
You carry their last tone of voice in your nervous system.
You replay conversations you never got to finish.
You imagine how they might be interpreting you.
You mentally rehearse what you’ll say when you see them again.
You fight battles that never leave your head.
And here’s the part no one really says out loud:
A distressed relationship doesn’t just make the relationship hurt.
It empties the color out of your life.
Food doesn’t taste the same.
Music doesn’t feel the same.
Friends don’t reach you the same.
Accomplishments don’t land the same.
Your body never truly settles.
Because when the person you love is emotionally distant, upset with you, shut down, or unreachable…
Your nervous system does not relax.
It *can’t.*
Every part of you is tracking,
“Am I safe with the person I love most?”
“Am I still wanted?”
“Am I still chosen?”
“Am I still worth staying for?”
You’re not dramatic.
You’re not needy.
You’re not weak.
You are human.
We are wired to bond.
We are wired to seek safety in connection.
We are wired to need emotional closeness.
So when the relationship is distressed, you don’t just lose harmony.
You lose your emotional home.
And that is individually devastating.
Not melodramatic.
Not exaggerated.
**Devastating.**
If you’re walking around trying to function while your heart is in crisis, I see you.
You’re carrying something huge.
And none of it means you’re broken.
It means your heart still knows love matters. See less

The last thing that has never repaired a romantic conflict is a discussion about it.
Read that again.
Because most couples do not actually “talk things out”…
They talk their nervous systems into collapse.
They talk in circles.
They stack logic on top of emotions that never got held.
They analyze each other instead of *feeling* each other.
They debate like lawyers while their hearts are starving for connection.
Here is the painful truth:
You do not fix romantic wounds with smarter sentences.
You do not repair emotional injuries with better arguments.
You do not restore safety with intellectual explanations.
Romantic conflict is not a mental problem.
It is a nervous system problem.
It is a connection problem.
And you cannot debate your way back into connection.
Real repair does not come from:
Who remembered the timeline correctly
Who structured their logic better
Who quoted a book more accurately
Who made the cleverer point
Repair happens when two bodies stop fighting and finally begin feeling again.
When one person says,
“I hurt you, and I can feel that.”
And the other says,
“I matter to you. I can feel that.”
That is when repair begins.
Not when you figure out who is right…
But when you remember how to be human with each other again.
Why “talking about it” makes things worse
* Because most “discussions” are disguised self-defense
* Because your partner does not feel heard, they feel examined
* Because talking often becomes a weapon instead of a bridge
* Because intellectual clarity without emotional presence feels like abandonment
* Because logic can explain pain but it cannot hold pain
What actually repairs romantic conflict
* Regulating your nervous system before opening your mouth
* Slowing down instead of speeding up
* Softening your tone, your face, your posture
* Letting yourself care before letting yourself speak
* Saying less words with more heart
* Touch, eye contact, closeness, breath
* Admitting impact instead of proving innocence
What partners secretly wish would happen instead of “discussing”
* “Please notice that I am hurting.”
* “Please show me I still matter to you.”
* “Please care more about connection than your point.”
* “Please do not analyze me. Be with me.”
* “Please help my nervous system feel safe again with you.”
If you want a relationship that heals instead of fractures
Stop trying to win the conversation.
Start trying to restore the bond.
Conflict does not destroy relationships.
A lack of emotional repair does.
The work is not learning how to “communicate better.”
The work is learning how to **stay emotionally present long enough to love each other again. See less

Couple in distress? Your nervous system is being harmed.
That’s the topic.
That’s the conversation.
That’s the truth nobody wants to face.
When your relationship is distressed, your nervous system isn’t just “uncomfortable.”
It is **injured.**
Not metaphorically.
Literally.
Your body does not experience relationship distress as an “emotional disagreement.”
It experiences it as a threat to survival.
Because for humans, love is not optional.
Connection is not decorative.
Emotional safety is not a luxury.
It is biology.
It is regulation.
It is homeostasis.
When the person you love becomes unpredictable, cold, distant, resentful, dismissive, unavailable, critical, explosive, silent, icy, or emotionally absent…
Your body registers it.
Your heart rate changes.
Your sleep becomes light and broken.
Your breathing tightens.
Your chest constricts.
Your muscles tense.
Your cortisol rises.
Your mind spins with worst-case scenarios.
Your stomach hurts for no medical reason.
Your immune system weakens.
Your appetite shifts.
And your soul feels like it’s living without oxygen.
This isn’t you being “dramatic.”
This is your nervous system saying:
“I am not safe here.”
You start scanning everything.
Tone of voice.
Body language.
Timing of texts.
How they looked at you.
How they didn’t.
Whether they rolled toward you in bed or turned away.
You’re not “obsessing.”
You’re trying to survive.
Your nervous system is wired to bond.
Your body is built to anchor to emotional safety.
Your brain was designed to interpret:
“Am I connected?”
“Am I wanted?”
“Am I loved?”
“Am I rejected?”
“Am I about to lose my person?”
When the answer to those is unclear, unstable, or painful, you don’t just lose relationship peace.
You lose regulation.
This is why people in distressed relationships:
Have trouble focusing at work
Feel emotionally exhausted
Stop feeling joy in things they used to love
Experience anxiety out of nowhere
Feel an ache in their chest that doesn’t go away
Cry at strange times
Laugh less
Feel smaller
Feel less alive
Because your nervous system can’t rest if love isn’t safe.
And let’s be honest:
A distressed relationship changes how you show up everywhere.
You bring it into your day.
You carry it into your friendships.
You drag it into your sleep.
You take it into your future.
You feel it in your body even when you’re alone.
That’s not weakness.
That’s human wiring.
Your system doesn’t care about “logic.”
It cares about **bonding.**
Your body wants repair.
Your body wants warmth.
Your body wants regulation.
Your body wants the nervous system of the person you love to say:
“You’re safe with me.”
“I care.”
“I’m here.”
“We’re okay.”
“I won’t disappear emotionally.”
When that doesn’t happen, your nervous system is left holding fear with nowhere to put it.
This is why repairing connection matters so deeply.
Not for “relationship goals.”
Not for Instagram quotes.
Not for appearances.
Because your health depends on it.
Your emotional integrity depends on it.
Your spirit depends on it.
A distressed relationship is not “just a relationship problem.”
It is a nervous system injury.
And you are allowed to take that seriously. See less

Body language.

Timing of texts.

How they looked at you.

How they didn’t.

Whether they rolled toward you in bed or turned away.

Feel emotionally exhausted

Stop feeling joy in things they used to love

Experience anxiety out of nowhere

Feel an ache in their chest that doesn’t go away

Cry at strange times

Laugh less

Feel smaller

Feel less alive

“Youre overreacting.”

You're not going to get your avoidant partner to do what you want.
Let me say that again, because this is the sentence nobody wants to hear:
You will not talk them into closeness.
You will not logic them into connection.
You will not guilt, shame, pressure, persuade, suggest, reframe, or therapize them into showing up the way you crave.
Not because you're weak.
Not because they're heartless.
Not because love isn't real.
Because nervous systems don't obey commands.
Here is the truth almost nobody tells you about avoidant partners:
They don't pull away to punish you.
They pull away because something inside their body tells them closeness is dangerous.
And when your body believes something is dangerous, you cannot “choose differently” any more than you can decide not to flinch when a fire touches your hand.
You want more closeness.
They want more quiet.
You want depth.
They want distance.
You want to talk until it feels better.
They want silence until their heart stops pounding.
And here is the part that hurts the most:
The more you chase, the more they retreat.
The louder you get, the quieter they become.
The harder you push, the more they disappear.
Not because they don't care.
But because your pursuit feels like being cornered in a burning room.
They learned this a long time ago.
Long before you.
Long before this relationship.
They learned that needing people is risky.
They learned that emotions aren't safe spaces.
They learned that vulnerability equals exposure, danger, overwhelm.
So when you say:
"Please talk to me." "Please feel with me." "Please stay with me in this moment."
They don't hear invitation.
Their body hears threat.
And here is the heartbreak:
You think they're choosing distance over love.
They're not.
They're choosing survival over collapse.
You keep thinking:
"If I word it better…" "If I just stay calm…" "If I explain it the right way…" "If I show them charts, videos, therapy concepts, attachment theory language…"
Then surely they'll understand.
Then surely they'll change.
Then surely they'll finally meet you where you are.
But avoidant systems do not move because of your clarity.
They move because of safety.
And safety is not built by force.
Here is what most people get wrong:
You think the problem is their behavior. The real problem is their body is terrified of needing you.
Avoidant partners are not emotionally empty. They're emotionally flooded.
They're not detached because they don't have feelings. They're detached because their feelings overwhelm their ability to stay present.
And when you demand emotional presence from a system already stretched past capacity…
It shuts down.
So let's speak the hardest truth:
You will never get your avoidant partner to do what you want by trying to make them.
Not with:
Explaining. Lecturing. Analyzing. Calling out patterns.
Diagnosing them with attachment labels. Telling them what a “healthy couple” should do. Citing something you saw on Instagram or heard in therapy.
Here's what actually shifts avoidant partners:
Safety. Time. Consistency. Non-attack presence. Connection that doesn't demand instant reciprocity. Moments where they are allowed to come forward voluntarily. Moments where they aren't punished for being slow. Moments where love doesn't feel like being swallowed whole.
Avoidant partners don't grow closer under pressure.
They grow closer when pressure leaves the room.
They open when connection stops feeling like a test they will fail.
They soften when they aren't constantly being measured, graded, corrected, analyzed.
They come forward when vulnerability stops feeling like walking into the courtroom of your disappointment.
And here's the hardest mirror if you're the pursuer:
You're hurting too.
You're terrified too.
You're just as flooded.
Your chasing is your nervous system screaming:
"Don't leave me."
Their withdrawing is their nervous system whispering:
"I can't survive if you get any closer."
Two nervous systems.
Both scared.
Both hurting.
Both protecting.
Not enemies. Just uncoordinated survival strategies.
So here's the real question:
Can you stop trying to change them long enough to understand them?
Can you stop trying to fix them long enough to see the small child inside them who's terrified of needing anyone?
Can you soften the “why aren't you more like me?” long enough to whisper:
"I know closeness is scary. I don't want to overwhelm you. I want to understand you."
Because here's the secret:
Avoidant partners don't need to be pushed. They need to be trusted.
They don't need to be cornered into openness. They need to feel like they can open without being consumed.
They don't need to be told to “show up.” They need to know it's safe to show up imperfectly.
You cannot drag them to connection.
But you can meet them at the doorway of their nervous system and say:
"I'm here. I'm patient. I'm human too. And I want to learn how we find each other without losing ourselves."
You won't get your avoidant partner to do what you want.
But you might invite them into something better:
A love that moves at the speed of safety. See less

You want closeness?
Real closeness?
Not just living together. Not just loving each other. Not just sharing a house, a bed, a last name, a history.
I am talking about the kind of closeness where your nervous systems trust each other. Where your heart relaxes inside the relationship. Where you do not constantly feel like you have to guard, defend, explain, convince, or perform.
Everyone says they want that.
Almost nobody understands what it actually requires.
Because here is the truth nobody tells you:
If you want closeness, you will have to learn the terrain of your partner’s pain.
Not the story they tell other people. Not the version they have intellectualized. Not the neat summary they give when they say, “Yeah, I had a rough childhood.”
I mean the living, breathing internal world that aches inside them. The part that still gets scared. The part that still braces. The part that still hides behind anger or withdrawal so nobody will see how much it hurts.
If you do not understand that, you do not understand them. And if you do not understand them, you cannot be close to them. Period.
Now here is the part that hurts to hear:
Most relationships do not fail because people stop loving each other.
They fail because people stop learning each other.
They fail because one or both partners start assuming: “You should be over this by now.” “You are too sensitive.” “You need to work on yourself.” “This is your issue, not mine.” “I did not mean it, so you should not feel so hurt.”
They fail because repair stops happening.
And that is the death of a relationship.
Not the yelling. Not the arguing. Not the tears.
Those are symptoms.
The real death happens quietly, over years, when you hurt each other and nothing meaningful changes.
When you trigger each other and you never really understand why.
When the same fight plays out like a rerun and each time you both secretly lose a little more hope.
You want the brutal truth?
Every time you hurt your partner and there is no deep repair, your bond weakens.
Not maybe. Not emotionally dramatic.
Fact.
Every unresolved moment leaves emotional residue. Every unprocessed rupture leaves a scar. Every “let’s just move on” stacks another layer on top of the last one.
And eventually, your relationship is not two people loving each other anymore.
It is two nervous systems quietly preparing for disappointment.
Two bodies bracing. Two hearts staying slightly guarded. Two people still there physically, but no longer fully available emotionally.
That is when couples say: “We drifted apart.” “We lost each other.” “We became roommates.”
They did not drift.
They eroded.
So let’s talk about what actually creates closeness.
It is not more conversations where you list what you do not like about them. It is not endless communication skills. It is not analyzing every fight for eight hours. It is not proving who is right.
Closeness comes from something far more intimate, far more courageous, and far more demanding:
Becoming a student of your partner’s hurt.
Learning their emotional language. Understanding what abandonment feels like in their body. Understanding what rejection does inside their chest. Understanding what criticism lands like in their nervous system. Understanding why certain tones slice them open. Understanding why certain faces remind them of every time they were dismissed growing up.
And then…
Choosing, again and again, to care.
Not defensively. Not resentfully. Not because you want credit.
But because this is the human you chose.
And here is the terrifying part:
Some of the deepest pain your partner carries will come from you.
Yes, you. Even if you love them. Even if you are kind. Even if you did not mean to.
Because nobody can wound you more deeply than the person whose love matters most.
And in that moment, when you realize, “I did this. I hurt someone I adore,”
that is the turning point.
That is where real love either grows
or dies.
Do you defend? Do you minimize? Do you explain? Do you tell them why they should not feel that bad? Do you make it about you?
Or…
Do you stay?
Do you breathe? Do you slow down? Do you let your heart hurt because theirs hurts? Do you care more about understanding them than proving yourself innocent?
This is where closeness is born.
Not in the not hurting. But in the way you respond when you do.
And I want to speak to something deeper here:
So many people tell themselves, “We will work on it later.” “It is not that bad.” “We will grow eventually.” “We love each other, so we will figure it out.”
Except that is not how human hearts work.
Every time pain gets ignored, your nervous system remembers.
It remembers tightening instead of softening. It remembers protecting instead of trusting. It remembers silence instead of safety.
And then one day, you wake up next to someone you still love…
but you no longer feel close to.
And here is the most devastating part:
By then, you do not just grieve the relationship.
You grieve the years you lost inside of it.
All the moments you could have had. All the warmth you could have lived inside. All the softness you could have shared. All replaced by emotional distance that never needed to exist.
That is regret.
Not the kind people post about online.
The real kind. The kind your body feels. The kind that sinks into your bones. The kind that whispers, “I wish I had learned how to love you better when I still could.”
So let me invite you into something rare:
Every once in a while, when you are driving. When you are scrolling. When you are sipping your coffee.
Pause.
Not to analyze. Not to shame yourself. Not to rehearse your arguments.
Pause to remember that your partner is a nervous system, not just a personality.
Ask yourself:
“What hurts them?” “What is still aching in them that I have never really slowed down enough to understand?” “What is it like inside their body when I shut down?” “What is it like inside their chest when I raise my voice?” “What is it like in their heart when I ignore them, dismiss them, joke at their expense, withdraw, roll my eyes, or act like what hurts them should not?”
And then…
Take it one level deeper again:
Can I become a guardian of their pain rather than a source of it?
Can I actively participate in reducing harm instead of accidentally repeating it? Can I care enough to soften my tone? Can I slow myself down long enough to stay present? Can I learn to apologize not to fix it, but to reconnect? Can I take responsibility without collapsing into shame?
This is what love actually is.
Not fireworks. Not romantic gestures. Not grand declarations.
Love is the willingness to be emotionally responsible with another human life.
And if you do this even once in a meaningful way…
It changes things.
One moment of deep awareness. One moment of slowing down enough to see their hurt. One moment of saying, “I know where I have wounded you and I am trying to understand you better,”
creates new wiring in their brain.
Their nervous system takes a new snapshot: “I am not alone here. I matter here. My pain counts here. I am safe enough to stay.”
And that is not theory.
That is bonding.
That is attachment.
That is how love deepens.
Not through perfection.
Through repair. Through tenderness. Through humility. Through courage. Through the willingness to stop living exclusively inside your own experience
and step, even for a moment, into theirs.
That is where closeness lives.
That is how love survives.
And that is how regret is prevented. Not by timing. Not by luck. Not by hoping things just get better.
By learning how to care about the deepest places in the person you chose. See less

Today I was walking my dog.
Training him.
Loving him.
Trying to help him learn how to move through the world without startling it.
He’s not aggressive.
He’s enthusiastic.
He’s a two-year-old nervous system with legs, joy bursting out of him in full force, wanting to connect before he knows how to regulate. So I do the work. I walk in circles. I redirect. I breathe. I teach him how to slow down his instinct so he doesn’t overwhelm another dog or another human.
And then it happens.
We come around a corner.
Another dog.
Another human.
No warning.
We’re in it instantly.
My dog lights up.
We pivot into training mode.
It is very obvious what I’m doing: structure, containment, presence.
And the woman says:
“You need to be farther away when you’re doing that training.”
I say, “thank you,” because she’s not wrong.
I’m already moving.
Already adjusting.
Already stepping into responsibility.
And while I’m literally taking a step — one step into doing exactly what she just suggested — she rolls her eyes.
Sharp exhale.
Dismissal.
Sarcasm.
Contempt in two seconds.
Two seconds.
Two seconds to erase respect.
Two seconds to strip someone of dignity.
Two seconds to decide, “I’m superior to you. You’re the problem. You’re inconvenient. And I don’t care who you are or what you’re trying to do.”
And this isn’t about a dog.
This is the human condition.
This is exactly how fast we hurt each other.
This is how fast connection collapses.
This is how fast we shift from “two humans sharing space” to “you’re the obstacle in my story.”
No war.
No catastrophe.
No traumatic backstory.
Just two seconds of ego.
And here’s what hit me walking away:
We aren’t just people trying to survive.
We are criticism engines, constantly scanning for where the world doesn’t align with our internal expectations.
We live in a culture that has convinced us that being right keeps us safe, and empathy is optional.
We walk through life judging: How people should move. How people should talk. How people should behave. How people should parent. How people should love. How people should exist.
We forget there’s a nervous system inside every body we criticize.
We forget someone is trying.
We forget there is effort happening we can’t see.
That woman didn’t just correct me.
She erased me.
Not because she’s evil. Not because she’s broken. But because she’s human.
And this is where relational wisdom starts:
The moment right before you react is sacred.
That’s the moment where you choose who you are.
That’s the moment where you decide whether you will deepen the wound between you and another human… or widen the possibility of connection.
Criticism is not simply “feedback.”
It is energy.
It’s tone.
It’s posture.
It’s eyes rolling. It’s breath scoffing. It’s the sound your nervous system makes when you forget another nervous system exists.
And criticism doesn’t just hurt the other person.
It damages the relationship itself. It breaks the bridge between two humans. It kills possibility. It collapses safety. It dissolves trust. It says, “Only one of us matters here, and it’s me.”
You don’t have to know that person to fracture connection.
Connection isn’t just intimate.
It’s social.
It’s communal.
It’s the fragile web that keeps the human race from feeling unbearably alone.
And we shatter it constantly.
Over dogs.
Over coffee orders.
Over parking lots.
Over dishes.
Over tone.
Over speed.
Over nothing.
We do it with our partners.
We do it with our children.
We do it with strangers.
We do it with ourselves.
And the tragedy is this:
The speed of our criticism is often faster than the speed of our compassion.
We could make the world safer.
We could make relationships safer.
We could make each other safer.
But that requires slowing down the reflex to be superior.
It requires humility. It requires humanity. It requires remembering that irritation doesn’t give you permission to dehumanize another person.
So if you want better relationships… If you want more connection… If you want to stop losing people you love… If you want to stop living in a lonely world of defensiveness and tiny emotional cuts:
Don’t just pay attention to what you disagree with.
Pay attention to: How quickly you roll your eyes. How fast your body moves into contempt. How immediately your tone sharpens. How instinctively you choose righteousness instead of kindness.
Because every one of those moments is a crossroads.
You can either criticize fast. Or you can care slow.
And here’s the part nobody says out loud:
We adore our dogs because they don’t do this to us.
They don’t shame us. They don’t humiliate us. They don’t punish us for imperfection. They don’t make us feel like a burden for simply existing.
They meet us with presence.
Humans could learn something here.
If you want to have better love… Better connection… Better chances at being deeply seen…
Start with this tiny piece of emotional maturity:
Notice the speed of your criticism. Interrupt it. Breathe. Choose dignity over dominance. Choose humanity over hierarchy. Choose care over ego.
Because the space inside those two seconds?
That’s where love lives. See less

Unprocessed emotion causes negative behavior.
And here is the deeper truth most people never talk about:
Emotion is not the problem.
Unfelt emotion is.
Unprocessed emotion does not disappear.
It reroutes.
It becomes sarcasm.
It becomes withdrawal.
It becomes irritability.
It becomes numbness.
It becomes control.
It becomes explosions that “come out of nowhere.”
It becomes distance in relationships that slowly turns into emptiness.
We do not hurt people because we are broken.
We hurt people because our hearts never learned how to safely feel what lives inside them.
Unprocessed sadness turns into anger.
Unprocessed fear turns into control.
Unprocessed shame turns into defensiveness.
Unprocessed disappointment turns into bitterness.
Unprocessed loneliness turns into neediness.
Unprocessed overwhelm turns into shutdown.
Every negative behavior started as a feeling that never got to be felt.
Most of us never grew up in homes where feelings were welcomed.
We were told to be strong.
We were told to calm down.
We were told we were too much.
We were told to get over it.
So we stopped processing emotions and started surviving them.
But here is the heartbreaking part…
When emotion is not processed, you cannot fully love, and you cannot fully feel loved.
Because love is not proven through logic.
Love is not proven through “everything’s fine.”
Love is not proven through fixing, explaining, rationalizing, or managing appearances.
We only know we are loved when our emotions are safe with someone.
When we break down and they do not run.
When we cry and they do not shame.
When we tell the truth and they do not punish.
When our nervous system melts in front of someone and they stay steady enough to hold us.
That is when the body finally whispers…
“I am safe.”
“I am not alone.”
“I am loved.”
Properly processed emotion is the language of love.
Love is when someone hears the tremble in your voice and leans closer.
Love is when you say, “I am not okay,” and they do not make it about them.
Love is when they can handle your mess without needing to fix or silence it.
Love is when your nervous system feels seen, not corrected.
We think we fall in love with personalities.
We actually fall in love with nervous systems that feel safe to our own.
When emotion is processed together…
Trust grows.
Intimacy deepens.
Resentment dissolves.
Walls fall.
Connection repairs.
And something sacred happens:
The emotional storms that used to destroy the relationship become the storms that fortify it.
This is why emotional processing is not optional.
It is foundational.
You cannot logic your way to closeness.
You cannot intellectualize your way to intimacy.
You cannot argue your way to safety.
You can only feel your way there.
If you want healthier behavior, you do not start by judging reactions.
You start by honoring the emotional life underneath them.
Sit with feelings.
Name what hurts.
Let grief be grief.
Let anger be acknowledged before you try to calm it.
Let fear be held before you try to reason with it.
This is not weakness.
It is relational strength.
Because when emotion finally gets processed, something beautiful happens:
The nervous system relaxes.
Love becomes easier.
Closeness feels natural.
Safety returns.
And for perhaps the first time in your life, your body finally says…
“This is love.
Because here, all of me is allowed to exist.” See less
