You don’t actually know what your relationship is made of…
until life stops being polite and starts being real.
Not when it is easy to love.
Not when affection costs nothing.
Not when problems are small and solvable by a good night’s sleep.
Not when you both still have energy, patience, and hope.
You learn what your love is built from
when something hits your world so hard that your nervous system can’t pretend anymore.
When death walks into your life.
When illness steals your illusion of invincibility.
When money disappears and shame creeps in.
When your partner collapses emotionally.
When your family becomes chaos and you cannot hide from it.
When your childhood wounds come roaring back.
When their unresolved trauma surfaces and fills the room.
When the story you thought your life would be shatters in front of you.
That is when the real relationship shows up.
Because crisis strips the relationship naked.
Every coping strategy appears.
Every defense mechanism wakes up.
Every childhood strategy for survival reactivates.
Every unhealed place inside both of you starts pulsing.
You see who runs.
Who freezes.
Who numbs.
Who blames.
Who attacks.
Who disappears behind stone walls of self-protection.
You also see something else:
Who softens instead of sharpens.
Who turns toward instead of turning away.
Who can stay in the room emotionally when pain is screaming.
Who can breathe with you instead of fixing you.
Who can say, “This is terrifying… come here,” instead of, “Figure it out.”
This is the moment you discover if your relationship was built for comfort
or built for life.
Because life will ask things of you that romance never mentions.
It will ask whether your partner can hold your shaking hands.
Whether they can tolerate your grief without needing it to be quieter.
Whether they can sit with your fear without making it your flaw.
Whether they can listen when your words are messy and your heart is bleeding.
Whether they can remain human with you, instead of becoming your judge, your fixer, or your ghost.
Crisis reveals something enormous:
Do you have compassion in your relationship
or do you only have preference?
Compassion is different from being nice.
It is different from giving advice.
It is different from trying to stay “positive.”
It is different from tough love.
It is different from telling someone to focus on gratitude while they are drowning.
Compassion is the ability to let another person’s experience matter inside your body.
It is the courage to feel with them, not around them.
It is the willingness to let their pain touch your nervous system without collapsing into panic, control, or dismissal.
It is the choice to protect connection instead of protecting your comfort.
We live in a world obsessed with improvement, productivity, hacks, fixes, optimization, spiritual bypassing, and emotional shortcuts.
We have tools, apps, programs, inspirational quotes, and endless books.
But none of those things teach you how to sit beside someone who is breaking apart.
No one teaches us how to look into the eyes of the person we love
and say:
“I do not know how to fix this. But I will not leave you in it alone.”
That is a human skill.
A nervous system skill.
A love skill.
And when you do not have it, crisis exposes you.
Some people discover in crisis that their partner never learned how to care.
Not deeply.
Not with presence.
Not with emotional attunement.
They discover they have a partner who can offer solutions, logic, harsh reality, lectures, distance, silence, or irritation…
but not soothing, not tenderness, not refuge.
Others discover the opposite.
They discover that when everything collapses, they are suddenly held in a way they have never been held before.
They discover depth.
Warmth.
Stability.
A groundedness that becomes sacred.
Crisis tells the truth.
It tells you whether your relationship has just been “functional companionship”
or “true attachment.”
It tells you whether you are bonded deeply
or simply coordinated well.
And it leaves you with questions that matter:
Does your partner rise in compassion
or drown in defensiveness?
Do they step toward your pain
or try to outrun it?
Do you become safer together
or lonelier together?
And let us be honest:
It is not just about them.
Crisis will expose you too.
It will show whether you can tolerate another person’s vulnerability.
Whether you can stop needing to control.
Whether you can stay instead of disappearing emotionally.
Whether you can soften instead of criticize.
Whether you can care without needing to turn the moment into a lesson, a debate, or a self-protection exercise.
Because relationships are not truly measured in the easy years.
They are measured in the moments when someone whispers:
“I am scared.”
“I am ashamed.”
“I am lost.”
“I am hurting.”
“I do not know what happens next.”
And the other person says, not perfectly, not heroically, but sincerely:
“Then we face it together. I am here. I am not leaving your heart alone in this.”
If your relationship has this… it has something rare.
If it does not… crisis will not be kind about revealing it.
Life will bring storms no matter how hard you try to avoid them.
The question is never, “Will we face hardship?”
The question is:
When the world shakes…
do we collapse into separation…
or do we become gentler, slower, more human,
and more together than we have ever been?

When someone cries, we rush to quiet them.
“Shh… shh… it’s ok. Calm down. Don’t cry. Take a breath. Settle. Be strong.”
We do this to children.
We do this to partners.
We do this to friends.
We do this to ourselves.
Not because we are cruel.
But because unfiltered pain makes us uncomfortable.
Because loud emotions wake up our own grief, fear, guilt, helplessness, and shame.
Because we have been trained our entire lives that big feelings are problems to control, not experiences to let exist.
But crying is not the problem.
Crying is the nervous system saying:
“This hurts.”
“This matters.”
“This is too big to hold quietly.”
“My body needs help carrying this.”
And instead of honoring that…
we teach silence.
We teach swallowing grief.
We teach numbing the scream.
We teach collapsing the sob into a tiny, acceptable whimper.
We teach emotional suffocation… and then wonder why people feel disconnected, depressed, numb, explosive, anxious, and ashamed of their own humanity.
What if we did the opposite?
What if we stopped trying to turn down the volume of pain…
and helped it release?
Instead of “shh, it’s ok,”
what if we said:
“It sounds awful. Let it out.”
“Make louder sounds.”
“Belt it. Scream it. Cry like your body is begging you to.”
“I won’t leave. I can handle your tears.”
“You don’t have to hold this alone.”
Do you know what happens when someone feels safe enough to cry fully?
Their breathing changes.
Their chest softens.
Their jaw unlocks.
Their nervous system unclenches.
Their body shakes out the trauma, instead of storing it.
Their shame melts because someone stayed with them instead of shrinking away.
Loud tears are truth finding air.
They are grief moving.
They are fear exiting the body.
They are heartbreak being honored instead of buried alive.
And yes… it’s raw.
Yes… it’s messy.
Yes… it’s uncomfortable.
Yes… it might break your heart to witness.
But this is what emotional intimacy actually is.
Not fixing.
Not managing.
Not silencing.
Not coaching someone out of their pain.
Staying.
Holding.
Hearing.
Letting the storm exist without shutting down the sky.
We don’t need quieter emotions.
We need safer spaces for louder truth.
So the next time someone cries, and you feel that instinct rise up to calm them, shrink them, tidy their grief…
Pause.
Maybe they don’t need to be calmed.
Maybe they need permission to be real. See less

17 Judgments That Make an Anxious Partner Spiral
(and Guarantee the Relationship Gets More Chaotic)
If you're anxious in love, you know exactly what it feels like to be set off by a single sentence, a single tone, a single eye roll. Your nervous system processes rejection at lightning speed. Your body reacts before your mind even understands what happened.

What Is Love Addiction Really?
We all need to be touched, loved, understood, seen... gotten.
The need is Universal.
Humans deeply need each other.
A baby that isn't touched will lose a part of his/her soul.
There are two components I want to break apart here, so you know the difference between them.
Component One: the Frozen Needs that occur when your needs are not met as a child.
Component Two: relating as adults, healing the Frozen Needs.
******************************
Frozen Needs
I consider a need to be frozen when a significant abuse or neglect happened as a child.
This need was frozen in time.
If you cried as a child, and your mother didn't have "enough" maturity to place your needs first AND understand how to tend to herself, her own needs... then she might have showed up for you, annoyed with you.
Annoyance coming at you as an infant from an unhealed mother permanently builds pathways in your brain.
You learn if you are worth being loved. Or. Not.
******************************
You Have Two Mothers
In adulthood, when you are triggered by another adult, it hurts, and it's terribly confusing.
Sometimes we blame mom (or dad, just sticking with mom for brevity).
It will help you OWN your own healing path if you know that the mom you are grieving is the one from childhood; actually about 90% of it is the first 2 years of your life.
(As a side note, in professional psychology, the debate has shifted from 6 months of age all the way up to 6 years old as the most critical years.
Currently, 6 months to 2 years is the popular opinion amongst psychologists.
It doesn't matter.
It's fucking young.)
So when I'm hurting, I think of young mom: scared, confused, not ready to be a mom.
Dealing with this directly, being hard on my mom as an adult, takes me away from owning the pain.
Leave the poor lady alone.
It's the one from childhood that hurt you, the one that set up your frozen needs.
From a different vantage point, healing the adult to adult mature relationship with your mother today can be a great path to maturity, if you're ready to learn something about her, what her struggles were as Young Mom.
I am in full agreement to spend a period of time blaming mom if you need to... young mom, old mom, all versions of mom.
But make an attempt to really get Young Mom is no longer in physical form in the way you think.
Young Mom is a neural net of pathways in your brain.
Those pathways can heal.
250,000 recovery books have made attempts to tell you how.
Very few describe vulnerability with another mature adult... I will get to that in a bit.
******************************
The Trigger Is Inside You
Mature adult love exists when giving/receiving is happening.
Without a trigger, and with present, clear, caught-up communication, you can FEEL the giving/receiving.
Triggers are faster than a speeding bullet.
When you get triggered, hurt, that's when you now have choices to make if you want to be conscious, and want people... to want to be close to you.
My favorite person talks about a "Gotsta Know Now" trigger.
If you hurt me, neglect me... it hurts, and I need to know... RIGHT NOW... how to fix it.
******************************
The Red Pill Or The Blue Pill
In my needing my immediate answer, I am hurting.
USUALLY, WELL, ALMOST ALWAYS, IF I HIT CONFUSION, I AM IN A FROZEN NEED.
What I literally need is a time machine.
I need my mom to come in and feed me while I was crying, in 1972.
I can be mad at 2021 mom, or 2002 mom, but she can't do anything.
It's mine.
If I take the Red Pill, I will stay stuck in trying to get Back To The Past.
I am in a frozen need.
Every defense from childhood, every brilliant method I created to manipulate these flawed humans to love me... I will pull out every method I can to get my needs met.
I am in emotional danger.
I will attack you back, lie, withhold the truth, not return your call, talk about you negatively to others, feel victimized... basically I will ruin my mature adult relationship if I stay in this frozen need.
I want my mommy.
I want her to change in 1972.
I will take it out on you in 2021, because you hurt my feelings.
******************************
The Blue Pill
I personally love the blue pill, because I know how to do it, it works, and it's the only thing that works.
I have spent 30 years cultivating how to grieve, feel my feelings, and take the risk to tell you that I am doing just that.
I have spent 30 years cultivating how to tell you what I did in childhood to protect myself.
In my adult mature relationships, I can detect when I am triggered, and I don't only have half the equation.
The self-help books teach how to go inside and love yourself.
It's not enough.
We need each other.
And if you were harmed in childhood like I was, you need positive feedback even more.
******************************
Falling On My Sword
Vulnerability means that I am putting myself in danger... temporarily.
It is Component Two of the equation of how to grow up.
Big people are scary.
They use big words.
It seems that if I admit something that I have done, I might be annihilated.
Yes, when you are this honest, people will respond back, and it will hurt.
That is part of your training, to detect that quickly, and eliminate them from your lives. Period.
If you want a good life, and you want the vulnerable path, you must learn to not allow people to get close to you... if they are not on that path.
You have your world of self-healing, but you also have millions and millions of souls on this planet that want closeness, that want depth.
When the brain is measured on an MRI and a person sees depth, realness, a person crying in a move, the pleasure centers light up (in addition to the pain centers).
We feel safe when we see another admit how flawed they are.
******************************
You Must Get A Microwave
When you risk sharing what you ARE ABOUT TO DO to destroy your relationship, you create safety for the other.
"I'm so embarrassed that I got so angry, and I was about to yell at you. I stopped myself. Would you hold me while I feel my anger?"
When you risk sharing your CONFUSION AND NON-CLARITY ABOUT YOUR FEELINGS, you create safety for the other.
"I want to be closer to you and I don't know how. Do you want that?"
When you risk sharing the EXACT THING THAT COMES TO YOUR MIND ABOUT WHAT YOU WISH YOU COULD SAY, you create safety for the other.
"I go all day long wishing we wouldn't argue. I feel more alone when you're in my bed than when you're not. I'm scared about that. Can we get some help?"
The only way to thaw out a frozen need is one moment at a time, one vulnerability at a time, one risk at a time.
I wish that I could help individuals heal super fast with one on one counseling with me.
What clients learn from me is how to do the above.
But nothing... nothing... nothing... will help you heal faster than a romantic partner that supports you... gently... in your continuous learning of how to move from a moment of a childhood Frozen Need... to vulnerability... a moment of sharing your coping mechanisms and your imperfections.
******************************
I love all of you that follow my posts.
And I would not say all this without having to do this myself.
Every single moment I have to do the same kind of risking, just as you do.
Every single moment I risk, I think you are going to walk away and not love me anymore.
So I go within, recognize that I have this Frozen Need, and I tell my beloved, "do you have a moment to listen to something I'm scared to say?"
If she says that she does have a moment, I might need another qualifier... "This is a deep one for me, and I'm in my fear of you going away part."
She knows not to say anything to me for a minute, because I am simply crying and struggling to say my next sentence about what I'm scared to say.
In all honesty, if I really slow down, I could stop there and sometimes not even say the next thing.
Because for that moment, adult to adult, I had a person be gentle with me, while I described my coping mechanism and my wound.
That is how to heal a Frozen Need.
It is frozen, it's really stuck in there, what happened in childhood.
For me, my wounding was very difficult.
I have come to peace that my whole life will be spent healing it.
I don't know another path other than this one.
I love it.
I get to be close to people, perhaps closer, more intense, deeper, than if I wasn't hurt in the first place.
******************************
So what is Love Addiction?
It is not understanding the above.
It is acting out too much from the Frozen Need without vulnerability.
It is having bad relationship after bad relationship and not understanding why. See less

 She stayed “strong” for 12 years. It cost her a decade of her life.

She said she could handle it.
She swallowed tears, compartmentalized hurt, performed normal, smiled for pictures.
She said she didn’t want to “feel weak,”
so she never let herself feel *anything.*
She thought avoiding emotional pain meant she was winning.
But here’s what actually happened:
The pain didn’t disappear.
It turned into chronic anxiety.
Into migraines.
Into exhaustion.
Into numbness.
Into a marriage where she no longer recognized the person she’d become.
She finally left.
And then said the sentence that destroys me every time I hear it:
“I thought I was avoiding pain by staying.
Now I realize I spent 12 years living inside of it.”
Avoiding pain didn’t save her.
It prolonged her suffering.

He thought emotional toughness = emotional maturity.
He prided himself on “not being sensitive.”
He stayed in abusive environments because he didn’t know it was abuse.
He stayed in cold relationships because he thought connection was optional.
He stayed disconnected from himself because feelings felt like weakness.
Then one day, someone loved him softly.
They didn’t yell.
They didn’t belittle.
They didn’t leave when it got hard.
And his body… broke.
He cried harder than he had in 20 years.
Not because it hurt.
But because for the first time his nervous system realized:
“Oh my God… THIS is what love feels like…

because it exposed how much harm he had normalized.

-

Not to process.
Not to grieve.
Not to be sad.
She just moved on.
Immediately into another relationship.
And the same dynamic repeated.
And again.
And again.
Different faces.
Same emotional pattern.
One day she finally said:
“I never stopped long enough to feel the pain of losing someone.
So I kept choosing people who would hurt me the same way.”
Avoiding grief didn’t make her strong.
It made her stuck.
Pain she refused to feel kept controlling her life anyway.

Never crying.
Never asking for help.
Never breaking down.

Protector.
Performer.

On the inside, full of pressure.

The problem wasn’t his heart.

He didn’t avoid pain.
He delayed it.

 Here is the truth all these stories share:

you do not escape it.

Leaving abuse is painful.

Learning to be loved instead of abused is painful.

Partner with pain instead of rejecting it.

Here’s why…

-

 She stayed “strong” for 12 years. It cost her a decade of her life.

She told herself she was fine.

She told herself it wasn’t “that bad.”

She said she could handle it.

She swallowed tears, compartmentalized hurt, performed normal, smiled for pictures.

She said she didn’t want to “feel weak,”

so she never let herself feel *anything.*

She thought avoiding emotional pain meant she was winning.

But here’s what actually happened:

The pain didn’t disappear.

It turned into chronic anxiety.

Into migraines.

Into exhaustion.

Into numbness.

Into a marriage where she no longer recognized the person she’d become.

She finally left.

And then said the sentence that destroys me every time I hear it:

“I thought I was avoiding pain by staying.

Now I realize I spent 12 years living inside of it.”

Avoiding pain didn’t save her.

It prolonged her suffering.

-

 He said therapy “wasn’t necessary.” Then cried the first time someone loved him gently.

He grew up being yelled at and criticized.

He thought emotional toughness = emotional maturity.

He prided himself on “not being sensitive.”

He stayed in abusive environments because he didn’t know it was abuse.

He stayed in cold relationships because he thought connection was optional.

He stayed disconnected from himself because feelings felt like weakness.

Then one day, someone loved him softly.

They didn’t yell.

They didn’t belittle.

They didn’t leave when it got hard.

And his body… broke.

He cried harder than he had in 20 years.

Not because it hurt.

But because for the first time his nervous system realized:

“Oh my God… THIS is what love feels like…

What have I been surviving instead?”

Learning to be loved hurt

because it exposed how much harm he had normalized.

Pain wasn’t his enemy.

Pain was telling the truth.

-

 She didn’t want to feel grief. So she kept repeating it.

After her breakup she decided not to “fall apart.”

Not to process.

Not to grieve.

Not to be sad.

She just moved on.

Immediately into another relationship.

And the same dynamic repeated.

And again.

Different faces.

Same emotional pattern.

One day she finally said:

“I never stopped long enough to feel the pain of losing someone.

So I kept choosing people who would hurt me the same way.”

Avoiding grief didn’t make her strong.

It made her stuck.

Pain she refused to feel kept controlling her life anyway.

-

 He told himself he was “fine.” Then had a panic attack at 48 years old.

Decades of holding everything in.

Never crying.

Never asking for help.

Never breaking down.

Provider.

Protector.

Performer.

On the outside, successful.

On the inside, full of pressure.

His body finally forced a shutdown.

Doctors said nothing was physically wrong.

The problem wasn’t his heart.

It was his history.

Years of emotional suppression collapsed his nervous system.

He didn’t avoid pain.

He delayed it.

And delayed pain compounds.

-

 Here is the truth all these stories share:

When you refuse to feel emotional pain,

you do not escape it.

You marinate in it.

Unfelt sadness does not disappear.

It becomes numbness.

Unfelt anger doesn’t dissolve.

It turns into resentment and explosion.

Unfelt loneliness doesn’t fade.

It turns into self-abandonment.

Unfelt grief doesn’t weaken.

It turns into emptiness.

Avoiding pain doesn’t protect you.

It enslaves you to it.

-

 Feeling pain isn’t suffering.

Feeling pain is completing it.

Pain processed becomes wisdom.

Pain honored becomes strength.

Pain moved through becomes healing.

Leaving abuse hurts.

But staying in abuse hurts forever.

Learning safe love hurts.

But staying with harmful love rewires your nervous system against intimacy.

Grieving hurts.

But refusing to grieve costs you your future happiness.

Pain is not proof you’re failing.

Pain is proof that you finally stopped abandoning yourself.

-

Stop rejecting pain like it’s the enemy.

Sit with it.

Partner with it.

Let it walk you out of the life that’s killing you.

Because the only thing more painful than change…

Be careful about what you think you know about a person
based only on a title, a credential, a rumor, or a Google search.
There’s a conversation happening in this screenshot that speaks to something way bigger than one thread, one name, or one debate about credentials.
It reflects a world where we’ve been trained to believe the only people worth listening to are the ones with letters after their name.
And listen… I love education.
I respect training.
I honor professionals and the incredible good they do.
But here’s a truth that makes people uncomfortable:
There’s book-smart wisdom
and there’s lived-body wisdom.
They’re not the same.
Both matter.
Neither cancels the other.
What worries me isn’t disagreement.
Disagreement is healthy.
Questions are valid.
Skepticism is human.
What worries me is certainty.
Certainty that “if a person isn’t licensed, they can’t possibly know what they’re talking about.”
Certainty that the human nervous system only trusts logos, institutions, and formal authority.
Certainty that credentials automatically equal emotional attunement, relational safety, and embodied understanding.
Your nervous system doesn’t attach to paper.
It attaches to resonance.
Presence.
Safety.
Truth you can feel.
I’ve worked with people who’ve got advanced degrees who’ve never once been emotionally available.
And I’ve worked with people who’ve got no degree at all who can sit inside raw human pain with steadiness, humility, accountability, and depth textbooks can’t even describe.
If you ask your nervous system instead of your fear, it usually knows the difference.
Sit still.
Breathe.
Ask yourself:
“When I listen to this human, do I feel safer? Calmer? Seen? Stronger? More honest inside myself?”
If the answer’s yes, your body’s telling you something real.
If the answer’s no, your body’s telling you something real.
Listen to it.
Every single day people sit with licensed professionals who talk at them but never truly meet them.
And every single day people meet someone who finally looks them in the eyes, sits in the dark with them, and says:
“I’m not leaving you in this.”
That doesn’t become “less” just because it isn’t certified, laminated, and stamped.
This isn’t about defending myself.
It isn’t about dismissing education.
It isn’t about discrediting people who’ve devoted their lives to formal clinical work.
It’s about humility.
It’s about remembering you don’t know someone’s depth, integrity, or capacity simply because you know their résumé.
And it’s about reclaiming a deeply human truth:
Sometimes your nervous system recognizes safety before your intellect gives you permission to trust it.
Sometimes real leadership isn’t granted by institutions.
It’s forged in lived experience.
In tears.
In mistakes.
In accountability.
In the sacred labor of actually caring for human hearts.
Honor the professionals who change lives.
They matter.
But also honor the embodied elders.
The wounded healers.
The ones who didn’t study pain from a distance, they lived it, walked through fire, and came back carrying lanterns.
If you slow down enough to listen…
Your body knows the difference. See less

I don’t often share posts on here, but this one really spoke to me. I spent six years studying to become a doctor, and I ultimately stepped away after a devastating heartbreak. Since then, life has consistently guided me away from credentials and certifications and toward direct, lived experience.
It hasn’t been easy. Developing a grounded sense of self-conviction has been part of my path. I’ve had many, many moments where I felt less than others with the shiny letters after their names. And then I come back to the present. I notice how often people soften, brighten, tell the truth, or breathe more fully when I’m with them. In those moments, my value becomes obvious.
We’ve been trained to trust letters more than lived experience. At the same time, I’m deeply aware of the harm that can happen without proper training. Training matters. Presence matters. Something essential is lost when we elevate one and dismiss the other.
Let’s not mistake the absence of letters for the absence of depth, wisdom, or beauty. Being deeply human is a potent capacity, one that long preceded institutions and quietly shaped them.
Thank you for speaking your truth here, Derek Hart See less

The “Good Person” Trap.
You don’t yell.
You don’t cheat.
You don’t name-call.
By all traditional standards, you’re a “good” partner.
So why’s your partner still lonely?
Why’re they still angry?
Why does it feel like there’s a thousand-mile canyon between you while you’re sitting on the same couch?
Here’s the truth that’s hard to swallow:
You can be a “good person” and still be a threatening partner.
Not threatening because you’re aggressive.
Threatening because you’re unavailable.
To a human nervous system, silence isn’t “peace.”
Withdrawal isn’t “giving space.”
Emotional neutrality isn’t “being calm.”
To the person who loves you, those things feel like abandonment.
And abandonment is a threat.
When your partner brings you their hurt, and you respond with:
“I didn’t mean it that way.”
“You’re overreacting.”
“I’m a good person, I’d never try to hurt you.”
You’re defending your reputation.
You’re not defending the relationship.
While you’re busy proving your innocence, your partner’s drowning in the experience of being unseen.
They don’t need to know you’re a good person. They already know that, and that’s why they’re still there.
They need to know you’re a safe person.
Safe means:
I can tell you I’m hurt without you making it about your intentions.
I can be messy without you shutting down.
I can find you when I’m lost, instead of finding a wall.
The “real death” of a relationship isn’t always a blow-up.
It’s the slow, quiet freezing over that happens when one person decides it’s safer to be “right” than to be “connected.”
It’s when you start prioritizing your “niceness” over their “wellness.”
If you want to save your marriage, stop trying to be the “good” partner.
Start being the present one.
Stop explaining why they shouldn’t feel that way.
Start wondering what it’s like to be them.
Because love isn’t a certificate you earn for good behavior.
It’s a living, breathing practice of staying when it gets uncomfortable.
Don’t just be a good person.
Be a sanctuary. See less

The anxious believes the avoidant is the problem.
The avoidant thinks the anxious is the problem, because the anxious one is the one driving them crazy.
Let's look at how solving this works.
The anxious:
They’re loud.
They’re pleading.
They’re emotional.
They’re relentless.
They’re critical.
They’re begging you to understand something you think you’ve already heard a hundred times.
But what almost nobody truly understands is this:
The anxious partner lives every day knowing they hurt you sometimes.
They know their tone cuts.
They know their intensity overwhelms.
They know their timing is awful.
They know their words land like arrows when they’re simply trying to scream out, “I’m scared you’ll leave.”
They already live with shame.
They replay conversations. They analyze moments. They hate themselves after the storm. They sit in the bathroom, or in their car, or in bed while you’re turned away from them, thinking:
“Why did I do that again?” “Why can’t I just stop?” “Why do I keep ruining the very thing I want most?”
So when they walk into counseling, their biggest fear isn’t that they’ve done too much.
Their biggest fear is:
“What if even therapy proves I really am the problem?”
And on the other side, you have the avoidant partner.
Calm. Composed. Rational. Logical. Measured.
They don’t explode.
They disappear.
Not physically. Emotionally.
They go quiet inside. They shrink their needs. They bury their feelings in layers of numbness.
They don’t shut down because they don’t care.
They shut down because:
They’re afraid care will drown them.
They’re afraid of being wrong.
They’re afraid they’ll try their best and it still won’t be enough.
They’re afraid of being controlled.
They’re afraid of failing love.
And inside that quietness is a hurricane nobody sees.
Because the avoidant partner doesn’t live in chaos… outside.
They live in chaos… inside.
They don’t lie awake saying, “How do I fix this right now?”
They lie awake wondering:
“Why do I always feel like I can’t do enough?” “Why is everything I give still not right?” “Why does love feel like walking into a courtroom instead of a home?”
So when the couple comes into counseling?
The avoidant partner usually says something like:
“Can we just calm this down?” “Can you help them not react so much?” “Can we learn better communication tools so they stop attacking?”
And to most of the world, that sounds reasonable.
But here is the raw, brutal truth most people never understand:
You cannot start healing by trying to slow the anxious partner down.
By the time you see their behavior, Their nervous system has already gone nuclear.
Their body believes: “I’m about to lose the person I love.”
Their brain believes: “If I stop, this relationship dies.”
And if you try to silence that panic with logic…
You don’t soothe it.
You terrify it.
So where does real healing start?
You don’t begin by fixing the anxious partner’s behavior.
You begin by bringing the avoidant’s humanity back into the room.
Not with criticism. Not with shame. Not with “you’re emotionally unavailable.” Not with “you’re the problem, too.”
But with tenderness.
With curiosity.
With the willingness to look beneath their quietness and say:
“I wonder where it hurts in you.”
Because here’s what the anxious partner rarely understands until it is gently revealed:
The avoidant didn’t stop needing love.
They stopped believing love was safe.
Their nervous system says: “If I feel too much, I’ll break.” “If I show too much, I’ll lose control.” “If I depend on you, you’ll eventually hurt me.” “If I open up, I’ll drown in something I don’t know how to survive.”
So they numb. They freeze. They disappear into silence. They tell themselves they’re fine. They convince themselves they don’t need much.
But inside?
There is loneliness. There is grief. There is exhaustion. There is a longing they barely dare admit they have.
And when therapy slowly uncovers this…
When the avoidant partner finally says something like:
“I do want you.” “I do miss closeness.” “I do feel overwhelmed, and it scares me.” “I back away not because I don’t love you… but because I’m terrified I’ll fail you.”
Something seismic shifts.
The anxious partner’s body does something miraculous: It softens.
Because for years, they believed:
“You don’t care.” “You don’t feel.” “You don’t love me as deeply.” “You don’t want closeness the way I do.”
And that belief is agony.
That belief is why they chase so hard. That belief is why their voice shakes. That belief is why their anger explodes. That belief is why their criticism burns.
They’ve been panicking in a relationship where they thought they were emotionally alone.
And suddenly…
They realize they weren’t alone.
They just couldn’t see the other person’s pain through their armor.
And the avoidant finally realizes something too:
The anxious one wasn’t trying to control them.
They were trying not to lose them.
They weren’t attacking them to destroy connection.
They were fighting to keep connection alive.
Two incredibly hurt nervous systems.
Both aching.
Both protecting themselves.
Both desperate for closeness…
But defending in opposite directions.
This is why skilled couples work does not begin with blame.
It begins with resurrection.
Resurrecting the avoidant’s heart. Resurrecting the anxious partner’s safety. Resurrecting the truth no one ever told either of them:
Avoidants want love just as deeply. They simply learned to survive without asking for it.
Anxious partners want peace just as much. They simply learned to fight for connection like their life depended on it.
When both of them finally see that…
That’s not simply conflict resolution.
That’s two humans finally recognizing each other’s humanity again.
That’s where repair begins.
That’s where compassion walks into the room and sits down between them.
That’s where love finally stops being a war, And starts becoming a place where two nervous systems Learn how to breathe again… together.
A portion of both their training is to grasp each other's entirely different style when emotions occur.
You don't stop being anxious and avoidant.
Ever.
Stop trying.
You help each other with this entirely different way of being. See less

Most people think the hardest thing in a healing relationship
is talking about the pain.
But sometimes the hardest, most vulnerable thing
is saying something *good*
and letting it actually land.
It’s unbelievably raw to say something loving to someone you’ve also been hurt by.
It’s terrifying to receive something loving from someone you’re still learning to trust again.
When a relationship has been distressed, your nervous systems are trained for danger.
You’re used to bracing.
You’re used to scanning for what’s wrong.
You’re used to waiting for the drop.
So when something tender shows up…
your body doesn’t always know what to do with it.
It feels almost *unsafe* to soften.
It feels dangerous to believe warmth.
It feels risky to let a moment of goodness actually affect you.
Because if you let it in, now your heart’s involved again.
Now you care again.
Now you’re open again.
And open has hurt before.
So what do couples do?
They joke it away.
They downplay it.
They deflect.
They argue with it.
They “yeah, but…” it to death.
Not because they don’t want love…
but because digesting love when you’ve been starving is overwhelming.
That’s why this matters:
When a distressed relationship is trying to heal,
it’s not just about talking through the hard things.
It’s about learning how to tolerate goodness again.
It’s about letting warmth sit in the room long enough for the nervous system to believe it.
It’s about letting a soft moment be real without sabotaging it.
It’s about saying:
“I see you.”
“I appreciate you.”

Most people think the hardest thing in a healing relationship

is talking about the pain.

But sometimes the hardest, most vulnerable thing

is saying something *good*

and letting it actually land.

It’s unbelievably raw to say something loving to someone you’ve also been hurt by.

It’s terrifying to receive something loving from someone you’re still learning to trust again.

When a relationship has been distressed, your nervous systems are trained for danger.

You’re used to bracing.

You’re used to scanning for what’s wrong.

You’re used to waiting for the drop.

So when something tender shows up…

your body doesn’t always know what to do with it.

It feels almost *unsafe* to soften.

It feels dangerous to believe warmth.

It feels risky to let a moment of goodness actually affect you.

Because if you let it in, now your heart’s involved again.

Now you care again.

Now you’re open again.

And open has hurt before.

So what do couples do?

They joke it away.

They downplay it.

They deflect.

They argue with it.

They “yeah, but…” it to death.

Not because they don’t want love…

but because digesting love when you’ve been starving is overwhelming.

That’s why this matters:

When a distressed relationship is trying to heal,

it’s not just about talking through the hard things.

They did not just fall in love.
They fell into recognition.
Two nervous systems that breathed,
Oh… there you are.
She loved with steady warmth,
believing relationships were places you tended,
like gardens you kept showing up for.
He loved with devotion that shook in his chest,
the anxious kind,
the kind that holds tight
because everything beautiful he had ever known
had once slipped through his fingers.
In the beginning
there was sunlight.
There were long talks with no clocks.
There were vows whispered into casual days
long before they spoke them at the altar.
Their wedding felt like relief.
He cried.
She trembled.
Everyone clapped
because it looked like forever.
They built a family.
Babies.
Soft cheeks.
Breath against collarbones.
Rooms painted in colors that sounded like hope.
He looked at her with awe
that she still chose him.
She looked at him with warmth
that believed love was a place you stayed.
And then, slowly, life pressed in.
The anxious part of him woke at night.
What if she leaves.
What if I ruin this.
What if I am not enough.
He began reaching harder,
needing reassurance like oxygen,
asking without asking:
Do you still love me.
Are we okay.
Please do not disappear.
She felt it.
Not the love.
The fear.
Fear became pressure.
Fear became weight.
Fear became the request
Prove I will not be abandoned
again
and again
and again.
Something inside her,
the avoidant part that had once learned
that closeness could mean losing herself,
started building walls disguised as calm.
She did not rage.
She did not scream.
She simply began stepping her heart
half a step back each day.
And when she stepped back,
his nervous system burned.
He panicked with love.
He tightened with tenderness.
He tried more affection, more words, more reaching.
But the closer he moved,
the more she needed space to breathe.
And here is the holy cruelty:
When the anxious lover feels abandoned,
they beg.
When the avoidant lover feels engulfed,
they criticize.
She began pointing out what was wrong.
Not because she did not care.
Because criticism creates distance.
It says,
Stay a little farther away
so I can feel safe.
So she softened less.
She sighed more.
She became calm and composed
but emotionally gone.
Her words turned precise and cool
in ways her heart did not fully mean.
He heard rejection.
He did not hear,
I am scared of closeness.
He only heard,
You are failing me.
His anxious heart broke quietly
again
and again
and again.
He cried in showers.
He tried harder.
He apologized for existing.
He shaped himself into versions
he thought might make her stay.
She did not want to hurt him.
But survival whispered,
Close up.
Stay composed.
Do not need.
Do not soften.
It is safer like this.
Secure love tried to hold them both.
It whispered,
You can repair.
You can come back.
You can tell the truth underneath your defenses.
But the defenses were louder.
He became abandonment.
She became criticism.
Both became heartbreak.
They stopped dancing in the kitchen.
They stopped lingering in hallways.
They stopped reaching for each other at night.
He kept asking with his eyes,
Do I matter.
Will you stay.
Please do not leave me.
She kept protecting herself with distance,
Do not come so close.
Do not drown me.
Do not need me so hard.
Two good people.
Two loving hearts.
Two terrified nervous systems.
They did not explode.
They did not shatter loudly.
They drifted
into parallel loneliness
inside a house they once filled with warmth.
The saddest part was not that they stopped loving.
Love was always there.
Sitting behind anxiety.
Hiding beneath criticism.
Waiting for safety
that never came.
One day they sat at a table,
hands shaking,
eyes tired,
souls worn out,
and whispered the truth neither wanted to speak.
He cried.
She shook.
There were no vows.
No applause.
No witnesses for the grief of we tried.
They kissed goodbye
like people mourning a miracle
their nervous systems could not hold.
They did not lose love.
They lost safety.
And love without safety
is a tragedy
that feels like fate. See less

John Gottman calls it contempt.
But let’s be more honest.
Contempt is just a very nice, academic, clinically acceptable word for quiet hatred creeping into a relationship.
Not dramatic hatred.
Not screaming hatred.
Not movie-scene hatred.
The slow kind.
The subtle kind.
The kind that smiles in public and dies in the kitchen.
Contempt is not eye rolling.
It is grief that gave up.
It is not sarcasm.
It is disappointment that turned hard.
It is not irritation.
It is love that stopped believing in repair.
Contempt is not anger.
Anger wants to fix something.
Contempt says there is nothing worth fixing anymore.
That is why Gottman calls it the biggest predictor of divorce.
Because contempt is the nervous system saying:
“I do not trust you anymore.”
“I do not respect you anymore.”
“I do not feel safe opening my heart to you anymore.”
And once the nervous system reaches that point,
it stops trying to repair.
It stops reaching.
It stops caring.
It survives instead of loves.
Contempt builds slowly.
It grows every time someone says
“You are too sensitive.”
“It is not a big deal.”
“You are overreacting.”
“Here we go again.”
It grows when the other person shuts down instead of leaning in.
It grows when repair never happens.
It grows when one partner feels unseen for too long.
And eventually…
Love does not explode.
It calcifies.
You still share a house.
You still share bills.
You still share kids, calendars, routines.
But you do not share a heart anymore.
Here is the heartbreaking truth:
By the time contempt shows up,
most people are not cruel.
They are exhausted.
They begged.
They tried.
They reached.
They softened.
And nothing changed.
So something inside closes.
And when it closes, it protects itself with superiority, sarcasm, distance, eye rolls, coldness.
Not because they hate you.
Because they are grieving the version of you
who they hoped would show up
and never came.
If you are in a relationship and you can feel contempt forming,
do not ignore it.
Do not justify it.
Do not normalize it.
Contempt is not a phase.
It is a warning siren.
It means there is pain that has never been heard.
It means repair never happened.
It means love is trying to survive by hardening.
Contempt is not the beginning of the end.
It is the middle
where someone quietly whispers inside themselves:
“I cannot keep breaking like this anymore.” See less

Forgiveness is easy.
That’s the lie.
Forgiveness is tidy.
Forgiveness is mature.
Forgiveness is enlightened.
Forgiveness is what emotionally evolved people do.
We’ve turned forgiveness into a performance,
a badge of spiritual superiority,
a social approval trophy.
Say the right calm words.
Say you’ve processed it.
Say you’re choosing compassion.
Say you’re letting go.
Say you understand why they did it.
And everyone nods and claps like you just achieved emotional sainthood.
But here’s the truth that makes people uncomfortable:
Most forgiveness is nothing but an intellectual exercise.
It’s not healing.
It’s not relational repair.
It’s not nervous system safety.
It’s logic pretending to be resolution.
It’s your mind giving speeches your heart isn’t ready to deliver.
“I understand.”
“I get it.”
“They had trauma.”
“They didn’t mean to.”
“I don’t want to hold onto anger.”
Meanwhile your body is screaming:
“I still don’t feel safe.”
“I still feel betrayed.”
“I still hurt.”
“I still flinch when I remember.”
“I still don’t trust you.”
Forgiveness is not hard because you are dramatic.
Forgiveness is not hard because you are immature.
Forgiveness is not hard because you are stubborn.
Forgiveness is hard because your nervous system does not care about your enlightened language.
Your body remembers.
Your body keeps score.
Your body does not release fear just because your brain thinks it is time to be spiritually impressive.
And nobody teaches us how to forgive.
They just preach that we *should.*
People tell you to forgive because it makes them comfortable.
They say “be the bigger person” because it helps them avoid depth.
They say “move on” because they do not want to sit in the truth of what was broken.
So what do you do?
You fake it.
You say the line.
You smile the smile.
You talk about healing like it already happened.
You swallow grief because it is inconvenient.
You bury anger because it is unattractive.
You silence truth because it is disruptive.
Then your resentment leaks.
Your trust cracks.
Your body tightens.
Your heart withdraws.
Your nervous system stays on guard.
And everyone calls you the problem when you “just can’t let it go.”
Let me say this clearly:
Not knowing how to forgive is the real truth.
And it is not weakness.
It is honesty.
It means your pain is not lying.
It means betrayal actually impacted you.
It means your nervous system has not found safety yet.
It means repair did not actually happen.
It means there is grief that never got witnessed.
It means accountability never fully occurred.
It means your heart refuses to sign off on a lie.
Forgiveness is not a sentence you repeat until it sounds believable.
Forgiveness is a physiological, emotional, relational process.
It is grief.
It is anger.
It is shaking.
It is naming reality.
It is letting yourself hate for a moment without shame.
It is facing what broke instead of decorating over it.
It is slow trust building.
It is truth-telling without gaslighting.
It is someone actually repairing the wound instead of just asking you to be spiritually mature enough to pretend it wasn’t deep.
If you haven’t forgiven yet,
stop letting people shame you.
You’re not failing.
You’re not immature.
You’re not weak.
You’re not bitter.
You’re honest.
You still hurt because something hurt you.
You’re still cautious because something threatened safety.
You hesitate because something inside you still bleeds when touched.
That’s not dysfunction.
That’s your nervous system doing its job.
Real forgiveness isn’t pretty.
Real forgiveness isn’t quick.
Real forgiveness isn’t intellectual.
Real forgiveness is earned.
Real forgiveness is felt.
Real forgiveness happens when the body finally sighs and says,
“Okay… now I believe it’s safe again.”
Until then…
You don’t need better forgiveness skills.
You need deeper truth,
real repair,
and permission to stop pretending that “letting go” is the same thing as healing. See less

You want to talk now.
I need a little time.
But I don’t tell you when I’ll be back.
And that silence… that uncertainty… that is where the pain is born.
People think the problem is disagreement.
It isn’t.
The real pain in relationships is the gap between two nervous systems trying to survive.
You want closeness because you’re scared of losing connection.
You want to talk because silence feels like abandonment.
You want to resolve it now because your heart can’t breathe in limbo.
I need space because my system is overwhelmed.
I need time because I don’t have words yet.
I need to step back so I don’t say something I’ll regret.
Both are valid.
Both are human.
Both are nervous systems trying to protect themselves.
But here’s where it breaks…
I disappear without anchoring you.
I retreat without giving you ground to stand on.
I leave and don’t say, “I will come back.”
So you don’t experience me as calming.
You experience me as gone.
Now your fear spirals.
Now your mind writes stories.
Now your body feels deserted.
And you’re no longer just waiting.
You’re grieving connection
while I’m trying to recover from it.
Do you see the tragedy?
You’re not “needy.”
You’re scared.
I’m not “cold.”
I’m scared too.
But when I walk away without giving you a path to find me again
I don’t just take space.
I take safety with me.
Healing doesn’t mean never needing time apart.
Healing means:
“I can’t talk right now…
but I will talk.
I’m coming back.
You’re not alone.
You’re still held in this relationship even while we pause.”
Time doesn’t hurt.
Uncertainty does.
Silence doesn’t break love.
Abandonment does.
We don’t need perfection.
We need reassurance.
We need attachment consciousness.
We need to remember that love collapses in the dark spaces
where one person disappears
and the other is left holding panic with no hand to reach for.
If you need time
take it.
But take them with you emotionally.
Say when.
Say how.
Say you’re still there.
Say,

11 Signs the Burned Out Pursuer Dynamic Will Not Heal
1. They no longer believe anything they say will land.
If the pursuer has rehearsed a hundred versions of the conversation and every version ends with disappointment, they stop trying. A relationship cannot heal when one partner doesn’t believe their voice makes impact.
2. Their numbness has replaced their urgency.
An anxious partner who stops panicking is not “better.” They’re done. Healing can’t begin when numbness has become the new nervous system baseline.
3. They’re carrying grief instead of hope.
Once the pursuer starts grieving the relationship while still in it, repair becomes nearly impossible. You can’t build connection on top of pre mourning.
4. They no longer trust repair attempts.
Small gestures, apologies, promises, none of them register anymore. Once a pursuer stops believing repair is real, the cycle is already in collapse.
5. They can’t feel their partner’s presence as soothing.
Touch, tone, proximity, what used to comfort now feels neutral or draining. Healing requires the nervous system to experience the partner as safety, not background noise.
6. They’ve internalized the belief: ‘Nothing will ever change.’
This is the death sentence for the pursuer withdrawer cycle. A relationship cannot heal when one partner’s internal world has fully closed the door.
7. They no longer fear losing the relationship.
The pursuer survives on hope. When that hope dries up, they don’t cling, they detach. If losing the relationship feels easier than trying again, the emotional system is already gone.
8. They feel more relief in silence than connection.
When quiet becomes the only place they can breathe, closeness feels threatening, not nourishing. Without safe connection, no healing can occur.
9. Every conversation feels like labor they can’t afford.

17 Judgments That Send a Disorganized Partner Into Emotional Chaos
(And Guarantee Panic, Shutdown, and Explosions)
A disorganized partner is the person who loves you deeply and fears you deeply at the same time.
They reach for closeness, then jerk away.
They want reassurance, then reject it.
They want comfort, then mistrust it.
They want safety, then feel suffocated by it.
Their nervous system isn’t confused because they’re dramatic or manipulative.
It’s confused because closeness has been intertwined with danger their entire life.
So when you judge them, even lightly, it can rip open every old wound at once.
Here are the 17 judgments that overwhelm them completely, followed by what to say instead so you stop triggering chaos in their system.
1. “You’re too emotional.”
What they hear:
Your feelings are wrong.
Inside:
Spiral into shame.
Say instead:
“I see how strong your feelings are. I want to move through them with you.”
2. “You’re overreacting.”
What they hear:
Your fear doesn’t matter.
Inside:
Panic and anger surface at once.
Say instead:
“Something feels big inside you. I’m here. We can slow it down.”
3. “You’re impossible to understand.”
What they hear:
You’re incomprehensible.
Inside:
Identity collapse.
Say instead:
“Let’s take a moment. I want to understand you better.”
4. “You make no sense.”
What they hear:
Your inner world is invalid.
Inside:
Fight and flight activate together.
Say instead:
“Your feelings matter. We can untangle this gently.”
5. “You’re crazy.”
What they hear:
You’re unsafe to love.
Inside:
Freeze, then rage, then collapse.
Say instead:
“You’re overwhelmed. Let’s breathe together.”
6. “You need to calm down.”
What they hear:
Your intensity is unacceptable.
Inside:
Panic spikes.
Say instead:
“I’m with you. Let’s slow our pace together.”
7. “You’re always suspicious.”
What they hear:
Your trauma reactions are defects.
Inside:
Hypervigilance increases.
Say instead:
“I get that safety feels fragile. Let’s talk through this gently.”
8. “You’re too much.”
What they hear:
Your existence is overwhelming.
Inside:
Shame storm.
Say instead:
“I want to be with you in this. We’ll take it slow.”
9. “You’re unstable.”
What they hear:
You’re unpredictable and wrong.
Inside:
They dissociate or explode.
Say instead:
“You’re hurting. I’m right here with you.”
10. “I can’t deal with you.”
What they hear:
I might abandon you.
Inside:
Attachment terror.
Say instead:
“This is hard, but I want to find our way through it.”
11. “Stop acting so paranoid.”
What they hear:
Your safety needs are invalid.
Inside:
Fear intensifies.
Say instead:
“I get why your alarm went off. Let’s look at it together.”
12. “You shut down and lash out.”
What they hear:
Your survival strategies are offenses.
Inside:
More chaos.
Say instead:
“When you shift states, I want to stay with you. We can make sense of it.”
13. “You’re too clingy.”
What they hear:
Your longing is a problem.
Inside:
Desperation or withdrawal.
Say instead:
“I see your need for closeness. Let’s find a pace that feels safe.”
14. “You’re too guarded.”
What they hear:
You’re failing at intimacy.
Inside:
Walls reinforce.
Say instead:
“I know opening up takes time. I’m patient.”
15. “You’re manipulative.”
What they hear:
Your attempts to get connection are bad.
Inside:
They feel monstrous.
Say instead:
“I see you reaching for connection. Let’s do it more gently.”
16. “You’re unpredictable.”
What they hear:
You’re scary and unreliable.
Inside:
Fear becomes shame becomes panic.
Say instead:
“I know things move fast inside you. I want to understand that rhythm.”
17. “I never know which version of you I’ll get.”
What they hear:
You’re a problem to navigate, not a person to love.
Inside:
Identity fragmentation.
Say instead:
“I see your different states. I want to stay steady so you don’t have to be.”
What disorganized partners never tell you
They’re not trying to confuse you.
They’re trying not to drown.
They’re trying not to repeat old terror.
They’re trying to love with a body that mistrusts love.
They’re trying to stay present while their system pulls them in two directions.
A gentle tone regulates them.
A slower pace grounds them.
A steady presence heals them.
When you remove judgment, they stop panicking.
When you stop amplifying their shame, they stop flipping states.
When you stay calm, they stop collapsing.
When you love their fear without pushing it away, you become the safest person they’ve ever known. See less

There is a shut-off valve in the human heart.
Most people don’t know it exists. Most couples don’t realize it’s operating. And by the time you notice it, it has already done enormous damage.
It doesn’t flip off because you’re dramatic. It doesn’t activate because you’re “too sensitive.” It doesn’t happen because you’re weak.
It happens because your nervous system decides: “This isn’t safe anymore.”
Not physically unsafe. Emotionally unsafe.
And when emotional safety drops low enough, something terrifying and deeply biological happens:
Your system blacks your partner out.
Not metaphorically. Not poetically. Literally.
The body does what trauma always does: it narrows awareness to survival only.
So suddenly… the person you once loved feels foreign. Their face doesn’t look warm anymore. Their voice doesn’t sound familiar. The softness disappears. Your nervous system cannot retrieve the memories of the sweetness, the laughter, the warmth, the closeness.
It’s not because you stopped loving them. It’s because your body stopped trusting them.
That’s what “enemy” really means in relationship. Not someone you hate. Someone you can no longer emotionally recognize.
Your chest doesn’t open when you see them. Your mind doesn’t fill in stories of love. There is no automatic lean-in. There is no natural tenderness.
Instead:
Your jaw tightens. Your stomach drops. Your muscles brace. Your thoughts harden into suspicion. Your heart moves into self-protection mode.
And then something even sadder happens:
You forget who they used to be to you.
Your nervous system pulls the curtains closed on all the good. The nights you laughed. The mornings you whispered. The moments you held each other like there was no one else on Earth.
Gone.
Not erased forever. But emotionally inaccessible.
Just like blackout drinking: You know life happened during that time… but you can’t feel it.
So when people say: “Just remember the good times…” you can’t.
When they say: “Just think of why you fell in love…” your mind goes empty.
When they say: “Just talk calmly…” your nervous system is screaming that you’re in danger.
Not danger of violence. Danger of rejection. Danger of shame. Danger of abandonment. Danger of emotional starvation.
And when this blackout state keeps happening, it doesn’t just destroy the relationship. It starts destroying you.
You start waking up with tension instead of hope. You start living in defense instead of openness. You start surviving love instead of being held by it.
Your world shrinks. Your joy shrinks. Your capacity shrinks.
And you begin to believe something is wrong with you.
But nothing is wrong with you.
Your system is telling the truth: “Connection has become unsafe.”
And yet…
Here’s the part that matters:
This isn’t a sign that love is gone. It isn’t proof the relationship is doomed.
It’s a signal. It’s a flare shot into the sky by your nervous system saying:
“We can’t keep living like this.”
Emotional safety isn’t a luxury in relationships. It isn’t a bonus feature. It is oxygen.
Without it, love can’t breathe. Memory can’t retrieve warmth. Compassion can’t come online. Repair can’t happen.
This year, this is the work:
Not pretending. Not coping harder. Not numbing out. Not “being strong.” Not telling ourselves stories about “it’s just a rough season.”
This year we work on emotional safety.
On learning how to repair instead of defend. On learning how to move toward instead of away. On learning how to speak pain without destroying each other. On learning how to hold fear and sadness in real time. On learning how to keep the shut-off valve from firing.
Because when emotional safety returns, the nervous system slowly opens. The blackout lifts. The warmth comes back. The memories reconnect. The heart remembers.
Not because you forced it.
Because safety allows love to breathe again.
This is what we’re working on now. This is the year we stop surviving relationships and start healing inside them. See less

We need to talk about spiritual bypassing.
Not as a buzzword. Not as a way to win an argument. As something that quietly keeps you from ever actually healing.
Spiritual bypassing is when you use spiritual ideas or practices to jump over the messy parts of being human. To skip your grief. Skip your anger. Skip your terror of being left. Instead of feeling what hurts, you reach for a quote, a mantra, a teaching, a higher perspective and climb out of your own body. 
And yes, sometimes you do it in the name of “love and light.”
You say things like: “Everything happens for a reason.” “Just let it go.” “Stay high vibration.” “Don’t give your power away.” “Detach from the story.”
It sounds wise. It even looks calm.
But your nervous system is on fire underneath. Your chest is tight. Your jaw is clenched. Your stomach is buzzing.
You aren’t at peace. You’re shut down.
And there’s a second layer almost nobody notices:
Calling someone “a spiritual bypasser” can also be a bypass.
You roll your eyes and say, “There they go again, bypassing their trauma.” You slap a label on them so you don’t have to feel how helpless you are watching them suffer. You diagnose instead of letting your heart break.
You avoid your own fear by criticizing how they avoid theirs.
So now you’ve got two people out of their bodies, arguing about who’s more awake.
Underneath all the spiritual language is something brutally simple:
There is grief that has never been held. There is terror that has never had company. There is shame that’s never been spoken out loud.
Spiritual bypassing is attractive because it gives you a shortcut. It lets you feel “above” the pain for a while. Meditation, prayer, breathwork, affirmations, rituals, plant medicine, yoga, church, crystals, retreats. None of these are the problem. Many of them are beautiful, powerful, sacred. The problem is how you use them. 
You can use them to come closer to what hurts. Or you can use them to stay just far enough away that nothing ever really changes.
In romantic love this gets vicious.
Your partner cries and says, “I feel abandoned.” You say, “You’re attached to your story. You need to work on your inner child.”
Your partner says, “I’m furious you lied to me.” You say, “Anger is low vibration. Can we stay in gratitude instead.”
Your partner says, “I’m scared you’ll leave.” You say, “Fear is an illusion. Trust the universe.”
You think you’re offering wisdom. Their body hears one thing: “Your pain is too much for me. Please stop feeling it.”
That’s spiritual bypassing in a relationship. It’s not just avoidance. It’s dressed up avoidance. Avoidance with a halo on.
And then there’s the quieter version.
You hurt. You feel the sting of criticism, or betrayal, or indifference. You feel yourself about to cry. And instead of saying, “That really hurts,” you tell yourself:
“I need to be more evolved.” “I should be over this by now.” “If I were really healing, this wouldn’t bother me.”
You shame your own pain in the name of growth.
So your body does what it has always done. It protects you. It numbs out. It tightens. It dissociates. It smiles while your eyes go empty.
Now your partner can’t find you. You can’t find yourself. But you can still quote a podcast perfectly.
Spiritual bypassing isn’t a character flaw. It’s a survival strategy. It’s what happens when your early life gave you more pain than you had support to process, and somewhere along the way you discovered that “meaning” hurts less than feeling. 
You turned your heartbreak into a philosophy so you wouldn’t have to feel it alone.
So what does real healing look like?
It doesn’t look glamorous. It doesn’t always look enlightened. It often looks like:
You sitting on the edge of the bed saying, “I feel small and stupid right now and I hate that I feel this way, but I don’t want to hide it from you.”
You pausing mid argument and saying, “Under all this logic, I’m actually terrified you don’t like me.”
You catching yourself about to say, “Just let it go,” and instead saying, “Tell me more. I want to understand why this cuts so deep.”
You noticing that you’re about to float up into ideas and choosing, instead, to drop into your body. Feel your feet. Feel your chest. Feel your throat. Let the feeling get 3 percent louder than your analysis.
It looks like bringing your spirituality down out of the clouds and into your voice, your tears, your shaky hands, your real-time honesty.
Healthy spirituality never erases your humanity. It sits on the floor with it. It keeps you company inside what hurts until you’re not alone there.
If you want to stop spiritually bypassing in love, start here:
When you feel the urge to offer a lesson, try offering presence. When you feel the urge to fix, try saying, “That sounds awful. I’m right here.” When you feel the urge to rise above, try dropping down instead.
Let your practice deepen your capacity to feel, not your ability to escape.
Because in the end, the relationship that will change your life isn’t the one where nobody ever hurts. It’s the one where both of you can say:
“I see your pain. I feel my own. I won’t use God, the universe, or any teaching to avoid sitting with you in this.”
That kind of love is spiritual. And there’s nothing bypassed about it. See less

You’ve got to separate two very different things.
Your hard day.
And how you bring it to your partner.
They are not the same thing.
And confusing them is one of the fastest ways couples hurt each other without meaning to.
Having a hard day is real.
Wanting to be heard is human.
Needing comfort is not wrong.
But the *way* you express it can either invite connection…
or turn your partner into a threat.
Here’s what often happens:
You come home overwhelmed.
Your body’s still carrying stress, frustration, disappointment, or hurt.
You don’t pause to unload it internally.
You don’t name what you actually need.
So it comes out sideways.
Tone sharpens.
Words get clipped.
Energy gets heavy.
Your partner feels attacked before they even know what’s wrong.
And now something tragic happens.
You think you’re saying,
“I’ve had a hard day and I need to be heard.”
Your partner hears,
“You’re the problem now.”
So they defend.
Or withdraw.
Or explain.
Or shut down.
And suddenly your hard day turns into a hard night…
and now the relationship is bleeding for something it didn’t cause.
Here’s the truth most of us were never taught:
**Your pain is valid.
Your need to be heard is valid.
But your partner is not responsible for absorbing your unprocessed emotion.**
That doesn’t mean you have to be perfect.
It means you have to be conscious.
It sounds like this:
“I had a hard day and I’m carrying a lot.”
“I don’t need fixing right now.”
“I just need you to hear me.”
“I’m not mad at you.”
That separation changes everything.
Now your partner can relax.
Now they can open.
Now they can actually show up for you.
Because when your pain is named without being aimed,
love stays safe.
Relationships don’t break because people have hard days.
They break when stress gets delivered as blame
and closeness gets sacrificed for relief.
You don’t have to swallow your feelings.
You just have to own them.
Separate your experience
from your expression.
That’s how being heard turns into being held. See less

Here’s the difficult part of loving someone.
One moment of invalidation
can outweigh a hundred loving ones.
One careless sentence.
One cold look.
One sigh that says “you’re too much.”
One moment where you turn away instead of toward.
And suddenly *that* is what your partner’s body remembers about you.
Not your effort.
Not your loyalty.
Not the years.
Not the way you showed up yesterday.
Just the moment you made them feel small.
Alone.
Unimportant.
Unsafe.
This isn’t fair.
But it’s how attachment works.
Your partner’s nervous system is not keeping a balanced scorecard.
It’s asking one ruthless question:
“Am I safe with you when it matters?”
And when the answer feels like no, even once, the body takes notes.
That’s why one dismissal can echo louder than a thousand “I love yous.”
That’s why one moment of meanness can make your partner pull back for weeks.
That’s why they suddenly seem distant and you don’t understand why.
It’s not punishment.
It’s protection.
And this is where couples get it wrong.
They argue the *fact* instead of repairing the *impact*.
“I didn’t mean it.”
“That’s not what I said.”
“You’re focusing on the wrong thing.”
“You know I love you.”
None of that helps.
Because love doesn’t survive on intent.
It survives on **goodwill**.
Goodwill is the invisible emotional cushion in a relationship.
It’s what allows your partner to say,
“That hurt, but I trust you.”
“That wasn’t okay, but I know your heart.”
“I’m upset, but I’m still here.”
When goodwill is strong, mistakes don’t become character assassinations.
When goodwill is thin, every rupture feels like proof.
And here’s the part couples don’t want to face:
You don’t build goodwill when things are calm.
You build it in the moments when you’re irritated, tired, triggered, or scared.
You build it when you choose:
* repair over being right
* softness over sarcasm
* curiosity over defense
* accountability over explanation
Because the truth is, you *will* mess up.
You *will* say something sharp.
You *will* miss the moment.
And when you do, goodwill is the only thing standing between
a painful moment
and a lasting wound.
If your partner seems overly affected by “one little thing,”
don’t minimize it.
That “one thing” landed on their heart.
Love isn’t about never hurting each other.
That’s a fantasy.
Love is about building so much goodwill
that when you hurt each other
the relationship can still remember who you are
instead of assuming the worst.
If you want your partner to stay close,
protect goodwill like your relationship depends on it.
Because it does. See less

THE TRUTH ANXIOUS PARTNERS ALMOST NEVER HEAR
(The version that speaks directly to the part of you that reaches)
Anxious partners don’t reach because they’re needy.
They reach because disconnection feels like suffocation.
You feel it in your chest first.
That tightening.
That ache.
That sudden awareness that something is off.
Your partner goes quiet and your body panics.
Their tone shifts and your mind starts racing.
They say, “I just need some space,” and your nervous system hears,
“I’m about to be left.”
You’re not trying to control your partner.
You’re trying to restore safety.
But no one sees that.
They see your questions and call them pressure.
They see your emotions and call them drama.
They see your need for reassurance and label it insecurity.
What they don’t see is the free fall inside you.
Because when you’re anxious, love doesn’t feel like comfort.
Love feels like something you could lose at any second.
Closeness is oxygen.
Distance is threat.
So when your partner pulls back, your body doesn’t wait for logic.
It reacts.
You ask more questions.
You seek clarity.
You try to talk it through.
You press for reassurance.
You raise the volume of connection because silence feels unbearable.
And then you’re told you’re too much.
Their withdrawal feels like rejection.
Their calm feels like indifference.
Their space feels like abandonment.
So you protest.
Not because you want to fight.
But because you want to matter.
Here’s the painful part that’s hard to face:
Your urgency can create the very distance you’re terrified of.
You think talking more will bring closeness.
Sometimes it overwhelms your partner and pushes them further away.
You think explaining your feelings will help them understand.
Sometimes it lands as criticism instead of vulnerability.
You think staying emotionally present at all costs will save the bond.
Sometimes it floods the room with fear instead of safety.
That doesn’t make you wrong.
It makes you unprotected.
Your nervous system learned long ago that connection can disappear.
So it watches constantly.
It tracks shifts.
It scans for danger.
It tries to prevent loss before it happens.
You’re not demanding.
You’re bracing.
You’re not clingy.
You’re terrified of being alone with your pain.
You’re not manipulative.
You’re trying to anchor the relationship when it feels like it’s slipping.
And underneath all of it is a very quiet truth:
You don’t need more words.
You need more safety.
You need to know that distance isn’t disappearance.
You need to know that silence isn’t abandonment.
You need to know that your partner is still emotionally reachable even when they need space.
There’s another version of you underneath the anxiety.
One that can wait when waiting doesn’t feel like punishment.
One that can soften when reassurance actually lands.
One that doesn’t have to chase closeness because it trusts it will return.
That version of you isn’t weak.
It just never learned how to feel safe in the pause.
And here’s the shift:
You don’t have to stop feeling.
You don’t have to become less emotional.
You don’t have to pretend you don’t care.
You just have to separate fear from pursuit.
One breath before you ask again.
One sentence that names fear instead of demanding reassurance.
One moment where you let yourself feel the panic without handing it to your partner to fix.
These tiny shifts change everything.
You don’t need to disappear.
But you don’t need to chase either.
Your partner isn’t asking you to stop needing.
They’re asking to feel chosen, not cornered.
Connection doesn’t grow from urgency.
It grows from presence that trusts it won’t be abandoned.
You’re not broken.
You’re activated.
You’re not too much.
You’re scared.
Let someone meet you in the fear, not the chase.
That’s the doorway out of the cycle.

That ache.

That sudden awareness that something is off.

Your partner goes quiet and your body panics.

Their tone shifts and your mind starts racing.

They say, “I just need some space,” and your nervous system hears,

“I’m about to be left.”

You’re not trying to control your partner.

You’re trying to restore safety.

But no one sees that.

They see your questions and call them pressure.

They see your emotions and call them drama.

They see your need for reassurance and label it insecurity.

What they don’t see is the free fall inside you.

Because when you’re anxious, love doesn’t feel like comfort.

Love feels like something you could lose at any second.

Closeness is oxygen.

Distance is threat.

So when your partner pulls back, your body doesn’t wait for logic.

It reacts.

You ask more questions.

You seek clarity.

You try to talk it through.

You press for reassurance.

You raise the volume of connection because silence feels unbearable.

And then you’re told you’re too much.

Their withdrawal feels like rejection.

Their calm feels like indifference.

Their space feels like abandonment.

So you protest.

Not because you want to fight.

But because you want to matter.

Here’s the painful part that’s hard to face:

Your urgency can create the very distance you’re terrified of.

You think talking more will bring closeness.

Sometimes it overwhelms your partner and pushes them further away.

You think explaining your feelings will help them understand.

Sometimes it lands as criticism instead of vulnerability.

You think staying emotionally present at all costs will save the bond.

Sometimes it floods the room with fear instead of safety.

That doesn’t make you wrong.

It makes you unprotected.

Your nervous system learned long ago that connection can disappear.

So it watches constantly.

It tracks shifts.

It scans for danger.

It tries to prevent loss before it happens.

You’re not demanding.

You’re bracing.

You’re not clingy.

You’re terrified of being alone with your pain.

You’re not manipulative.

You’re trying to anchor the relationship when it feels like it’s slipping.

And underneath all of it is a very quiet truth:

You don’t need more words.

You need more safety.

You need to know that distance isn’t disappearance.

You need to know that silence isn’t abandonment.

You need to know that your partner is still emotionally reachable even when they need space.

There’s another version of you underneath the anxiety.

One that can wait when waiting doesn’t feel like punishment.

One that can soften when reassurance actually lands.

One that doesn’t have to chase closeness because it trusts it will return.

That version of you isn’t weak.

It just never learned how to feel safe in the pause.

And here’s the shift:

You don’t have to stop feeling.

You don’t have to become less emotional.

You don’t have to pretend you don’t care.

You just have to separate fear from pursuit.

One breath before you ask again.

One sentence that names fear instead of demanding reassurance.

One moment where you let yourself feel the panic without handing it to your partner to fix.

These tiny shifts change everything.

You don’t need to disappear.

But you don’t need to chase either.

Your partner isn’t asking you to stop needing.

They’re asking to feel chosen, not cornered.

Connection doesn’t grow from urgency.

It grows from presence that trusts it won’t be abandoned.

You’re not broken.

You’re activated.

You’re not too much.

You’re scared.

Let someone meet you in the fear, not the chase.

That’s the doorway out of the cycle.
