How Do I Know When To Leave A Relationship?
My client Letisha is in an abusive relationship.
And if that was all a person needed to know to leave, everybody would at the first signs of abuse.
But Letisha chose Ben as her partner.
She has been struggling for 3 years to leave.
What does Ben do that is abusive?
He threatens to leave her, with the feeling of vengeance in his voice, every time they have any argument, even if it's a tiny one.
Letisha believes that Ben "gets off" on how much she suffers when he threatens her.
As a marriage counselor, I learned long ago not to diagnose any man or woman with a label.
He's abusive.
She's codependent.
He's a liar.
She's manipulative.
He's a control freak.
She's narcissistic.
This list goes on and on, and is irrelevant.
Ben threatened to leave Letisha on their fourth date, 14 years ago.
And that's when Letisha signed up to play this game.
Letisha did the following, from the fourth date up until now, 14 years later, when Ben threatened her:
1) She argued with him about it.
2) She called him an asshole.
3) She threatened to leave him first.
4) She begged him not to leave.
5) She got caught talking poorly about him to his friends, and to his father.
6) She criticized him over 100 times (she emailed me a list of 100 criticisms, and put a fancy watermark on it that said "Proof This Man Is Abusive.")
7) She cried, but when he asked her about it, she attacked.
This list could also go on and on.
The list above BINDS HER TO HIM with Krazy Glue.
She cannot escape this awful pattern between them because when she argues and fights, she leaves every time with more doubt and guilt and confusion.
There is only one way to know the truth of this situation.
There is only one way to feel 100% clear that it is time to leave Ben.
And that's by doing one thing.
Okay.
Three things.
Vulnerability.
And then Silence.
And then Witnessing.
VULNERABILITY:
"I get so scared when you tell me you're going to leave me.
It's been happening for a long time, and I've been fighting and fighting about it with you.
I've never really just sat here and looked into your eyes and told you that it feels like I die inside each time you say this to me.
I'm so hurt and angry that I've let this go on for so long, and I believe I've probably spent years doing mean things to you because I didn't know what else to do.
I am terrified that you're going to leave, but I'm more terrified to just be honest and tell you how much I hurt inside all the time anticipating that this same argument will happen.
I'm sorry I've contributed to this fight in any ways that may have hurt you."
SILENCE:
Letisha has to now do nothing.
Bite her tongue.
NO MATTER what Ben does next, she needs to not engage in any fight about this topic.
There are no details to discuss.
She told him what it does to her, with tears pouring down her face (she did this in front of me and Ben).
It's painful for Letisha to not get hooked back into convincing him of things, and doing all the 7 items above.
Quiet time.
WITNESSING:
There is an unspecified amount of time need to see who Ben wants to now become.
Maybe one day.
Maybe one month.
She needs to wait to see what he says next.
Or possibly the next 5 things he says next on 5 different days.
She needs to slow down until something meaningful comes out of Ben's mouth.
Letisha and Ben did not come to see me for 2 months.
I thought the whole thing failed and that they quit counseling with me.
Ben was secretly going to a counselor for those 2 months.
I don't know what counselor he saw, but he did not say his first words to Letisha until the 2 months had passed.
Then they came to see me.
He said the right things to her.
Her vulnerability disarmed his ability to attack further.
He had no idea she even loved him anymore.
He threatened to leave to try to get attention from her.
After further work with me, Ben knows how to get attention from her by asking.
They cancelled their legal separation, and they are currently in Hawaii taking a honeymoon they never took.
Letisha did not have to leave Ben because he was abusive.
I did not diagnose Ben as being abusive, and taught Letisha to stop labeling him as abusive.
Her vulnerability stopped the whole pattern.
And if Ben did not recognize his part, and Letisha was able to do the silence and witnessing well, then she would have been able to leave him, without guilt or confusion.
But she didn't need to.
People leave relationships in other ways, but this method is direct, takes little time, and preserves the heart of the person leaving.
If you want to see who the person in front of you really is, you must learn vulnerability, or else you're diagnosing them, judging them, and arguing with them.
And it will take a really long time to leave. See less

There’s a moment in every distressed relationship that changes everything.
It’s not when someone yells.
It’s not when someone cries.
It’s not even when someone walks away.
It’s the moment one person says, in words or in energy,
“Just leave me alone.”
And the other person hears,
“I will not connect with you.”
“Not now.”
“Go away.”
That’s not a boundary.
That’s a nervous system shutting the door.
Here’s what people don’t understand about that moment.
The person asking for space isn’t trying to be cruel.
They’re overwhelmed beyond their capacity.
Their body is flooded.
Their heart is buried under panic, shame, fear, and overload.
And the person reaching for connection isn’t trying to be needy.
They’re trying to survive the terror of disconnection.
They’re offering their most vulnerable, open-hearted self.
And it’s landing on someone who literally cannot feel it.
So one partner shows vulnerability.
The other feels nothing.
Not because they don’t care.
But because their system is maxed out.
This is where couples break.
Because one person thinks,
“I finally opened my heart and you still didn’t move.”
And the other thinks,
“I’m drowning and you keep asking me to swim toward you.”
Both are right.
And both are alone.
This is the moment where love doesn’t die.
It goes offline.
The compassion that’s needed can’t happen yet.
The reassurance that would save the moment isn’t available.
The tenderness that could heal the wound is locked behind overwhelm.
And then something tragic happens.
The vulnerable partner starts believing,
“My pain doesn’t matter.”
The overwhelmed partner starts believing,
“I can’t do this. I’ll never get it right.”
That’s when couples stop fighting about the dishwasher.
And start fighting about survival.
This is the work nobody teaches.
Not how to talk better.
Not how to argue less.
Not how to explain more clearly.
But how to sit in that brutal space where one heart is open and the other is flooded.
How to slow the moment down before it becomes permanent damage.
How to help one partner feel safe enough to feel.
And the other feel seen enough to stop screaming for connection.
Because the real heartbreak isn’t conflict.
It’s when vulnerability meets overwhelm
and both people walk away believing they’re the problem.
They’re not.
They’re just two nervous systems trying to survive love.

Imagine meeting someone who wanted to learn your past not to punish you, but to understand how you needed to be loved.
That's a powerful statement that cuts right to the heart of what real intimacy looks like. Most people dig into your history to build a case against you. To collect evidence for why you're broken or difficult or wrong.
But imagine someone who looks at your wounds and thinks "Oh, now I understand why you flinch when I raise my voice" instead of "You're too sensitive."
Someone who learns that your dad left when you were eight and thinks "No wonder you panic when I'm quiet" instead of "You're clingy."
That's the difference between punishment and understanding. Between using your past as ammunition or as a roadmap to your heart.
Most relationships die because people weaponize each other's histories. The right person sees your scars and learns how to love you better because of them, not despite them. See less

If you’re trying to prove anything in your relationship, you’re already in trouble.
Prove you’re trustworthy.
Prove you won’t do it again.
Prove how much you love them.
Prove you’re loyal.
Prove you’re ready for commitment.
Prove you can handle monogamy.
All of that sounds mature.
All of that sounds responsible.
All of that sounds like growth.
And almost all of it is coming from the wrong place.
Because proving is an intellectual strategy.
Love is not.
Proving lives in your head.
Connection lives in your nervous system.
You can explain forever why you’re different now.
You can outline rules, agreements, contracts, timelines, expectations.
You can swear you’ll never cross that line again.
You can promise the future with perfect words.
And none of that reaches the place where trust actually lives.
Trust doesn’t live in logic.
It lives in your partner’s body.
Trust is not built when someone understands you.
Trust is built when someone feels safe with you.
That’s why the moment you start working hard to prove something, your relationship is already telling you the truth.
It’s telling you that safety isn’t there yet.
And here’s the part nobody wants to hear.
If you’re having to negotiate monogamy, you’re already late.
Not because monogamy is impossible.
But because when a relationship is truly ready for it, it doesn’t need to be argued into existence.
The human heart doesn’t arrive at commitment through contracts.
It arrives through resonance.
It arrives through the felt experience of being chosen without pressure.
Of being seen without performance.
Of being held without fear that you’ll disappear.
You don’t decide to be faithful with your mouth.
You decide with your nervous system.
When you feel safe.
When you feel connected.
When you feel known.
When you feel valued without having to audition.
That’s when monogamy becomes natural.
Not forced.
Not negotiated.
Not proven.
Not defended.
Just lived.
This is why so many couples get it backward.
They think the rules create safety.
They think the agreements create trust.
They think the words create commitment.
But it’s the opposite.
Safety creates trust.
Trust creates commitment.
Commitment makes the rules unnecessary.
When a relationship is truly alive, you don’t need to prove you’re loyal.
You’re loyal because you don’t want anywhere else to go.
When a relationship is truly safe, you don’t need to prove you love them.
They feel it when you walk in the room.
When a relationship is truly connected, you don’t need to promise the future.
The future is already being built in how you treat each other today.
Proving is what we do when we’re scared we won’t be chosen.
Explaining is what we do when we’re scared we’ll be misunderstood.
Negotiating is what we do when we’re scared the bond isn’t strong enough to hold.
And none of that is wrong.
But it’s information.
If you’re trying to prove you’re trustworthy, it means trust is broken.
If you’re trying to prove you won’t leave, it means safety is shaky.
If you’re trying to prove you’re committed, it means connection is fragile.
So don’t shame yourself for proving.
Just understand what it’s pointing to.
It’s pointing to the place that actually needs attention.
Not your words.
Not your promises.
Not your agreements.
Your presence.
Your consistency.
Your emotional availability.
Your willingness to be seen when you’d rather perform.
Because in the end, the human heart doesn’t believe what you say.
It believes what it feels when it’s with you.
And no amount of proof can replace that. See less

A missed text.
A look that lingered a second too long.

Human things.

She felt unseen.

She didn’t push because she wanted control.

The truth about why you keep choosing people who hurt you the same way your parents did:
When you weren't seen as a child, your body learned what "love" feels like:
• Trying desperately to be heard
• Never quite mattering enough
• Always almost getting what you need
• Being told you're "too sensitive"
So now your nervous system only recognizes "love" when it feels exactly like that.
The person who listens? Boring.
The one who's consistent? No chemistry.
The partner who actually sees you? Something must be wrong with them.
But that person who's just distant enough? Just critical enough? Just unavailable enough?
Your whole body lights up: "THIS IS IT. THIS IS LOVE."
Then you spend years trying to get from them what you couldn't get from mom or dad. And when they can't give it (because you chose them SPECIFICALLY for their inability to give it), you point and say: "See? Nobody understands me."
You're not crazy. You're brilliant. Your nervous system is doing EXACTLY what it learned to do - finding the familiar and calling it home.
Here's what breaks my heart:
You push away the very people who could heal you because your body literally cannot recognize safety.
It thinks love is supposed to hurt. It thinks you're supposed to chase.
It thinks "almost but not quite" is what connection feels like.
Until you see this pattern, REALLY see it, you'll keep proving yourself right that nobody cares.
But you're not broken.
You're just speaking the wrong language of love.
The person you need isn't another one who makes you work for crumbs.
It's someone whose consistency feels so foreign that your body wants to run.
That's how you know you're finally choosing different. See less

You know the feeling.
Not in your head.
In your gut.
That quiet, unmistakable knowing that something has expired… even though no one’s said it out loud yet.
A relationship doesn’t end the day someone leaves.
It ends the day your body stops believing repair is possible.
You can feel it when the conversations start looping instead of opening.
When every effort feels heavier instead of hopeful.
When trying harder only makes you more tired, not more connected.
That’s when people get confused.
They think they’re failing because they’re giving up.
But most of the time, they’re not giving up.
They’re finally listening.
Listening to the part of them that’s been saying for months, sometimes years,
“I can’t keep jumping hurdles just to feel okay with the person who’s supposed to feel like home.”
Here’s the truth nobody wants to say out loud.
Some relationships don’t die from one big betrayal.
They die from emotional exhaustion.
From trying to fix everything.
From explaining yourself one more time.
From hoping this conversation will finally be different.
Until one day your nervous system just… stops believing.
And when you reach that place, letting go isn’t cruelty.
It’s mercy.
Mercy for the part of you that’s been trying to survive instead of live.
Mercy for the heart that’s been carrying more than it should have to.
You don’t have to hate someone to outgrow the relationship.
You don’t have to demonize them to leave.
You don’t have to prove they’re bad to admit that this isn’t good anymore.
Sometimes the bravest thing you’ll ever do
is stop trying to resurrect something
that your body already knows has ended.
Not every ending is a failure.
Some endings are the moment you finally stop abandoning yourself. See less

When your relationship is struggling, it’s actually far more dangerous than most people realize.
Not dangerous in the dramatic, obvious way.
Dangerous in the slow way.
The quiet way.
The way that changes you while you’re still telling yourself you’re fine.
Because most people think relationship pain is an emotional problem.
It’s not.
It’s a biological problem.
A nervous system problem.
A survival problem.
You weren’t built to simply exist next to another person.
You were built to bond.
To attach.
To give care and receive care.
To feel the relief of being held in someone’s mind.
Love is not a hobby.
Love is a system.
It’s why we survived.
There were nearly twenty species that once walked upright like we do.
Stronger bodies than ours.
Better hunters than us.
More physically dominant than us.
And yet only one made it.
Not because we were stronger.
Not because we were faster.
But because Homo sapiens learned how to bond in larger groups.
We learned how to cooperate.
We learned how to care beyond the immediate moment.
We learned how to build trust, emotional alliance, and repair after rupture.
That’s what beat raw strength.
So when your closest bond is breaking down, it’s not just sad.
It’s not just stressful.
It’s a direct contradiction of what your body is built to do.
And here’s the part that gets under people’s skin once they really see it:
In a struggling relationship, it’s not only that your needs aren’t being met.
It’s that you can’t give love the way you’re wired to give it.
People talk about being unloved like it’s the main injury.
It’s not.
The injury is that you become unable to love freely.
You become unable to offer your natural care without it turning into a fight.
You start holding back your tenderness.
You start rationing your generosity.
You start pausing before you do the kind thing, not because you’re cold, but because you’re tired of it being used against you.
You stop reaching.
Not because you stopped loving.
Because reaching became dangerous.
And this is what makes relationship distress so devastating.
When your partner is someone you once wanted to give everything to, and now you have to protect yourself from them, your biology goes into conflict.
Your body is running two opposing programs at once.
Program one says: bond, connect, soften, care, repair.
Program two says: brace, defend, scan, keep score, don’t be stupid.
That internal clash is exhausting.
And most people never name it.
They just slowly become a smaller version of themselves.
They become a version that doesn’t laugh as easily.
Doesn’t trust their own instincts.
Doesn’t feel confident.
Doesn’t feel safe being fully alive.
They become someone who’s constantly thinking about their partner, but not in the beautiful way.
They think about their partner like a threat map.
What mood are they in today?
What did I do wrong?
What’s coming next?
How do I avoid the next conflict?
How do I get through dinner without it turning into something?
Even if you only fight twice a month, your nervous system is fighting every day.
Because unresolved conflict doesn’t end when the conversation ends.
It keeps going in your body.
It replays in the shower.
It replays in the car.
It replays when you see their name pop up on your phone.
It replays when you hear their footsteps in the hallway.
It’s like living with a low grade alarm system that never turns off.
And then people wonder why they can’t sleep.
Why they snap at their kids.
Why they can’t focus at work.
Why they don’t feel joy like they used to.
Why they feel numb.
Numb isn’t nothing.
Numb is a shutdown.
Numb is what happens when your system has had too much.
And if you want proof that care isn’t optional for humans, you don’t even need adult psychology.
You can look at infants.
Researchers show a three-month-old baby two puppets.
One puppet helps another puppet with a problem.
The other puppet refuses.
No words.
No moral lecture.
No life experience.
And the baby almost always chooses the helper.
Three months old.
That means something in us is born already oriented toward care.
We are wired to move toward the one who helps.
We are wired to prefer kindness.
We are wired to detect safety and cooperation as if our life depends on it.
Because it does.
So what happens when the person you’re closest to becomes the person you can’t relax around?
What happens when the person who should be your safe place becomes the person your body braces for?
This is why distressed relationships don’t just hurt your feelings.
They change your identity.
Because your identity is tied to your bonding system.
You become who you are in the presence of your closest attachment.
If you’re constantly criticized, you internalize it.
If you’re constantly ignored, you internalize it.
If you’re constantly walking on eggshells, you internalize it.
And people are taught all this garbage like,
don’t take it personally,
just focus on yourself,
it’s their opinion,
it’s none of your business what someone thinks of you.
That is not how attachment works.
If the person whose love you depend on is consistently unkind, you don’t get to just rise above it.
Your system absorbs it.
It goes into your bloodstream.
It goes into your breath.
It goes into how your eyes look when you look in the mirror.
And the most tragic part is this:
In a distressed relationship, both people usually still have the instinct to care.
They just can’t access it.
Or they access it for ten seconds, and then pain hijacks them.
One person reaches with criticism.
The other person protects with distance.
One person begs for contact by pushing.
The other person begs for safety by withdrawing.
And both of them are losing the thing they were built for.
Not sex.
Not romance.
Not date nights.
Care.
Simple, human, obvious care.
The kind of care that makes you feel like you exist in someone’s mind.
So when you’re in a fight and you don’t know how to solve it, please don’t minimize it.
It isn’t just a bad conversation.
It’s your biology trying to find a way back to safety.
And the reason this matters so much is because you don’t get unlimited years to live in this state without it costing you.
It costs you your softness.
It costs you your patience.
It costs you your openness.
It costs you your hope.
And eventually, it costs you your ability to feel love without fear.
That’s why a struggling relationship is dangerous.
Because it doesn’t just make you unhappy.
It interrupts the most human thing about you.
You were built to bond.
You were built to give care and receive care.
And when your closest bond becomes a place you cannot safely do that, your system knows something is wrong.
Long before your mind admits it.
That’s why this is urgent.
Not because you’re broken.
Because love is oxygen.
And you can’t thrive while you’re holding your breath. See less

They don’t look like they’re drowning.
That’s what makes it so hard to understand.
The avoidant pain isn’t loud.
It isn’t dramatic.
It isn’t messy.
It’s quiet.
Contained.
Invisible.
And that’s exactly why no one believes how heavy it is.
The avoidant doesn’t pull away because they don’t care.
They pull away because caring feels like too much to carry.
Every emotional need feels like another wave.
Every conflict feels like proof they’re failing.
Every moment of closeness feels like pressure they can’t survive.
So they go still.
They go silent.
They go inward.
Not because they’re cold.
Because their nervous system is screaming,
“I can’t breathe in here.”
This is the part nobody sees.
While the anxious partner panics out loud,
The avoidant panics in secret.
One begs for connection.
The other begs for space.
Both are terrified.
Both are exhausted.
Both feel misunderstood.
And both walk away thinking,
“If I were different, maybe love wouldn’t hurt this much.”
But here’s the truth.
Avoidants aren’t running from love.
They’re running from the feeling that love will cost them themselves.
They learned early that needing was dangerous.
That depending meant disappointment.
That being seen meant being overwhelmed.
So now, even when love shows up safe,
Their body still braces like the flood is coming.
If you’re avoidant, hear this.
You’re not heartless.
You’re not broken.
You’re not incapable of intimacy.
You’re someone who learned to survive by staying afloat alone.
And now you’re trying to learn how to let someone hold you without sinking.
The healing isn’t forcing yourself to need more.
It’s learning that closeness doesn’t have to drown you.
That love can feel steady, not suffocating.
That you don’t have to disappear to stay safe.
And one day, you won’t have to choose between freedom and connection.
You’ll finally learn you can breathe in both.

A bill gets paid late.
Eighteen dollars.
That’s it.
And if your relationship is already distressed, that tiny fee doesn’t stay tiny.
It ignites a universe.
Not because you’re dramatic.
Not because you’re “bad at communication.”
Not because one of you is “too sensitive.”
Because a romantic relationship isn’t two minds exchanging information.
It’s two nervous systems touching.
And once the bond gets less safe, everything becomes a threat.
The $18 isn’t the problem.
The $18 is the match.
And the fire is older than the fee.
It’s the look your partner gives you when they’re disappointed.
It’s the tone you hear that says, “Here we go again.”
It’s the split second where your body decides you’re about to be blamed, or abandoned, or seen as incompetent, or not cared about.
So you don’t react to the fee.
You react to the meaning.
And then you do what humans do when meaning hurts.
You protect.
You get sharp.
You get cold.
You get loud.
You get quiet.
You get logical.
You get moral.
You get sarcastic.
You get “fine.”
And the tragedy is this:
Most couples think they’re fighting about the bill.
They’re actually fighting about what happens inside them when they feel alone with pain.
Because that’s the real crisis in love.
Not pain.
Not conflict.
Not mistakes.
The real crisis is when pain shows up and neither of you knows how to hold it without making the other person the enemy.
So the fee turns into a fight.
The fight turns into a story.
The story turns into a file folder in your brain labeled:
“Here’s why I can’t trust you.”
“Here’s why you’re unsafe.”
“Here’s why I’m alone.”
“Here’s why love doesn’t work.”
And then the relationship starts dying by paperwork.
One moment at a time.
This is why couples don’t fall apart from one big event.
They fall apart from a thousand small moments where one of them is hurting and the other one doesn’t know what to do with it.
A late fee.
A forgotten text.
A sigh.
A slammed cabinet.
A “Whatever.”
A long pause.
A look away.
And every time, the same thing happens.
Not on the surface.
In the body.
Your chest tightens.
Your stomach drops.
Your throat closes.
Your mind speeds up.
You start building a case instead of building a bridge.
And what’s wild is how early this pattern shows itself.
The same couple that collapses under the grief of losing a child… didn’t start collapsing at the funeral.
They started collapsing at the $18.
They started collapsing at the moment they didn’t know how to say, “I’m overwhelmed” without sounding like blame.
They started collapsing at the moment they didn’t know how to respond to overwhelm without defending.
This is what nobody wants to admit:
Words won’t save you once the bond is scared.
Words are late.
Words come after your body has already decided.
Psychology is obsessed with explanations and interpretations and “communication.”
But your nervous system doesn’t care about your explanation.
It cares whether you are safe.
It cares whether your partner’s pain has room to exist without punishment.
It cares whether you can be near emotion without turning it into war.
That’s why the beginning of repair isn’t a better sentence.
It’s a different state.
Breathing that actually changes your physiology.
Slowing down enough to feel the panic in your own body before you export it onto your partner.
Learning to stay present with their discomfort without trying to fix it, dismiss it, or prove them wrong.
Not because you’re becoming “spiritual.”
Because you’re becoming real.
Because your body is where the truth lives.
And if you’ve never learned this, please hear this gently:
You’re not failing.
You’re untrained.
You were taught to talk.
You weren’t taught to regulate in the presence of someone else’s pain.
You weren’t taught how to stay soft when you feel accused.
You weren’t taught how to stay close when you feel ashamed.
You weren’t taught how to be a safe place while your own body is screaming for safety.
So you do what most couples do.
You try to solve emotion with words.
And you keep wondering why it keeps getting worse.
Here’s the shift that changes everything:
When your partner is upset, don’t start with the topic.
Start with the universe.
Start with the body.
Start with one breath that says, “I’m here.”
Start with the courage to ask one question that your relationship has been starving for:
“What’s happening inside you right now?”
Not “What did I do wrong?”
Not “Why are you like this?”
Not “Can we just move on?”
But:
“What’s happening inside you… and can I be with you there?”
Because that’s the beginning of a relationship that survives.
Not the absence of pain.
But the presence of a partner who can sit beside pain without making it a courtroom.
And if you can do that with eighteen dollars…
You can do it with anything.
That’s the whole point.
That’s the whole universe. See less

Dear trauma,
I don’t like how you sabotage my relationships.
I don’t like how you sneak into moments that are supposed to feel safe and turn them into something heavy.
I don’t like how you show up even when I’ve done everything “right.”
Read the books.
Learned the language.
Studied my triggers.
Practiced the insight.
And still, there you are.
I can understand you intellectually and still feel powerless when you take over my body.
I can know exactly what’s happening and still not know how to stop it.
I can take responsibility for my reactions and still feel like I’m watching myself fall into the same patterns I promised I’d outgrow.
That’s the part no one prepares you for.
That healing doesn’t mean you stop being triggered.
It means you become painfully aware of how triggered you are while it’s happening.
And some days, that feels worse.
I don’t like how even when I love people, even when I feel good with them, even when something beautiful is happening, you whisper your old prophecy into my nervous system.
This won’t last.
They’ll leave.
Something will ruin this.
Don’t get too comfortable.
Don’t get too attached.
So I grieve before anything is gone.
I grieve in advance.
I grieve the ending of moments that are still happening.
I grieve the loss of people who are still right in front of me.
I grieve futures that haven’t even had the chance to breathe yet.
Sometimes I think I’m grieving my childhood.
Sometimes I think I’m grieving the parts of me that never got to feel safe enough to relax into joy.
Sometimes I think I’m grieving the version of myself I wish I could be, the one who can feel happy without bracing for impact.
I’m tired of how you turn love into vigilance.
I’m tired of how you make closeness feel like something I have to manage instead of something I get to receive.
I’m tired of how you turn tenderness into a countdown clock.
And I’m especially tired of how lonely this makes me feel.
Because from the outside, it looks like I’m strong.
It looks like I’m insightful.
It looks like I’m healed.
But inside, I’m constantly negotiating with fear.
Constantly reminding myself that the present moment isn’t a threat.
Constantly trying to convince my body that safety doesn’t always end in disaster.
People think trauma is about the past.
They don’t understand it’s about the future you’re always afraid of losing.
They don’t see how exhausting it is to love with one foot already braced for the fall.
They don’t see how brave it actually is to keep opening your heart when your entire nervous system learned that love disappears.
So dear trauma, here’s the truth I’m finally learning how to say to you.
You made sense once.
You protected me when I had no other protection.
You taught me how to survive when I didn’t know how to feel safe.
But you don’t get to run my love life forever.
You don’t get to decide how much joy I’m allowed to feel.
You don’t get to decide how close I’m allowed to get.
You don’t get to turn every good moment into a rehearsal for loss.
I may still feel you.
I may still hear you.
I may still struggle with you.
But I’m learning something you never taught me.
That grief doesn’t have to live in advance.
That love doesn’t have to be paid for in fear.
That happiness doesn’t always come with a bill.
And that maybe being “normal” isn’t about never hurting.
Maybe it’s about learning how to let yourself be happy without apologizing for it.
Even when you’re scared.
Even when you’re trembling.
Even when you don’t fully trust the ground beneath you yet.
I’m still here.
I’m still loving.
I’m still choosing connection.
And this time, trauma, you don’t get to be the narrator of my story anymore. See less

Do you know what the biggest problem in relationships is today?
It’s not cheating, it’s not lack of commitment, and it’s not even communication. It’s something more invisible, and it’s shaping every modern love story.
We have never had more freedom in relationships, yet we have never had fewer relational skills.
We want to be deeply known, without ever saying who we really are. We want our partner to know how to love us, without ever explaining what love actually looks like to us.
We crave intimacy, but we avoid the friction that creates it.
I was listening to a therapist once who said something that shook me to my core. They called it social atrophy. The room went still because everyone felt the weight of those words.
We can date, work, shop, even leave a marriage without leaving our couch. We have removed friction from our lives, but the truth is, friction is the very thing that teaches us how to love.
Without it, we lose the muscle to navigate differences. We lose the tolerance for discomfort. We lose the ability to sit across from someone and say, “This is what I need, can you meet me here?”
And instead, we wait silently, secretly hoping our partner will read our minds, while quietly resenting them when they do not.
But here is the reality, your partner is not a mind reader. They are a person with their own wiring, their own story, their own way of understanding love. And unless you tell them how to love you, they are only guessing.
So no, the problem in your relationship is not that you don’t have enough love. The problem is that we have been sold the fantasy that closeness should not require effort. That if it is real, it should be easy. That if it is love, it should feel natural. That if it is meant to be, they should just know.
But real intimacy is not effortless, it is earned.
The most extraordinary relationships are not the ones that glide along without conflict. They are the ones that learn how to repair after rupture. They are the ones where two people are willing to sit in discomfort long enough to grow something deeper. They are the ones that expand because both partners choose honesty, vulnerability, and the courage to stay open.
We don’t need more chemistry, we need more capacity.
Capacity to tell the truth, capacity to hear the truth, capacity to stay in the fire of connection long enough to let it transform us.
That is where love becomes unshakable. See less

Regret
Regret doesn’t usually arrive with fireworks.
It sneaks in quietly, disguised as something small.
Something ordinary.
Something you barely notice in the moment.
It starts with the way you corrected your partner over the dishwasher.
Not because it really mattered.
Not because it was important.
But because you were tired, tense, a little irritated, and it felt easier to be right than to be kind.
So you pointed out the plates.
The cups.
The wrong order.
And in that tiny moment, you chose control over connection.
You don’t regret it that day.
You regret it later.
When you realize how many times you turned daily life into a performance review.
Then there’s the regret that feels even quieter.
The day you didn’t go on that hike.
You actually had the time.
You just didn’t take it.
You stayed busy.
You stayed distracted.
You stayed “productive.”
And the memory you didn’t make becomes heavier than the work you did.
You don’t regret it that night.
You regret it years later when you can’t remember what you were so busy doing, but you can remember exactly how your partner looked when they asked you to come.
Then there’s the regret that lands sharper.
The time you criticized your partner in front of their friends.
You didn’t mean to humiliate them.
You just wanted to make a point.
To get a laugh.
To feel justified.
And you watched the smile on their face fade just enough that you pretended not to see it.
You don’t regret it in the moment.
You regret it when you realize that safety dies in public first.
And then there are the regrets that come with silence.
All the times you didn’t say thank you.
All the times you assumed they knew you cared.
All the times you let resentment build instead of courage.
All the times you chose distance because closeness felt like too much work that day.
You don’t regret those moments individually.
You regret them collectively when you wake up one morning and realize the relationship feels colder, and you can’t remember when the warmth started slipping away.
Then there are the regrets that change the shape of your life.
The moment you say something in anger that you can’t take back.
The moment you break trust and tell yourself you’ll fix it later.
The moment you start confiding in someone else instead of the person who promised you their heart.
The moment you stand on the edge of betrayal and tell yourself you deserve this because you’ve been hurting too long.
You don’t regret it when you’re justifying it.
You regret it when the damage becomes real.
When you see what it does to the person who loved you.
When you see what it does to who you become afterward.
And then there’s the regret no one wants to talk about.
The day something tragic happens.
The phone call.
The diagnosis.
The accident.
The loss.
The day you would give anything to go back and undo every petty correction, every missed hike, every public criticism, every silent resentment, every harsh word.
The day you realize that repair is important, but awareness before damage is priceless.
Because regret isn’t just about what you did wrong.
It’s about what you didn’t do when you still had time.
It’s about the kindness you delayed.
The affection you withheld.
The patience you thought you’d give later.
The love you assumed would always be there to receive it.
So this isn’t a post about guilt.
It’s a post about consciousness.
About realizing that the smallest moments are training you for the biggest ones.
That the way you handle irritation today becomes the way you handle heartbreak tomorrow.
That the way you treat your partner in ordinary moments is exactly how you’ll remember yourself when everything is on the line.
Regret doesn’t start with betrayal.
It starts with the dishwasher.
With the hike you skipped.
With the joke that went too far.
With the moment you chose being right over being gentle.
And the good news is this.
You don’t have to wait for tragedy to change.
You don’t have to wait for loss to learn what matters.
You don’t have to live your life backward wishing you’d loved better.
You can choose now.
To speak softer.
To pause longer.
To correct less.
To appreciate more.
To love in the small moments like they’re sacred.
Because one day, they will be.
With your work, you're replaceable immediately in this world.
With your loved ones, there’s never going to be a replacement...
...for you. See less

But because you were tired, tense, a little irritated, and it felt easier to be right than to be kind.

So you pointed out the plates.

The cups.

The wrong order.

And in that tiny moment, you chose control over connection.

You don’t regret it that day.

You regret it later.

When you realize how many times you turned daily life into a performance review.

Then there’s the regret that feels even quieter.

The day you didn’t go on that hike.

You actually had the time.

You just didn’t take it.

You stayed busy.

You stayed distracted.

You stayed “productive.”

And the memory you didn’t make becomes heavier than the work you did.

You don’t regret it that night.

You regret it years later when you can’t remember what you were so busy doing, but you can remember exactly how your partner looked when they asked you to come.

Then there’s the regret that lands sharper.

The time you criticized your partner in front of their friends.

You didn’t mean to humiliate them.

You just wanted to make a point.

To get a laugh.

To feel justified.

And you watched the smile on their face fade just enough that you pretended not to see it.

You don’t regret it in the moment.

You regret it when you realize that safety dies in public first.

And then there are the regrets that come with silence.

All the times you didn’t say thank you.

All the times you assumed they knew you cared.

All the times you let resentment build instead of courage.

All the times you chose distance because closeness felt like too much work that day.

You don’t regret those moments individually.

You regret them collectively when you wake up one morning and realize the relationship feels colder, and you can’t remember when the warmth started slipping away.

Then there are the regrets that change the shape of your life.

The moment you say something in anger that you can’t take back.

The moment you break trust and tell yourself you’ll fix it later.

The moment you start confiding in someone else instead of the person who promised you their heart.

The moment you stand on the edge of betrayal and tell yourself you deserve this because you’ve been hurting too long.

You don’t regret it when you’re justifying it.

You regret it when the damage becomes real.

When you see what it does to the person who loved you.

When you see what it does to who you become afterward.

And then there’s the regret no one wants to talk about.

The day something tragic happens.

The phone call.

The diagnosis.

The accident.

The loss.

The day you would give anything to go back and undo every petty correction, every missed hike, every public criticism, every silent resentment, every harsh word.

The day you realize that repair is important, but awareness before damage is priceless.

Because regret isn’t just about what you did wrong.

It’s about what you didn’t do when you still had time.

It’s about the kindness you delayed.

The affection you withheld.

The patience you thought you’d give later.

The love you assumed would always be there to receive it.

So this isn’t a post about guilt.

It’s a post about consciousness.

About realizing that the smallest moments are training you for the biggest ones.

That the way you handle irritation today becomes the way you handle heartbreak tomorrow.

That the way you treat your partner in ordinary moments is exactly how you’ll remember yourself when everything is on the line.

Regret doesn’t start with betrayal.

It starts with the dishwasher.

With the hike you skipped.

With the joke that went too far.

With the moment you chose being right over being gentle.

And the good news is this.

You don’t have to wait for tragedy to change.

You don’t have to wait for loss to learn what matters.

You don’t have to live your life backward wishing you’d loved better.

You can choose now.

To speak softer.

To pause longer.

To correct less.

To appreciate more.

To love in the small moments like they’re sacred.

Because one day, they will be.

With your loved ones, there’s never going to be a replacement...

An attachment problem in a relationship ALWAYS has anxious-avoidant at its core. Tomorrow begins the journey to solution.

You do know, now, if your relationship is on track to end.
Especially if you glance into your own eyes in the mirror as you read this.
Emotional safety is the real measure of your relationship.
Not chemistry.
Not attraction.
Not “how much you love each other.”
Not whether you still have good days.
The measure is simpler and harsher:
How safe do you feel inside your body when it’s time to be honest.
And I don’t mean “safe” like nobody ever gets offended.
I mean safe like you can touch the dangerous topics without losing each other.
Because every couple has them.
The landmines.
The subjects you both know, without even saying it, will light the whole room on fire.
Money.
Sex.
Parenting.
Exes.
Porn.
Drinking.
Spending.
The way your mother talks to you.
The way you shut down.
The way you get sharp.
That one thing that happened three years ago that still lives in the air like smoke.
You already know your partner’s triggers.
You know what happens to their face.
You know the exact tone that makes them disappear.
You know the sentence that makes them go cold.
You know the look that means, “I’m about to defend myself,” before they’ve even had a thought.
And here’s the part that should scare you a little:
Most couples quietly organize their entire relationship around avoiding those moments.
Not because they’re lazy.
Because they’re trying to survive.
So you do what every distressed couple does, without realizing you’re doing it.
You build a treaty.
You stop bringing things up.
You stop asking the real questions.
You stop naming what hurts.
You stop telling the truth at the edge of the truth.
You call it “keeping the peace.”
But it isn’t peace.
It’s emotional debt.
It’s fear in a nicer outfit.
And debt always collects interest.
At first it looks small.
You don’t mention the comment that stung.
You swallow the disappointment.
You tell yourself, “It’s not worth it.”
You tell yourself, “I’ll bring it up later when it’s calmer.”
Later never comes.
Because “calm” becomes the avoidance strategy.
You start living in what I call the safe zone.
And the safe zone feels fine, until you realize it’s also where intimacy goes to die.
Because intimacy requires risk.
If you can’t risk being misunderstood, you can’t be known.
If you can’t risk your partner having a reaction, you can’t be honest.
If you can’t risk touching the painful places, you can’t heal them.
So the relationship starts shrinking.
Not dramatically.
Quietly.
You talk about logistics.
You talk about schedules.
You talk about the kids.
You talk about the dog.
You talk about work.
And you stop talking about the part that actually matters.
What it feels like to be you with them.
And what it feels like to be them with you.
This is why couples say, “We don’t even fight that much.”
They think it’s a good sign.
Sometimes it’s the worst sign.
Because the absence of conflict isn’t always safety.
Sometimes it’s resignation.
Sometimes it’s both people learning, unconsciously, that honesty costs too much.
So they pay for it with distance.
Then something happens that forces the truth.
A bill comes in.
A message is seen.
A tone is misread.
A family member crosses a line.
Someone makes an offhand remark that hits a bruise you’ve been protecting for years.
And suddenly the topic you’ve been avoiding isn’t just a topic anymore.
It’s a pile of years.
Now you’re not arguing about the bill.
You’re arguing about being alone in this relationship.
You’re not arguing about sex.
You’re arguing about feeling unwanted.
You’re not arguing about chores.
You’re arguing about whether you matter.
And because you’ve avoided the truth for so long, you don’t have the skill to touch it gently.
So you do the only thing your nervous system knows how to do in threat.
You attack.
Or you disappear.
One partner gets louder and sharper, because they’re desperate to be heard.
The other partner gets colder and quieter, because they’re desperate to not be harmed.
Both of them are trying to survive.
Both of them are terrified.
Both of them feel alone.
And here’s the tragedy.
They don’t realize the avoidance was the beginning of the end.
Not the argument.
The avoidance.
Because every time you don’t say what hurt, you don’t just keep the peace.
You teach your body a lesson:
“It isn’t safe to be real here.”
And every time your partner doesn’t respond with care, even if they don’t mean to, they teach your body a lesson too:
“My pain won’t be held here.”
That’s emotional safety.
It isn’t a vibe.
It’s a pattern.
It’s what your nervous system learns after hundreds of small moments.
It’s the difference between:
“I can tell you something hard and you’ll stay with me.”
Versus:
“If I tell you something hard, I’ll lose you.”
So let me get painfully specific.
A relationship is emotionally unsafe when you find yourself doing any of these:
You rehearse what you’re going to say for hours, and still don’t say it.
You start with a “joke” because you’re afraid to be direct.
You bring it up in a fight because calm honesty hasn’t worked.
You soften it so much it becomes invisible, then feel resentful they didn’t get it.
You wait until you’re furious because you needed courage and didn’t have it.
You feel your chest tighten before you speak, because your body expects punishment.
You decide it’s easier to not need anything.
And you can tell it’s unsafe by what happens afterward.
Do you feel closer after you tell the truth.
Or do you feel ashamed for having needs.
Do you feel seen.
Or do you feel like a problem.
Do you feel like you can stay human.
Or do you have to become a lawyer and prove your case.
Now the hard truth.
Some topics must be talked about.
Not because communication is magic.
Because silence is poison.
If you don’t have a way to talk about the hard things without hurting each other, the relationship will eventually train you into one of two futures:
You’ll explode.
Or you’ll slowly go numb.
And numb isn’t neutral.
Numb is the body’s way of saying, “This costs too much.”
So what’s the point.
The goal isn’t to never trigger each other.
You will.
The goal is to be able to touch the triggers with care.
To be able to say, “We’re in the danger zone,” without turning each other into enemies.
To be able to feel the nervous system alarm and still choose gentleness.
That’s emotional safety.
Not comfort.
Not agreement.
Not perfection.
Safety is when you can tell the truth and still feel like you belong.
Safety is when hard topics don’t become character assassination.
Safety is when repair is so normal that a rupture doesn’t feel like the end of love.
And if you’re reading this and realizing, “We avoid everything,” please don’t turn that into shame.
Turn it into clarity.
Because the couple that admits, “We don’t feel safe,” is closer to healing than the couple still pretending, “Everything’s fine.”
If you want to measure your relationship, don’t measure how often you fight.
Measure this:
How many parts of your heart have you been forced to hide just to keep the peace.
That number tells the truth.
And if it’s high, it doesn’t mean you’re doomed.
It means it’s time.
Time to stop living around the landmines.
Time to stop paying interest on emotional debt.
Time to learn how to talk about the hard things without losing each other.
Because the relationship doesn’t break when you bring up the hard topic.
It breaks when you don’t. See less

Your need to correct the details of what I share is why I pull away from you.
Not because I can’t handle feedback.
Not because I don’t care about the truth.
Not because I’m fragile.
But because every time I open my mouth and you rush to fix the facts, my body hears something very different than what you think you’re saying.
It hears:
“You’re wrong.”
“You’re unreliable.”
“You’re not safe to listen to.”
“You’re not safe to feel with.”
And after a while, I stop sharing.
Not dramatically.
Quietly.
I share less of the story.
Less of the emotion.
Less of the moment that mattered to me.
Because when I’m trying to tell you how something felt and you correct what happened, you’re not helping me feel understood.
You’re teaching me that my inner world isn’t welcome here.
You think you’re protecting accuracy.
I’m losing connection.
You think you’re being logical.
I’m becoming invisible.
You think you’re being helpful.
I’m learning how to disappear in front of you.
And this is the part most people miss.
Correction feels small to the person doing it.
It feels surgical.
Clean.
Precise.
But to the person sharing, it feels like being cut off mid-heartbeat.
Because when someone finally risks saying, “This hurt me,” what they need isn’t a footnote.
They need a witness.
They don’t need you to be a fact-checker.
They need you to be present.
And the tragedy is this:
Most people don’t pull away because they aren’t loved.
They pull away because they don’t feel met.
They pull away because every vulnerable moment turns into a debate.
Every feeling turns into a technicality.
Every story turns into a courtroom.
So they stop telling the story.
And then they stop telling you about themselves.
And then they stop letting you in.
Not because they want distance.
Because distance becomes the only way to protect what’s left of their heart.
If you want to know why someone you love is growing quieter around you, don’t ask what they’re hiding.
Ask how often you’ve corrected them when they were trying to be seen.
Because sometimes the deepest damage in a relationship isn’t betrayal.
It’s being right at the cost of being close. See less

THE MIND OF SOMEONE WHO’S BEEN CONSTANTLY CRITICIZED
Over time, their brain learns five core rules:
1. Emotion is dangerous
2. Mistakes cost love
3. Defending makes it worse
4. Withdrawal keeps me safe
5. Silence is survival
This turns into a hidden operating system:
Before they speak, they scan for danger.
Before they feel, they check if it’s allowed.
Before they respond, they brace for impact.
They don’t solve problems by fixing them.
They solve problems by reducing exposure.
That’s the tragic version.
But there’s another version that emerges in people who heal.
-
THE HEALED VERSION OF THIS MINDSET
People who survive criticism and heal don’t become louder.
They become deeper.
They develop three extraordinary capacities:
• They can separate impact from intention
• They can stay present in emotional intensity
• They can regulate themselves while staying connected
That’s the system you want to wire.
-
HOW TO THINK LIKE A HEALED VERSION OF SOMEONE WHO WAS CRITICIZED
Here’s the internal logic you want to practice:
Instead of
“Am I wrong?”
They think
“What’s happening inside me right now?”
Instead of
“I need to explain myself”
They think
“I need to stay with myself”
Instead of
“I have to fix this”
They think
“I have to stay connected”
Instead of
“I messed up”
They think
“Something important is happening in me”
Instead of
“I’m being judged”
They think
“My nervous system is activated”
-
PRACTICAL MENTAL EXERCISES TO REWIRE YOUR BRAIN
These are not affirmations.
These are nervous system drills.
-
1. THE PAUSE BEFORE PROOF
When you feel criticized, do not explain. Do not defend.
Instead say silently: “I’m safe enough to feel first.”
Then breathe into your chest for 10 seconds.
You’re teaching your system that survival doesn’t require justification.
-
2. THE INTERNAL WITNESS
Once a day, ask yourself: “What did I feel today that I didn’t express?”
Not what happened.
Not what they did.
What you felt.
Write one sentence. No solutions.
This retrains your brain to value experience over performance.
-
3. THE SEPARATION PRACTICE
When you’re criticized, say internally: “This is information. Not identity.”
Feel where the criticism lands in your body. Chest. Throat. Gut.
Breathe into that exact spot.
You’re teaching your system: “Feedback does not equal danger.”
-
4. THE COURAGE LOOP
Once a week, say one true feeling without defending it.
Example: “When you corrected me, I felt small.”
Stop.
No explanation.
No justification.
No backstory.
You’re training your nervous system to survive being seen without armor.
-
5. THE REPAIR IMPRINT
After conflict, place a hand on your chest and say: “I stayed. I didn’t disappear.”
This wires a new identity: “I am someone who stays connected under pressure.”
-
6. THE DEACTIVATION RESPONSE
When you want to shut down, do this instead:
Slow your breath
Relax your jaw
Drop your shoulders
Soften your eyes
This tells your nervous system: “Connection is not threat.”
-
7. THE NEW PROBLEM SOLVER
Practice solving problems like this:
Old way
“What should I say to fix this?”
New way
“What do I need to feel to stay present?”
That’s how healed people who were criticized become powerful.
They don’t lead with defense.
They lead with regulation.
They don’t lead with explanation.
They lead with presence.
They don’t lead with proving.
They lead with grounding.
-
THE CORE REWIRE
Here’s the sentence that changes everything:
People who heal from criticism stop trying to survive conversations
and start learning how to stay inside themselves while staying with others.
That’s the skill.
Not thicker skin.
Not better arguments.
Not smarter words.
A nervous system that can feel and stay.
That’s how you replicate the healing versionn of someone who was constantly criticized.
Not by copying their pain.
By copying their strength. See less

You don’t notice when safety leaves the relationship. It doesn’t slam the door or make a dramatic exit. It slips quietly out the back while you’re arguing about dishes or scrolling through your phone. It leaves in the pause before you say what you’re really feeling.
It leaves when you decide it’s easier to be silent than to risk being misunderstood. And one day, you wake up next to someone you love deeply and realize that, somehow, you no longer feel safe with them.
At first, you try to explain it. You tell them you’re fine, that you’re just tired, that work is stressful. But deep down you know it isn’t any of that. It’s the way your body braces before you speak.
It’s the way your chest tightens when you need comfort. It’s the way you rehearse your feelings before you share them because you don’t trust that they’ll be held gently. Safety isn’t a concept. It’s a physical experience. And your body always knows the truth before your mind is ready to admit it.
You stop reaching for their hand first. You stop sharing the little things that used to spill out easily. You start managing the version of yourself they see, trimming away the parts that might be too sensitive, too angry, too needy.
And slowly, without ever deciding to, you shrink. You shrink into the spaces where you’re sure you won’t be judged. You shrink into silence because silence is easier than explaining. You shrink into being “fine” because “fine” is safer than being real.
The strange part is that you still love them. You still want them. You still crave their closeness. But love without safety doesn’t feel like love. It feels like performance. It feels like tension humming just beneath the skin.
It feels like longing for someone who is right beside you. And if you stay in that space long enough, love becomes a place where you’re constantly trying to protect yourself instead of rest.
It’s not that they’re cruel or unkind. It’s that somewhere along the way, the small moments stopped being safe. The laugh at the wrong time. The “you’re overreacting” when you were trying to open up.
The dismissal of something that mattered deeply to you. Each one on its own felt minor. But they stacked quietly, one on top of the other, until the foundation of safety crumbled. And now, even when they’re trying, even when they say all the right things, your body still doesn’t believe them.
This is the part no one warns you about: love cannot thrive where safety has vanished. Passion can. Chemistry can. Even commitment can. But real love, the kind that softens you, that lets you be fully known, needs safety the way lungs need air.
It needs to know that the parts of you that are hardest to love will not be turned away. It needs to know that anger can exist without punishment, that sadness can exist without being dismissed, that fear can exist without being shamed.
And here’s the thing about safety: it’s not built by never hurting each other. It’s built by how you come back. It’s built by what happens after the hurt. It’s built in the way you say, “I see that I scared you” instead of “I didn’t mean it.”
It’s built in the way you stay and listen when the conversation gets uncomfortable. It’s built in the way you reach for each other again and again until your bodies learn that closeness is no longer a risk.
If you want love that lasts, stop asking how much you love each other and start asking how safe you feel with each other. Stop measuring the strength of your bond by how many vacations you’ve taken or how many anniversaries you’ve celebrated, and start measuring it by how freely you can speak your truth.
Can you say “I’m lonely” without it starting a fight? Can you say “I’m scared” without being told you’re too sensitive? Can you let your voice shake, your tears fall, your body tremble, and still feel held?
Because love without safety will eventually starve. It will become cautious. It will become quiet. It will survive, maybe, but it will not grow. But love with safety is a place where you can unfold. Where you can speak before you edit.
Where you can show the ugliest parts of yourself and know they won’t be weaponized. Where you can finally exhale and rest in the knowledge that you are seen and still chosen.
Love without safety isn’t love. It’s a performance wrapped around fear. It’s two people trying to hold on while hiding the most important parts of themselves. And love like that is exhausting.
But love with safety, real, deep, unwavering safety, is where everything changes. It’s where walls come down, where hearts soften, where vulnerability stops feeling like a risk and starts feeling like a home. And that’s where love truly begins. See less

A love letter from a man to a woman.
I love you.
But I digress.
It started with your smile.
That’s all I knew.
My brain lit up.
I was unable to get the smile off my face.
Then I noticed your hair.
Then you looked at me, and the flirt happened. You’re interested.
I’m nervous.
Relationships have been hard.
But something different is happening this time.
I can rest in your eyes.
I’m not scared of them.
I don’t want to take from you.
I want to give to you.
How do I know you won’t hurt me?
I don’t know.
But I know there’s no way I will hurt you.
The little things don’t seem to matter.
I have trauma, you have trauma, I have addiction, you have 
addiction.
But something is different.
I don’t seem to want my crutches.
I don’t need them.
I can be in my own skin.
I want to be in my own skin.
It’s never felt this comfortable.
I make choices that are sometimes a little kookoo.
And so do you.
But this time, I’m going to do something different.
I’m not going to make you wrong.
I’m not going to judge you.
I’m going to learn a new way.
I supposed things bother me, but I will not feel complete at the end 
of my life if I spent time telling you that your choices are bad.
They might be bad.
My perception is probably flawed.
It doesn’t matter.
Because the center of our love is that we supported each other in the impossibly difficult choices life brings.
I support you in your painful struggles.
I do not criticize you because I’m uncomfortable with watching you struggle.
It is your struggle, and my heart will pour out to you, and I will sit by your side while you move through your trials and tribulations.
I will hope for the same for me, but we’re both imperfect.
I will manage my expectations of receiving this level of care, and I hope you forgive me when I mess up.
Because I will.
Where I cannot yet see, I will update my prescription.
The years have moved on, and we ask each other if we can remember any time when we were hard on each other, when judgment was stuck for more than one day.
We remember one, and it was probably my fault.
But the sweetness of my apologies made up for it.
We became closer on that one babe, because we shared a couple of the deeper wounds of the past.
We’ve cauterized our hurts, because we never forget step one:
Treat each other with as much loving-kindness as we can find in the moment, no matter the issue.
We’re getting older.
I recall a story from the past.

I never knew, as a man, I could have the experience of knowing I would adore every inch of your body, even before I saw it.
We went slow.
I fell in love with you first, then we made love.
I don’t get a lot of things right, but I got that order right.
We’re rocking in our chairs on the porch.
We made love recently, but my hip replacement still aches a bit.
We hold hands.
How does holding hands never stop increasing our love?
It’s just hands.
I love how you see me.
I hope you love how I see you.
We’re still coachable.
We can suggest things to each other, and we know it’s a real reaching for the other to grow.
Sweetheart… our anxiety didn’t get the best of us.
We beat it.
It wanted to run the show, but we made the details and the stories unimportant.
Our hearts came first.
In spite of myself, my Hart was loved.
We had losses.
We might have made a few better decisions if the focus was on the details.
We lost a little money.
We gained a little weight.
(I always liked when you were a little overweight, it was comforting, I should have said that more)
But we made our communication the priority each and every day.
Thank you so much for not creating a life of arguments.
Thank you for exceeding any dream I could have had for my life partner.

Most couples don’t fail at couples therapy.
They never even make it into couples therapy.
They walk into an office, sit on a couch, start telling the story, and everyone in the room pretends the work has begun.
It hasn’t.
What’s actually happening in those first sessions, especially with a high-distress couple, is what I call pre-couples work.
And if your therapist or coach can’t name this, you’re in danger of wasting months, money, and hope.
Because here’s the uncomfortable truth.
Real couples work is not talking about your relationship.
Real couples work is being led into new interactions you cannot create on your own.
Interactions that touch the underlying emotion.
Interactions that reveal the hidden injury.
Interactions that train the nervous system, not the intellect.
Interactions that create a lived experience of, “Oh… you actually get me.”
That’s what permanently changes a distressed bond.
But high-distress couples can’t do that yet.
Not because they’re dumb.
Not because they don’t care.
Because their nervous systems are already organized around survival.
They aren’t walking into session ready to be close.
They’re walking in ready to defend.
Ready to prove.
Ready to protect.
Ready to not get humiliated.
Ready to not get blamed.
Ready to not lose.
So what do they do?
They do what they’ve done for years.
They report events.
They litigate details.
They correct each other’s memory.
They try to convince the third person in the room that their version is the true one.
And the therapist nods thoughtfully.
And the couple thinks, “Good, we’re finally doing the work.”
No.
That’s not couples work.
That’s two people still trapped in the same room, just with an audience.
Here’s the subtle part most people miss.
If you try to stage closeness too early, it doesn’t create intimacy.
It creates harm.
Because asking for vulnerability when the relationship isn’t safe doesn’t feel like healing.
It feels like exposure.
It feels like standing naked in front of the very person who’s been hurting you and being told, “Now open your heart.”
And the body says, absolutely not.
So a seasoned couples practitioner has to know something that almost nobody teaches.
There are stages.
Distinct stages.
And you cannot skip them without making the relationship worse.
Stage 1: Pre-couples work
Pre-couples work is not romance.
It’s not repair.
It’s not tenderness.
It’s triage.
It’s two people who cannot even agree on reality.
One says, “You always dismiss me.”
The other says, “I never dismiss you, you’re too sensitive.”
One says, “You’re controlling.”
The other says, “I’m just trying to keep us alive.”
One says, “You abandoned me.”
The other says, “I needed space or I would’ve exploded.”
At this stage, the couple isn’t fighting about the dishwasher.
They’re fighting about whether they’re even allowed to have feelings.
They’re fighting about whether their inner world counts.
They’re fighting about whether their pain is real.
So pre-couples work has one main job.
Not to solve the relationship.
Not to fix communication.
Not to build closeness.
The job is to build the first fragile thing that makes later work possible:
A shared narrative.
Not the perfect narrative.
Not the whole truth.
Not a courtroom verdict.
Just enough of a shared map that both nervous systems stop screaming, “This is insane.”
Because without a shared narrative, you can’t create shared intention.
And without shared intention, you cannot stage the kind of interactions that heal.
Stage 2: The first real turning point
This is the moment most couples never reach.
It’s the moment they stop trying to win.
And they start trying to understand.
It’s the moment they can say something like:
“Okay. We don’t see it the same way. But something did happen between us. And we’re both suffering.”
That sentence alone is a nervous system event.
Because it’s the first time the relationship stops being a battleground and becomes a shared problem.
This is when intention becomes possible.
Not fake intention.
Not “We’ll try harder.”
Not “We’ll communicate better.”
Real intention sounds more like:
“I don’t want to keep destroying us.”
“I don’t want to keep becoming someone I hate.”
“I want to learn how to do this differently, even if I don’t know how yet.”
That’s the inkling of the beginning.
It’s not couples work yet.
But it’s the doorway.
Stage 3: Actual couples work
Now, and only now, do we enter the real thing.
This is where I stage interactions.
This is where I have you face each other and speak in a way your pattern has never allowed.
This is where the work stops being analysis and becomes experience.
This is where someone learns to say:
“When you look away from me, my body panics.”
And the other learns not to defend.
Not to explain.
Not to fix.
But to stay.
To let the impact land.
To offer recognition.
Because the only thing that heals a distressed relationship is not a clever insight.
It’s not a new rule.
It’s not a better boundary.
It’s a new emotional experience between the two of you that your nervous systems register as real.
And here’s the part that’s going to land hard if you’ve been in therapy for a while.
Sometimes five to seven sessions in, a couple realizes:
“We haven’t done any of this.”
They’ve paid.
They’ve cried.
They’ve fought in the parking lot after sessions.
They’ve done homework.
They’ve learned vocabulary.
And they still don’t feel closer.
Because they were never in couples work.
They were in pre-couples work, spinning their story, hoping the therapist would somehow magically turn it into connection.
A seasoned couples coach should be able to tell you, clearly, what stage you are in.
They should be able to name what has to happen before deeper work is safe.

Most couples don’t fail at couples therapy.

They never even make it into couples therapy.

They walk into an office, sit on a couch, start telling the story, and everyone in the room pretends the work has begun.

It hasn’t.

What’s actually happening in those first sessions, especially with a high-distress couple, is what I call pre-couples work.

And if your therapist or coach can’t name this, you’re in danger of wasting months, money, and hope.

Because here’s the uncomfortable truth.

Real couples work is not talking about your relationship.

Real couples work is being led into new interactions you cannot create on your own.

Interactions that touch the underlying emotion.

Interactions that reveal the hidden injury.

Interactions that train the nervous system, not the intellect.

Interactions that create a lived experience of, “Oh… you actually get me.”

That’s what permanently changes a distressed bond.

But high-distress couples can’t do that yet.

Not because they’re dumb.

Not because they don’t care.

Because their nervous systems are already organized around survival.

They aren’t walking into session ready to be close.

They’re walking in ready to defend.

Ready to prove.

Ready to protect.

Ready to not get humiliated.

Ready to not get blamed.

Ready to not lose.

So what do they do?

They do what they’ve done for years.

They report events.

They litigate details.

They correct each other’s memory.

They try to convince the third person in the room that their version is the true one.

And the therapist nods thoughtfully.

And the couple thinks, “Good, we’re finally doing the work.”

No.

That’s not couples work.

That’s two people still trapped in the same room, just with an audience.

Here’s the subtle part most people miss.

If you try to stage closeness too early, it doesn’t create intimacy.

It creates harm.

Because asking for vulnerability when the relationship isn’t safe doesn’t feel like healing.

It feels like exposure.

It feels like standing naked in front of the very person who’s been hurting you and being told, “Now open your heart.”

And the body says, absolutely not.

So a seasoned couples practitioner has to know something that almost nobody teaches.

There are stages.

Distinct stages.

And you cannot skip them without making the relationship worse.

Stage 1: Pre-couples work

Pre-couples work is not romance.

It’s not repair.

It’s not tenderness.

It’s triage.

It’s two people who cannot even agree on reality.

One says, “You always dismiss me.”

The other says, “I never dismiss you, you’re too sensitive.”

One says, “You’re controlling.”

The other says, “I’m just trying to keep us alive.”

One says, “You abandoned me.”

The other says, “I needed space or I would’ve exploded.”

At this stage, the couple isn’t fighting about the dishwasher.

They’re fighting about whether they’re even allowed to have feelings.

They’re fighting about whether their inner world counts.

They’re fighting about whether their pain is real.

So pre-couples work has one main job.

Not to solve the relationship.

Not to fix communication.

Not to build closeness.

The job is to build the first fragile thing that makes later work possible:

A shared narrative.

Not the perfect narrative.

Not the whole truth.

Not a courtroom verdict.

Just enough of a shared map that both nervous systems stop screaming, “This is insane.”

Because without a shared narrative, you can’t create shared intention.

And without shared intention, you cannot stage the kind of interactions that heal.

Stage 2: The first real turning point

This is the moment most couples never reach.

It’s the moment they stop trying to win.

And they start trying to understand.

It’s the moment they can say something like:

“Okay. We don’t see it the same way. But something did happen between us. And we’re both suffering.”

That sentence alone is a nervous system event.

Because it’s the first time the relationship stops being a battleground and becomes a shared problem.

This is when intention becomes possible.

Not fake intention.

Not “We’ll try harder.”

Not “We’ll communicate better.”

Real intention sounds more like:

“I don’t want to keep destroying us.”

“I don’t want to keep becoming someone I hate.”

“I want to learn how to do this differently, even if I don’t know how yet.”

That’s the inkling of the beginning.

It’s not couples work yet.

But it’s the doorway.

Now, and only now, do we enter the real thing.

This is where I stage interactions.

This is where I have you face each other and speak in a way your pattern has never allowed.

This is where the work stops being analysis and becomes experience.

This is where someone learns to say:

“When you look away from me, my body panics.”

And the other learns not to defend.

Not to explain.

Not to fix.

But to stay.

To let the impact land.

To offer recognition.

Because the only thing that heals a distressed relationship is not a clever insight.

It’s not a new rule.

It’s not a better boundary.

It’s a new emotional experience between the two of you that your nervous systems register as real.

They’ve paid.

They’ve cried.

They’ve fought in the parking lot after sessions.

They’ve done homework.

They’ve learned vocabulary.

And they still don’t feel closer.

Because they were never in couples work.

They were in pre-couples work, spinning their story, hoping the therapist would somehow magically turn it into connection.

They should be able to name what has to happen before deeper work is safe.

Your heart learns a terrible kind of math in childhood.
Distance equals safety because mom couldn't handle your needs.  
Criticism equals love because that's how dad showed he cared.  
Walking on eggshells equals connection because quiet meant everyone was okay.
Then you grow up and fall in love.
Except you don't fall in love with kindness.
Kindness feels foreign. Wrong. Like wearing someone else's clothes.
You fall in love with the familiar ache.
The way she goes quiet when you need her most - just like mom.  
The way he sighs when you're excited about something - just like dad.  
The way they look right through you when you're hurting.
Your body goes "Yes. This. I know this dance."
Not because you want to suffer.  
Because suffering is the only language your nervous system speaks fluently.
You don't pick someone who treats you well and think "this could work."
You pick someone who hurts you in that specific, childhood way and think "if I can just get THEM to love me differently, I'll finally be okay."
Like your heart is still trying to fix that eight-year-old's broken world.
So you chase the unavailable one.  
Fight for the critical one.  
Beg the distant one to see you.
Same pattern. Different face.
Meanwhile, the person who'd actually cherish you?  
They feel boring. Safe. "Not my type."
Translation: "Doesn't match my damage."
Your brain literally cannot compute someone being gentle without wanting something back.
Someone listening without getting frustrated.  
Someone staying close when you're messy.  
Someone choosing you without you having to earn it.
That's not love to your nervous system.  
That's suspicious.
Real healing?  
Learning to let your heart hurt in a completely different way.
Not the familiar hurt of being unseen.  
The terrifying hurt of being seen and staying.

One of the strangest things about relationship distress is how much you learn to live with.
Not because it’s okay.
Because you adapt.
You adapt to the tightness in your chest when your phone buzzes and it’s them.
You adapt to rehearsing conversations in your head that never actually happen.
You adapt to feeling more alone next to someone than you ever felt single.
You adapt to the way your body braces when they walk into the room.
You adapt to not bringing things up because it’s “not worth it.”
You adapt to hoping things will improve without knowing how.
And the most dangerous adaptation of all?
You stop noticing how much of you isn’t there anymore.
Your confidence narrows.
Your curiosity dulls.
Your sexuality goes quiet.
Your world gets smaller.
Not because you’re weak.
Because your nervous system is conserving energy.
This is the part no one tells you:
You don’t stay stuck because you don’t know enough.
You stay stuck because your body has learned how to survive here.
And survival feels deceptively stable.
Until one day, you realize you don’t recognize yourself anymore. See less
