I want to tell you about a couple I work with who figured this out after nineteen years of marriage. And I want to tell you specifically about what happened the first night after the wife understood what his reaching had actually been about. Because what happened between them lasted about two minutes. It wasn't s*x. It wasn't a conversation. It wasn't dramatic or cinematic or anything that would look like a turning point if you were watching from the outside.
But both of them told me, separately, on our next Zoom call, that it was the most intimate experience of their entire marriage.
Two minutes.
After nineteen years.
Let me give you the backstory first, because the backstory is what makes the two minutes land the way they landed.
They'd been in the pattern for years. The exact pattern I've been describing. He reaches physically. She interprets it as s*x. She pulls away. He absorbs the rejection. The physical vocabulary between them shrinks. She notices the distance. He can't explain the distance. Both of them conclude the other one is the problem.
Nineteen years of this.
By the time they came to me, the physical dimension of their marriage was essentially dead. Not hostile. Dead. They didn't fight about it. They didn't argue about s*x or intimacy or who initiates or who rejects. They'd moved past all of that. They'd arrived at the place couples arrive when the fighting about it has been replaced by a mutual, unspoken agreement to stop trying.
He'd stopped reaching for her physically about three years before they called me. Not a decision he made consciously. His body just stopped. The way I described it in the earlier post. The gate closed. The half-second calculation before every bid eventually produced the same answer enough times that the system shut down.
And she'd noticed the shutdown and concluded it was about her attractiveness. That he didn't want her anymore. That nineteen years and two kids and the changes in her body had made her someone he no longer desired. She'd been carrying that conclusion for three years without saying it out loud because saying it out loud would make it real and she wasn't ready for it to be real.
So they were living in this quiet, polite, physically dead space. Functioning. Co-parenting. Running the household. Sleeping in the same bed without touching. Not angry. Just absent from each other's bodies.
We'd been working together for about two months when I brought up the closeness bid.
I didn't use that language. I didn't give them a lecture about attachment or bids or mistranslation. I just asked him a question during one of our Zoom sessions.
I said, "When you used to reach for her physically, before you stopped, what were you reaching for?"
He didn't answer right away. He sat with it. She was watching him from her side of the screen. And I could see him doing the thing men do when they're trying to find language for something they've never been asked to put into words.
He said, "I don't know. Just to be close to her."
I said, "Close how? What did the closeness feel like when it worked?"
He was quiet for a while. Then he said, "Safe. It felt safe. Like everything that was loud all day got quiet when I was touching her. Not s*x. Just the touching. Like my body could finally stop running."
She made a sound. Small. Almost inaudible. But I heard it through the speakers and I could see her face change.
She said, "That's what it was?"
He looked at her.
She said, "I thought you were trying to start something. Every time. I thought it was always about s*x. And I was tired. And I didn't want s*x most of those times. So I pulled away. And I thought I was saying no to s*x. I didn't know I was saying no to..."
She didn't finish the sentence.
He finished it.
He said, "To me."
The room went very still.
Not the kind of still that happens when something goes wrong. The kind of still that happens when something true lands in a space that's been filled with a lie for nineteen years and the lie finally dissolves and what's left is just two people looking at each other through a screen realizing they've been hurting each other by accident for almost two decades.
She said, "I've been pushing you away for nineteen years and I didn't know what I was pushing away."
He said, "I stopped reaching because I thought you didn't want me near you."
She said, "I wanted you near me every single night. I just didn't want it to lead to s*x every single night. And I didn't know those were two different things. I didn't know you were offering the first one without needing the second one."
That was the session. That was the moment of recognition. Both of them saw the mistranslation at the same time and both of them understood, in real time, that the physical death of their marriage wasn't about desire or attraction or s*x drives or any of the things they'd been privately blaming for three years.
It was about a misread reach.
Nineteen years of misread reaches.
I ended the session by saying one thing. I said, "Tonight, when you're in bed, I want him to reach for you the way he used to. And I want you to let him. And I want both of you to let it be what it is without it needing to go anywhere."
That was the assignment. No instructions. No technique. No framework. Just reach and receive with no agenda.
Here's what happened.
She told me about it first. On a call the next morning. She was crying before she started talking, which I've learned to recognize as the specific cry that means something good happened that the body doesn't know what to do with yet.
She said they got into bed that night the way they'd been getting into bed for three years. On their own sides. Facing away from each other or staring at the ceiling. The perfunctory "good night" that doesn't mean good night, it means "I'm here but I'm not here and we both know it."
She said she lay there for a few minutes waiting. And he lay there for a few minutes not moving. And she could feel the tension in the bed because both of them were aware that something was supposed to happen and neither of them knew how to start it.
She said she almost gave up. Almost rolled over and went to sleep and let the moment pass the way every other moment had passed for three years.
And then she felt his hand.
On her hip.
Not moving. Not sliding. Not going anywhere. Just his hand. Resting on her hip. The way it used to rest there years ago when they were still in the stage of marriage where bodies find each other in the dark without thinking about it.
She said his hand was shaking.
She told me that and had to stop talking for a minute.
His hand was shaking. Because the man who'd stopped reaching three years ago was reaching again. And the reaching was so terrifying, so loaded with the accumulated weight of every rejection his body had stored, that his hand was physically trembling against her hip.
She said, "I could feel how scared he was. In his hand. I could feel it. And I realized I'd never known he was scared. I thought he was distant. I thought he'd checked out. I thought he didn't want me anymore. And his hand was shaking because he wanted to be close to me so badly that the wanting was making his body shake."
She didn't pull away.
She didn't stiffen.
She didn't calculate whether the hand on the hip was going somewhere.
She moved toward the hand.
She rolled toward him. Slowly. And she pressed her back against his chest. And she took his shaking hand from her hip and moved it to her stomach and held it there with both of hers.
And she said, "Stay."
One word.
And his body broke.
Not in the way bodies break during a fight. In the way bodies break when something that's been held too tightly for too long finally gets released. She said she felt it happen against her back. His chest. Something inside his chest let go. And the shaking in his hand stopped. And his breathing changed. And his arm tightened around her. Not pulling. Not initiating. Holding. Holding like a man who just found something he'd been convinced was lost.
She said they lay there for about two minutes.
Neither of them said anything else.
Neither of them moved.
Neither of them tried to turn it into anything.
His chest against her back. His arm around her. His hand on her stomach held by both of hers. Both of them breathing.
That's it.
That's the whole thing.
Two minutes of a man holding his wife in the dark with his hand on her stomach.
That's what they both described to me as the most intimate experience of their nineteen-year marriage.
Not a vacation. Not a wedding. Not a night of passion. Not any of the things that are supposed to be the peaks of a marriage.
Two minutes of being held.
After three years of not being held.
By a man whose hand was shaking because the reaching was that frightening and that necessary.
I asked him about it on our next Zoom call. Separately. Before the couples session.
I said, "What happened in your body when she said 'stay'?"
He was quiet for a long time.
Then he said, "Something melted."
He couldn't elaborate much more than that. He's not a man who has a lot of language for internal experience. But he said, "I've been holding something in my chest for three years. Maybe longer. And when she rolled toward me instead of away from me, and she took my hand and put it on her stomach and said that one word, the thing in my chest melted. I don't know what it was. But it's been there for years and it melted in about ten seconds."
He said, "I didn't know my hand was shaking until she told you. But I believe it. Because I was terrified. I was terrified she was going to pull away again. And I knew if she pulled away one more time I was never going to reach again. That was going to be the last one. And she didn't pull away. She came toward me. And the direction of her body told me something that no words could have told me."
I said, "What did it tell you?"
He said, "That I'm still welcome there."
That I'm still welcome there.
That's what the two minutes were about.
Not s*x. Not desire. Not passion. Not attraction.
Welcome.
The experience of a man reaching for the safest place he knows and discovering that the safest place still wants him there.
After three years of believing it didn't.
That's what closeness bids are about.
That's what the hand on the waist is reaching for.
That's what the pull in bed is asking.
That's what the hug that lasts too long is saying.
"Am I still welcome there?"
And the answer to that question, delivered not in words but in the direction of a body in the dark, is the thing that determines whether a man stays open or closes permanently.
She rolled toward him.
That's the answer.
That's the whole answer.
Not a conversation. Not an apology. Not a twelve-step repair plan.
A body moving toward a reaching hand instead of away from it.
Two minutes of holding in the dark.
And a one-word sentence that told a shaking man that home was still open.
"Stay."
If you take one thing from everything I've written about bids and closeness and the physical dimension of marriage, let it be this.
The next time his hand finds your hip in the dark, move toward it.
Not away.
Toward.
And if you can, hold the hand.
And if you can, say the word.
And give him two minutes of knowing that the safest place on earth didn't close while he wasn't looking.
Two minutes.
That's all it takes to bring a man back from three years of silence.
Not therapy. Not a conversation. Not a weekend away.
Two minutes of being welcome.
In the dark.
In the bed you've been sharing but not sharing.
Let him back in.
He's been waiting at the door with a shaking hand for longer than you know.

She made a sound. Small. Almost inaudible. But I heard it through the speakers and I could see her face change.

She said, "That's what it was?"

He looked at her.

She said, "I thought you were trying to start something. Every time. I thought it was always about s*x. And I was tired. And I didn't want s*x most of those times. So I pulled away. And I thought I was saying no to s*x. I didn't know I was saying no to..."

She didn't finish the sentence.

He finished it.

He said, "To me."

The room went very still.

Not the kind of still that happens when something goes wrong. The kind of still that happens when something true lands in a space that's been filled with a lie for nineteen years and the lie finally dissolves and what's left is just two people looking at each other through a screen realizing they've been hurting each other by accident for almost two decades.

She said, "I've been pushing you away for nineteen years and I didn't know what I was pushing away."

He said, "I stopped reaching because I thought you didn't want me near you."

She said, "I wanted you near me every single night. I just didn't want it to lead to s*x every single night. And I didn't know those were two different things. I didn't know you were offering the first one without needing the second one."

That was the session. That was the moment of recognition. Both of them saw the mistranslation at the same time and both of them understood, in real time, that the physical death of their marriage wasn't about desire or attraction or s*x drives or any of the things they'd been privately blaming for three years.

It was about a misread reach.

Nineteen years of misread reaches.

I ended the session by saying one thing. I said, "Tonight, when you're in bed, I want him to reach for you the way he used to. And I want you to let him. And I want both of you to let it be what it is without it needing to go anywhere."

That was the assignment. No instructions. No technique. No framework. Just reach and receive with no agenda.

Here's what happened.

She told me about it first. On a call the next morning. She was crying before she started talking, which I've learned to recognize as the specific cry that means something good happened that the body doesn't know what to do with yet.

She said they got into bed that night the way they'd been getting into bed for three years. On their own sides. Facing away from each other or staring at the ceiling. The perfunctory "good night" that doesn't mean good night, it means "I'm here but I'm not here and we both know it."

She said she lay there for a few minutes waiting. And he lay there for a few minutes not moving. And she could feel the tension in the bed because both of them were aware that something was supposed to happen and neither of them knew how to start it.

She said she almost gave up. Almost rolled over and went to sleep and let the moment pass the way every other moment had passed for three years.

And then she felt his hand.

On her hip.

Not moving. Not sliding. Not going anywhere. Just his hand. Resting on her hip. The way it used to rest there years ago when they were still in the stage of marriage where bodies find each other in the dark without thinking about it.

She said his hand was shaking.

She told me that and had to stop talking for a minute.

His hand was shaking. Because the man who'd stopped reaching three years ago was reaching again. And the reaching was so terrifying, so loaded with the accumulated weight of every rejection his body had stored, that his hand was physically trembling against her hip.

She said, "I could feel how scared he was. In his hand. I could feel it. And I realized I'd never known he was scared. I thought he was distant. I thought he'd checked out. I thought he didn't want me anymore. And his hand was shaking because he wanted to be close to me so badly that the wanting was making his body shake."

She didn't pull away.

She didn't stiffen.

She didn't calculate whether the hand on the hip was going somewhere.

She moved toward the hand.

She rolled toward him. Slowly. And she pressed her back against his chest. And she took his shaking hand from her hip and moved it to her stomach and held it there with both of hers.

And she said, "Stay."

One word.

And his body broke.

Not in the way bodies break during a fight. In the way bodies break when something that's been held too tightly for too long finally gets released. She said she felt it happen against her back. His chest. Something inside his chest let go. And the shaking in his hand stopped. And his breathing changed. And his arm tightened around her. Not pulling. Not initiating. Holding. Holding like a man who just found something he'd been convinced was lost.

She said they lay there for about two minutes.

Neither of them said anything else.

Neither of them moved.

Neither of them tried to turn it into anything.

His chest against her back. His arm around her. His hand on her stomach held by both of hers. Both of them breathing.

That's it.

That's the whole thing.

Two minutes of a man holding his wife in the dark with his hand on her stomach.

That's what they both described to me as the most intimate experience of their nineteen-year marriage.

Not a vacation. Not a wedding. Not a night of passion. Not any of the things that are supposed to be the peaks of a marriage.

Two minutes of being held.

After three years of not being held.

By a man whose hand was shaking because the reaching was that frightening and that necessary.

I asked him about it on our next Zoom call. Separately. Before the couples session.

I said, "What happened in your body when she said 'stay'?"

He was quiet for a long time.

Then he said, "Something melted."

He couldn't elaborate much more than that. He's not a man who has a lot of language for internal experience. But he said, "I've been holding something in my chest for three years. Maybe longer. And when she rolled toward me instead of away from me, and she took my hand and put it on her stomach and said that one word, the thing in my chest melted. I don't know what it was. But it's been there for years and it melted in about ten seconds."

He said, "I didn't know my hand was shaking until she told you. But I believe it. Because I was terrified. I was terrified she was going to pull away again. And I knew if she pulled away one more time I was never going to reach again. That was going to be the last one. And she didn't pull away. She came toward me. And the direction of her body told me something that no words could have told me."

I said, "What did it tell you?"

He said, "That I'm still welcome there."

That I'm still welcome there.

That's what the two minutes were about.

Not s*x. Not desire. Not passion. Not attraction.

Welcome.

The experience of a man reaching for the safest place he knows and discovering that the safest place still wants him there.

After three years of believing it didn't.

That's what closeness bids are about.

That's what the hand on the waist is reaching for.

That's what the pull in bed is asking.

That's what the hug that lasts too long is saying.

"Am I still welcome there?"

And the answer to that question, delivered not in words but in the direction of a body in the dark, is the thing that determines whether a man stays open or closes permanently.

She rolled toward him.

That's the answer.

That's the whole answer.

Not a conversation. Not an apology. Not a twelve-step repair plan.

A body moving toward a reaching hand instead of away from it.

Two minutes of holding in the dark.

And a one-word sentence that told a shaking man that home was still open.

"Stay."

If you take one thing from everything I've written about bids and closeness and the physical dimension of marriage, let it be this.

The next time his hand finds your hip in the dark, move toward it.

Not away.

Toward.

And if you can, hold the hand.

And if you can, say the word.

And give him two minutes of knowing that the safest place on earth didn't close while he wasn't looking.

Two minutes.

That's all it takes to bring a man back from three years of silence.

Not therapy. Not a conversation. Not a weekend away.

Two minutes of being welcome.

In the dark.

In the bed you've been sharing but not sharing.

Let him back in.

He's been waiting at the door with a shaking hand for longer than you know.

100 Truths a Marriage Counselor Wishes Every Couple Knew Before the First Session
The Truths About Why You're Actually Here
1. You didn't come here because of the fight last Tuesday.
2. You came here because of a thousand Tuesdays before that one.
3. The presenting problem is almost never the problem.
4. The thing you're arguing about is rarely the thing you're arguing about.
5. You've been lonely in this marriage longer than you've admitted.
6. So has the person sitting next to you.
7. One of you has been quietly planning an exit for a while.
8. The other one has been quietly hoping you'd stop.
9. You're not here to be right. You're here because being right hasn't worked.
10. If you came here to win, you've already lost.
The Truths About What You Brought With You
11. You married your mother. Or your father. Or both.
12. You married the wound you haven't finished with.
13. The things that drive you craziest about them are usually old business.
14. You're reacting to your spouse and to someone from thirty years ago at the same time.
15. Your nervous system doesn't know the difference.
16. Neither does theirs.
17. Most fights in a marriage are two frightened children in adult bodies.
18. You didn't choose them by accident.
19. You chose someone who would bring the wound up so you could finally look at it.
20. They chose you for the same reason.
The Truths About Communication
21. You don't have a communication problem. You have a safety problem.
22. Nobody opens up to someone who feels dangerous to them.
23. Being right is not the same as being heard.
24. Being heard is not the same as being agreed with.
25. Most couples don't listen. They wait.
26. Most couples don't talk. They deliver verdicts.
27. The tone you use with them is the tone they learn to brace against.
28. You've been teaching each other how to avoid you for years.
29. You are both fluent in each other's worst self by now.
30. You've forgotten how to speak to the best of each other.
The Truths About Fighting
31. Every couple fights. The healthy ones fight cleaner and repair faster.
32. It's not conflict that ends marriages. It's contempt.
33. Eye-rolling is a warning sign. So is the sigh.
34. So is the silence that goes on too long after.
35. Stonewalling is not peace. It's a slow-motion leaving.
36. When you shut them out, you teach them to stop reaching.
37. When you punish them for reaching, they eventually stop.
38. Criticism is not feedback. Criticism is character assassination.
39. Defensiveness is just fear in a suit and tie.
40. The fight after the fight is always the real one.
The Truths About Repair
41. Nothing predicts the future of a marriage more than how you repair.
42. Couples who repair badly don't last, even if the original hurts were small.
43. Couples who repair well can survive enormous hurts.
44. "I'm sorry, but" is not an apology.
45. "I'm sorry you feel that way" is not an apology.
46. "I'm sorry I was late, you always make a big deal out of nothing" is not an apology.
47. A real apology has no escape hatch in it.
48. A real apology names the thing.
49. A real apology doesn't ask to be forgiven before the other person is ready.
50. A real apology is the beginning of the repair, not the end.
The Truths About S*x and Intimacy
51. The s*x problem is almost never a s*x problem.
52. It's a resentment problem wearing s*x clothes.
53. You can't be emotionally shut out all week and physically open at night.
54. Desire follows safety. Not the other way around.
55. The lowest-desire partner sets the pace. That's biology, not punishment.
56. Chasing someone who's pulling away makes them pull further.
57. Your partner is not withholding. They're protecting themselves from something they haven't been able to name yet.
58. The bedroom is the scoreboard for the rest of the marriage.
59. If you want more in the bedroom, look at what's happening in the kitchen.
60. Most couples wait until the intimacy is nearly gone before they ask for help.
The Truths About What You Don't See
61. Your partner is lonelier than you think.
62. Your partner has been trying to tell you something for years.
63. You've been missing it because it doesn't sound like how you would've said it.
64. Your partner has a private sadness you haven't noticed.
65. Your partner is tired in a way they haven't explained.
66. Your partner has been bracing for the next version of you that hurts them.
67. Your partner remembers things you said that you don't.
68. They replay them at night when they can't sleep.
69. You do the same to them.
70. Both of you are walking around with a file of evidence against the other.
The Truths About What Each of You Needs
71. One of you needs to feel wanted. The other needs to feel safe.
72. One of you needs to feel seen. The other needs to feel trusted.
73. One of you pursues. The other withdraws.
74. This is not a flaw in either of you. It's the dance.
75. The pursuer is not needy. The pursuer is terrified of being left.
76. The withdrawer is not cold. The withdrawer is terrified of being consumed.
77. When the pursuer slows down, the withdrawer can finally come forward.
78. When the withdrawer stays, the pursuer can finally rest.
79. Most couples never learn each other's fear language.
80. They only learn each other's attack language.
The Truths About the Marriage Itself
81. Your marriage has a third presence in the room. It's not either of you.
82. The marriage has its own nervous system now.
83. You have been feeding it or starving it for years.
84. Most couples don't kill their marriage. They neglect it to death.
85. A marriage dies by inches, not by blows.
86. The day the marriage ended in your heart was probably years before either of you admitted it.
87. Or it hasn't ended yet, and you're here to find out.
88. There's no neutral in a long relationship. You're either moving toward each other or away from each other.
89. Every day you don't repair is a day the distance gets a little more familiar.
90. Familiar distance is how couples end up as roommates.
The Truths About What Comes Next
91. Therapy is not a referee. I'm not here to decide who's right.
92. I'm here to help you see what you can't see while you're inside of it.
93. Both of you will feel misunderstood by me at some point. That means it's working.
94. This will get harder before it gets easier. That's not a sign of failure.
95. Some of what you'll learn about yourself will be hard to sit with.
96. Some of what you'll learn about each other will be harder.
97. Not every marriage survives this work. The honest ones do.
98. Some couples discover they want to stay. Some discover they want to leave.
99. Either way, you'll leave here clearer than you came in.
100. The goal is not to save the marriage. The goal is to tell the truth. If the truth wants the marriage, the marriage will come back.

My Parents 
In our classes in The Relationship Lab, we learn a lot of things from Derek Hart  in the 30min lectures before individual sessions. One thing he said is that most Relationship issues begin in the first 6 months. 
I cringed. 
My parents issues began on Day 3 of their Honeymoon.  Somehow Mom learned that Dad had had sex with other women, and she was angry because he said he had never been married. He said, "I told you the truth, I haven't." She very heatedly said "You knew what I meant." 
She felt betrayed.
If you understand religion and their views about sex outside of marriage, particularly the cult I was raised in, the same one my Mom was raised in, that my Dad married into, you see how much shame she had now for marrying a man she thought was "pure".
Besides the fact this triggered her deep insecurities that Dad didn't choose her because he loved her, she had been chosen because she was the best on a list.
You see, my Dad made a list of all available single woman in the cult and all their attributes. He spent 2 years visiting each assembly and getting to know people. There was a woman named Helen that he really was attracted to, but she wore pants and my Mom didn't; since pants weren't allowed in the cult, that ruled out Helen. Dad always told Mom that he chose her from the list, but Mom I guess never felt chosen. She felt qualified because of a list of his prerequisites like Bible knowledge and desire to have kids, because he possibly wanted to be a Preacher. He had gone to Biola Bible College in California, but dropped out when he learned the cult didn't care about any degree.
She was so angry, she didn't speak to him the next 3 days of their Honeymoon. 
Can you imagine how punished he felt?
My heart grieves for my Dad. 
And my Mom. 
That's some deep intense pain. From my witnessing of things, I don't believe it ever got repaired. 
I don't know what changed. I don't know, or maybe just don't remember what she said that made her tell Dad she forgave him, but she really didn't. She made him "pay" the rest of his life.
My Dad was 31 and my Mom 19 when they got married, after 2 years of dating, in 1975.
She stopped her BCPs to get pregnant because she didn't want him to leave her. Dad wasn't ready for kids yet. He wanted time alone. I was born 1.5 years after they were married. I am 9 months old in this photo.
My Dad admitted to me later in life, at age 14, that he really never wanted kids. He only had them because Mom wanted them. All he wanted to do was work and study the Bible. He didn't want to be a Preacher because that was too much pressure and authority. But Mom wanted him to be one. So she put pressures on him to address "issues" he had with the church leadership, particularly with modesty and hypocrisy she saw. 
In one of these meetings, "The Men" (term for those in leadership) asked my Dad some questions about why this was such an issue with him, he told them about my Mom's concerns and his responsibility to protect his home.
Ohhhhh shit.
Wrong thing to say. 
When she learned of this, she chastised him and beat him over the head, micromanaging his every move. If they went for coffee, which was a rare thing, maybe they did 4 times in my childhood, she would demand why he looked at the waitresses butt as she walked away from the table or try to see down her blouse when she poured them a cup of coffee. This escalated to "The Men" having a "Private Conversation" with my Mom without my Dad present, which defied their laws of headship in the church, and when they questioned her about her concerns being brought to "The Men" through my Dad, she enlightened them that my Dad had a problem lusting after other woman.
Now a war had begun between them. A war that Dad never stood a chance to win. Not once.
In 1993, the modesty issues became so great, my Mom demanded my Dad "make a statement". He had told "The Men" that if things didn't change, he would have to take a stand. He chose to do that June 13th,1993 when Hans & Shelley got married. When the bride walked down the isle, with a neckline "too low", we walked out.
And yes, I as a 16 year old daughter knew what was likely to happen, but was told to not make a scene, just observe Daddy out of the corner of my eye, instructed to not make eye contact with anyone, and simply follow suit. We marched out with out heads held high, beeming that we were doing a "righteous act of God". 
My heart broke that day.
Tears slid down my face as we drove home.
I felt so empty inside. Worse than I ever had, and I didn't know why.
The following Friday Night, my Mom answered the phone to some lady telling her that she was pregnant by her husband. Mom went into shock and struggled to ask questions, and the lady hung up. We didn't have caller ID back then on rotary dialed phones. My Mom went into a full-blown rage. She already had been suspicious and accusing my Dad of having an affair. Now she had proof.
The irony? 
She opened the phonebook and called every R Gilbert, Randall Gilbert, Randy Gilbert, or Russell Gilbert and asked if they were married, how long they had been married, and if their relationship was solid because she got this call and she knew it couldn't be her husband as he would never have an affair on her!!!
I am not fucking joking with you.
The situation with Dad got worse, way worse, and she kicked him out of the bedroom to sleep on the couch. When that didn't give her enough room or feeling of safety, she made him sleep at work, on the floor in a sleeping bag. When Dad's boss caught him doing this, he put a stop to it. Dad & Mom then bought a mini-motorhome and Dad slept in that on work property, with the pretense we were eventually going to travel to the assemblies, but it was to give Dad a place to live. 
We never did travel.
We would go every weekend and take Dad groceries and gather his laundry and take it back home and wash it. 
After a period of time and no progress in the relationship, with lots more fights, Mom told Dad we were not going to do anything for him - he was on his own. This meant when Dad came to wash his clothes each weekend, we had to be gone because Mom wouldn't want to see him.
She then began threatening divorce. Pitting us kids against each other when my brother wanted to live with Dad, but us girls would get no choice because she already never left us alone with my Dad as it was, even before all of this. 
I questioned my Mom if she really loved my Dad. I asked her what evidence she had beyond the phone call that I believed was a prank, likely by girlfriends of Shelley. I made her squirm so deeply that she told me to stop asking questions and that I would understand "when I became an adult".  I risked being beaten to fight for their relationship. I said some things that made her utterly hate me and lash out in the worst rage I ever saw, until I was raped at age 17.
My parents eventually figured things out and Dad moved back in, but there is more to the story of the back and worth crazy making chaos.
No easy way to write all of this painful life I have witnessed and lived. But it is the reason why I swore I didn't want to get married for a long time because I didn't want a relationship like my parents had.
It is what drove me to read relationship books and do courses and work on me long before a man came into my life. 
Yet as I sit with the question of where do I have "Shards of Sadness" stored in my body, I am finding some really difficult memories that had to be stuffed down to just get through them. There wasn't any room for someone to tend to me and the big feelings eating me alive. 
It also is very eye opening to review your life on this kind of level. 
To feel the oppression. To sense the deep level of obligation to follow rules. To uncover all the ways I had no choice. To see how many things I had to do like an adult in a child's body. To see how much was up to me. To feel the intense pressure. To observe the responsibility I had to figure it all out. To rise to the demands to succeed and not fail. To see how I never once felt safe. To recognize that nobody had my back. To see how I was not seen, heard and held and the depth of loneliness this created. To know how hurt and scared I was. To see how much of my life, the spirit within me, has been suffocating. 
I lay on my bed and hold little Omar and sob, sob out layers of shards of sadness, releasing this pent up grief. 
It's difficult to discuss "the rest of the story" like Paul Harvey could do. Maybe because there is no good ending.

You see, my Dad made a list of all available single woman in the cult and all their attributes. He spent 2 years visiting each assembly and getting to know people. There was a woman named Helen that he really was attracted to, but she wore pants and my Mom didn't; since pants weren't allowed in the cult, that ruled out Helen. She felt qualified because of a list of his prerequisites like Bible knowledge and desire to have kids, because he possibly wanted to be a Preacher. She was so angry, she didn't speak to him the next 3 days of their Honeymoon.

Can you imagine how punished he felt?

My heart grieves for my Dad.

And my Mom.

That's some deep intense pain. From my witnessing of things, I don't believe it ever got repaired.

I don't know what changed. I don't know, or maybe just don't remember what she said that made her tell Dad she forgave him, but she really didn't. She made him "pay" the rest of his life.

He didn't want to be a Preacher because that was too much pressure and authority. But Mom wanted him to be one. So she put pressures on him to address "issues" he had with the church leadership, particularly with modesty and hypocrisy she saw.

In one of these meetings, "The Men" (term for those in leadership) asked my Dad some questions about why this was such an issue with him, he told them about my Mom's concerns and his responsibility to protect his home.

Ohhhhh shit.

Wrong thing to say.

If they went for coffee, which was a rare thing, maybe they did 4 times in my childhood, she would demand why he looked at the waitresses butt as she walked away from the table or try to see down her blouse when she poured them a cup of coffee. Now a war had begun between them. A war that Dad never stood a chance to win. Not once.

He chose to do that June 13th,1993 when Hans & Shelley got married. When the bride walked down the isle, with a neckline "too low", we walked out.

We marched out with out heads held high, beeming that we were doing a "righteous act of God".

My heart broke that day.

Tears slid down my face as we drove home.

I felt so empty inside. Worse than I ever had, and I didn't know why.

The irony?

We never did travel.

She then began threatening divorce. Pitting us kids against each other when my brother wanted to live with Dad, but us girls would get no choice because she already never left us alone with my Dad as it was, even before all of this.

I made her squirm so deeply that she told me to stop asking questions and that I would understand "when I became an adult".  I risked being beaten to fight for their relationship. I said some things that made her utterly hate me and lash out in the worst rage I ever saw, until I was raped at age 17.

It is what drove me to read relationship books and do courses and work on me long before a man came into my life.

To see how much of my life, the spirit within me, has been suffocating.

It's difficult to discuss "the rest of the story" like Paul Harvey could do. Maybe because there is no good ending.

The Slow Demotion: How You Got Replaced in Your Own Marriage by Your Partner's Friends, Podcasts, and Hobbies
There's a moment, sometimes, when you realize something about your marriage that you didn't expect to ever have to realize.
You realize you've been replaced.
Not by another person, in the way the culture has language for. Not by an affair. Not by someone they fell in love with at work. The replacement is more diffuse than that, and quieter, and in some ways more devastating, because it's been happening for years and you didn't notice it as it was happening.
You've been replaced by your partner's friends. By their hobbies. By their podcasts. By the people they follow on social media. By their book club. By their golf buddies. By the woman from their running group. By the guys they play poker with on Thursdays. By the parasocial relationship they have with the host of the show they listen to on their commute.
Slowly, over years, the things that used to flow between the two of you have been redirected to other people and other places. The energy. The curiosity. The wit. The vulnerability. The aliveness. The version of them that used to be activated by being near you is now being activated by other rooms. Other voices. Other relationships. And the version of them that comes home to you is the leftover. The drained one. The one with nothing much left to give.
You didn't catch it as it was happening. The redirection was gradual. There was no specific Tuesday when they decided to give the most interesting parts of themselves to people who weren't you. It just happened, slowly, through a thousand small choices, and now you're standing in your own kitchen looking at the person you've been married to for fifteen years and realizing they're more alive when they're texting their friend group than they are when they're talking to you.
This is the demotion.
Most people who experience it can't articulate what's happening. They feel something is wrong. They feel jealous in a way that doesn't quite fit the situation. They feel small. They feel like they've become irrelevant inside their own marriage. They wonder if they're being unreasonable. They tell themselves it's good that their partner has friends. It's good that their partner has hobbies. It's good that their partner has interests outside the marriage. They're right about all of that.
But what they're missing is that there's a difference between a partner who has a full life outside the marriage and brings the energy of that life back into the marriage, and a partner who has a full life outside the marriage and brings the leftover crumbs back into the marriage. The first one enriches the marriage. The second one slowly empties it.
Most people who feel this can't quite distinguish between the two. They just feel the absence of something they can't name.
Let me describe what the demotion actually looks like, because once you can see it, you can stop wondering if you're being crazy.
It looks like your partner laughing harder at something on a podcast than they laugh at anything you say.
It looks like them telling a story to their friend on the phone with a kind of animation and detail and aliveness that they haven't brought to a dinner conversation with you in months.
It looks like them coming home from a long day, exhausted, but somehow finding energy to text their friend group at length while only managing to grunt a few words at you when you ask how their day was.
It looks like them planning trips with friends that they wouldn't have the energy to plan with you. Booking flights. Coordinating schedules. Researching restaurants. Putting together the kind of detailed itinerary that, in your relationship, has been your job for the entire marriage because they were too tired to participate.
It looks like them remembering the small things their friends have told them, and forgetting the small things you've been telling them for years.
It looks like them being the version of themselves you fell in love with when they're at work, or with their book club, or with their college roommates, and being a flatter, more depleted version of themselves when they're home with you.
It looks like you watching them light up at a podcast guest in a way they haven't lit up in your kitchen in five years.
It looks like the conversations you used to have with them, the ones about ideas and meaning and what they're thinking about, now happening between them and someone else. They're having those conversations. They're capable of having them. They're just having them with their cousin. With their colleague. With the woman they sit next to on the train. Not with you.
You can sense all of this without being able to name it, and the not-naming it is part of what makes it so disorienting. Because if you brought it up, you'd sound paranoid or controlling or insecure. They have friends. They have a podcast they like. They have a hobby. None of these are betrayals in the conventional sense. There's nothing to point to. Nothing to confront. Nothing that would justify the size of the feeling you've been carrying.
But the feeling is real.
You've been quietly replaced.
Not by any single thing. By the cumulative redirection of everything that used to flow between you to a hundred other rooms.
Now I want to tell you why this happens, because if you understand the why, you can sometimes do something about it.
Most marriages start with the partners as each other's primary aliveness source. You're the most interesting person in each other's lives. The conversations between you carry the most current of your interior worlds. The energy of your day is brought home and metabolized in the relationship.
Then life happens. Kids. Mortgages. Jobs that consume more than they should. Bodies that get tired. Schedules that fragment. The bandwidth that used to be available for the relationship gets eaten by logistics. And in the absence of the bandwidth, both of you start, without realizing you're doing it, to find smaller, more manageable sources of aliveness elsewhere.
A friendship becomes the place where the parts of you that don't fit into the marriage's logistics get to live. A hobby becomes the place where you get to be a fuller version of yourself than the marriage has time for. A podcast becomes a substitute for the long talks you used to have. A workout group becomes a substitute for the play that used to live between you. A coworker becomes a substitute for the witness you used to have at home.
None of these things are wrong by themselves. The wrongness is the cumulative effect. You've quietly built a life where the most alive parts of you are happening in rooms your partner is not in. And your partner has done the same. And both of you are slightly relieved by the arrangement, because the marriage was getting heavy, and the lightness of these other rooms is welcome.
But the marriage starts to die.
Not from anything dramatic. From the quiet exodus of aliveness to elsewhere.
You're both still inside the marriage. You're both still committed. You're both still going through the motions. But the part of you that used to be the marriage is now distributed across a dozen other rooms, and the marriage itself is just the place where the depleted versions of both of you converge at the end of the day.
This is what I mean by being replaced.
You weren't replaced by a person.
You were replaced by an entire ecosystem.
And the ecosystem is harder to fight than a person would have been. You can't ask them to stop having friends. You can't ask them to delete the podcast. You can't make them quit their hobby. The ecosystem has legitimate reasons to exist. The problem is the ratio. The problem is what's left for you when the ecosystem has taken its share.
If you've recognized yourself in this, I want to tell you what to do.
You don't try to compete with the ecosystem.
You can't out-podcast a podcast. You can't out-friend a friendship. You can't make yourself more interesting than a hobby that's been honed over years. Those rooms have advantages your marriage doesn't have. They're voluntary. They're new. They don't carry the accumulated friction of fifteen years of shared history. They get to be light because they don't have to also handle the dishes.
What you do instead is name the demotion.
Carefully. Without accusation. Without competition.
You can say to your partner, on an ordinary night, "I've been noticing something I want to share with you. It's not a complaint. It's an observation. I feel like the most alive parts of you are happening in places I'm not. With your friends. On the show you listen to. In your hobby. And I miss the version of you that used to live in our marriage. I'm not asking you to give those things up. I'm just noticing that I've been getting the leftovers, and I miss being the place where you bring the alive stuff."
That sentence is hard to say. It's vulnerable. It admits something that feels small. It risks being dismissed.
But it's the only way to start a conversation about a demotion that no individual incident justifies.
Because the demotion isn't about any single thing. It's about the ratio. And the only way to address the ratio is to name it directly.
If your partner can hear that, the conversation can deepen. They can examine, with you, where their aliveness has been going. They might recognize that they've been replacing you too, and that the replacement was unconscious, and that they want to bring their fullest self back into the marriage.
If they can't hear it, you have important information. You're now seeing that the redirection isn't reversible from your side alone. You'll need to decide what to do with that information over time.
But the conversation is worth having.
Because the demotion is real. And it's been killing your marriage quietly for years. And the only way to stop the bleed is to name it and ask, together, whether the marriage can become a place again where both of you bring your alive selves home, instead of leaving them in other rooms.
Most couples never have this conversation.
Most couples just keep being demoted, slowly, year after year, until the marriage is a hollow administrative arrangement and both of them are confused about why it feels so empty when nothing dramatic has gone wrong.
Don't be one of those couples.
Name the demotion.
It might be the most important thing you say to your partner this year.

When You Set a Boundary and the Marriage Ends
I want to write directly to a woman who left a comment on one of my posts, because what she described is happening in marriages all over the country right now, and almost nobody has the language for it.
Here's what she said, summarized.
She's been living with a husband who'd been quietly checking out for a long time. He took a job far from home that required him to be gone for two weeks. While he was gone, she carried the household alone. Two daughters, three and six. A full-time job. The constant low hum of being on alert because there was nobody else there to hand the children to. Two weeks of being a single parent while still wearing the costume of being married.
He came home and didn't look at her.
Didn't ask how it had been.
Didn't acknowledge what she had carried.
Just went to sleep. Talked to the kids. Treated her presence in the house as an inconvenience, or maybe just as scenery.
She left work early the next day to confront it. She told him she couldn't keep doing this. That she couldn't keep protecting their daughters from his absence. That she couldn't keep absorbing the cost of his indecision. That if he didn't want to be in the marriage, he needed to leave, because the children could feel his shutdown and she couldn't keep pretending it wasn't affecting them.
And he, in that moment, decided.
Not in any of the moments before that. Not in the years of slow withdrawal. Not in the months when his body was clearly already gone. Not when she was alone with two small children for two weeks. Not when he came home and didn't see her.
He decided when she finally drew a line.
He suddenly knew, in that moment, that he was done. Ten years of marriage. Two children. Done.
Because she had asked, with her whole body, to be seen. And his response was to leave instead of to look.
And then, because he couldn't take responsibility for the leaving, he made it her fault. He said he couldn't trust her anymore. He refused to explain how, or what that meant, or what he'd been trusting before that suddenly broke.

Currently, about 12% of couples that come to me should no longer be together.
This is almost never a general incompatibility problem.
This is because the wounds on both sides make it impossible to move towards the solution I offer, my vulnerability framework.
They just can't do it.
If you ask why, that is not the correct question.
The human condition is to be risk averse, and revealing ourselves takes monumental courage.
So then we have the question, are these two people ready to one day find a better relationship?
Yes.
They must.
They must learn what this relationship has taught them to choose a slightly less Trauma-Bond-ish relationship.
You will be a better person when the invalidation you get is not so harsh.
That might not seem like something to strive for next time... a less harsh partner.
It absolutely is the journey you must take, seeing red flags that you can only see now.
And you can only see those red flags after you entirely exit the relationship.
But we have a problem.
Exiting, for those highly sensitive people (including Derek Hart by the way), is like getting your wisdom teeth pulled without Novocaine.
It's so painful for a trauma-childhood-inflicted adult to leave a relationship...
...that they often take multiple years to leave.
During those multiple years, misery runs their relationship lives.
One of the most painful parts is the level of regret that you will have just "topping off" your relationship with a few more years to see the above.
This is nobody's fault, and you're both at fault.
Read the sentence above again.
Even if there was fault, it will not help you make a decision.
Forget fault.
Fault is irrelevant.
What is relevant is that as you talk to everybody, trying to find the answer... the truth is...
That you are talking to everybody else... except your partner.
Once your partner does not have your back...
...meaning that they are not the one you go to each day to reveal your personal life difficulties and your conflict difficulties with THAT PARTNER...
...your relationship is in far more trouble than you can recognize.
You need support to:
1. Make the break from trying to find the answers in the eyes of your partner. They are not available for this, as they navigate their dissatisfaction.
2. Grieve the loss... during the loss.
3. Make the connection that you must take these steps so you can begin again with a better choice.
The above writing might not be the most profound explanation of leaving a relationship.
But the above writing is the most profound wisdom you are going to have to learn by doing it.
I have had to do this in my past.
I describe me.
I describe hundreds of my couples.
You deserve love.
And the path to love is agony when you have a trauma bond in your life.
You will not find the perfect partner next time.
You will find a perfect understanding on your path...
...of how to choose someone who says AWWW when you're hurting...
...about anything in your life...
...including your struggle that day...
...with your partner.
Sometimes the only chance you have...
For long term happiness....
Is a brief moment in time of ripping off the bandaid. See less

The Phone in the Bedroom Is the Third Person in Your Marriage
I want to write about something that's happening in almost every long-term marriage in the developed world right now, and that almost nobody is naming as a marriage problem because it doesn't look like a marriage problem.
The phone has become the third person in your bedroom.
Not in a metaphorical way. In a physical, structural, nervous-system-shaping way. The bedroom you used to share with your partner has slowly become a co-working space with two screens and a shared bed. The space that used to be the most intimate room in your house has become the place where two adults lie next to each other scrolling, each in their own private content world, each becoming less available to the other one with every minute that passes.
You probably don't experience this as a marriage crisis. You experience it as how things are. The phone in bed has become so normal that the absence of the phone in bed feels notable, when in fact, the presence of the phone in bed is the historical aberration.
Your grandparents didn't lie next to each other staring at separate luminous rectangles for the last hour of every day for fifty years. Nobody in human history did that until very recently. And the speed at which this practice has become the norm has been faster than the speed at which we've understood what it's doing to long-term relationships.
It's doing something profound.
I want to walk you through what's actually happening when you and your partner spend the last hour of every night next to each other on phones, because once you can see it, you can decide whether you want to keep doing it.
Here's what's happening to the bedroom itself.
The bedroom used to be a sanctuary. A specific kind of room with a specific function. A place where two people transitioned from the public-facing demands of the day into the private, undefended space that only the two of them got to inhabit together. The bedroom was where you brushed your teeth next to each other. Where you talked about the day's small moments. Where you laughed about something stupid that happened at dinner. Where you rolled toward each other and made physical contact that wasn't necessarily about s*x but was about reentering each other's bodies after a day of being apart. The bedroom was where intimacy lived, in its broadest sense. Not just the s*x. The closeness. The unguarded presence. The being-known.
The phone has rewired all of that.
The bedroom is no longer a sanctuary. It's an extension of the public-facing world. Your work emails come in there. Your social feeds come in there. The news comes in there. Strangers' opinions come in there. Algorithms that have been engineered by some of the smartest minds in the world to capture and hold your attention come in there. All of that arrives in the room that used to belong only to you and your partner.
And here's the brutal thing about the algorithms. They are better at capturing your attention than your partner is. They were designed by teams of engineers whose entire job is to make sure you do not look up from the screen. Your partner cannot compete with that. No human can compete with that. Asking your partner to be more interesting than the algorithm is asking them to outperform a system that was built specifically to outperform humans.
So the algorithm wins.
Every night.
Without you noticing.
And every minute the algorithm wins, you're spending in your most intimate room not being intimate with the person you're supposed to be intimate with.
Here's what's happening to your bodies.
Bedtime used to involve a specific physiological transition. The lights went down. The day ended. The body began to shift from sympathetic activation, the nervous system state that runs you through your day, into parasympathetic recovery, the state that lets you sleep and lets your body restore itself. That transition used to happen alongside the rituals of being with your partner. The brushing teeth together. The talking about the day. The lying down and reaching for each other. The physical proximity that signaled to both nervous systems that the day was over and you were now in the safe space.
Phones disrupt this transition.
Blue light tells your body to stay awake. The dopamine hits from notifications and feeds keep your sympathetic nervous system activated past the point where it should have downshifted. Your body doesn't get to do the wind-down it's supposed to do, because you're holding a device that's actively keeping you in the state your body needed to leave.
And here's the part most people don't realize. When you and your partner are both on your phones in bed, you're not just keeping yourselves activated. You're keeping each other activated. Two nervous systems in the same room, both wound up, both unable to do the parasympathetic shift, both signaling to each other that it isn't safe to let down yet.
You are co-regulating each other into a state of chronic low-grade alert in the very room that used to be the place where you co-regulated each other into rest.
This is one of the reasons so many couples are tired in a way that better sleep doesn't fix. The room where they used to recover has become a room that depletes them further. They wake up not having truly rested, because their bodies didn't get to do the restoration they were supposed to do.
Here's what's happening to your conversations.
The bedroom used to be where the small daily debriefs happened. The thirty seconds of, "I forgot to tell you the weird thing that happened at lunch." The moment of, "Did you see what your sister posted today?" The quiet, "Are you okay? You seemed off at dinner." The brief check-in that closed out the day for both of you and made sure neither of you was carrying anything unexamined into sleep.
Those debriefs don't happen anymore.
The window for them is gone. It's been replaced by scrolling. The thirty seconds that would have held a small important exchange between you is now thirty seconds of TikTok or Instagram or news. Multiplied by hundreds of nights a year. For years. Adding up to thousands of small debriefs that didn't happen because there was always a screen instead.
Most couples don't notice this loss. They don't experience the absence of the small debriefs as a specific thing. They just experience a slow drift into not knowing what's going on in their partner's life. They start to feel like they don't really know what their partner has been thinking about lately. They start to feel like the marriage has become more functional and less alive. They can't trace the change to anything specific because the change happened in fragments, thirty seconds at a time, every single night, while a screen was lighting their face.
Here's what's happening to physical intimacy.
This is the part people understand most easily, but I want to name it precisely.
When you're on a phone, your body is engaged with the screen. Your hands are holding it. Your eyes are tracking it. Your attention is in it. Your body is not available to the body of the person next to you, because your body is occupied. Even when nothing s*xual is happening, the constant low-grade physical occupation of phone-holding means your body has stopped being available for the casual, automatic physical contact that used to happen between two bodies sharing a bed.
The hand that used to find your partner's hip in the dark is now holding a phone.
The leg that used to wrap over theirs is now still because you're propped up on your elbow looking at a screen.
The face that used to turn toward them as you drifted toward sleep is now angled toward the device.
The body habits that used to keep you tethered to each other physically have been replaced by body habits that keep you tethered to a screen. And after years of this, the bodies stop reaching for each other automatically, because they've forgotten how. The physical default has become two bodies separately engaged with their devices instead of with each other.
When you do try to reach for each other physically, after years of this, it feels disruptive. You have to put the phone down. You have to interrupt the scroll. You have to redirect attention. 100 Reasons You're in Deep Trouble If You're in a Relationship to Have Your Needs Met Instead of to Connect and Repair
If the primary reason you're in your relationship is to have the other person meet your needs, you are in much deeper trouble than you know. Most people don't understand the difference between using a partner as a need-meeting machine and being in a relationship of connection and repair. The difference is the whole thing. It's the difference between a marriage that becomes more alive over time and one that quietly hollows out while looking fine on the surface.
I'm going to list a hundred reasons this orientation will eventually destroy your relationship. Some of them will sound similar. That's intentional. The pattern is fractal. It shows up in a thousand small ways, and you have to see it from many angles before you really catch yourself doing it.
1. Needs are infinite. Connection is sustainable. A partner can never meet enough needs to fill you, because the well is bottomless. Connection feeds something different and doesn't require constant replenishment.
2. Need-based relationships make your partner a service provider. Service providers can be replaced. People you're connected to can't.
3. The moment your partner stops meeting a need, you experience them as failing you, even if they're doing everything else well. Connection survives a partner not meeting a need. Need-based love doesn't.
4. You start keeping score without realizing you're keeping score.
5. You measure the relationship in transactions instead of in moments.
6. Your partner becomes an instrument of your wellbeing instead of a person whose interior life matters to you.
7. You stop being curious about who they actually are. You only care about what they can do for you.
8. The conversations between you get reduced to whether they're meeting your needs that day.
9. You experience their independent activities as a threat. Anything they do that doesn't serve your needs feels like abandonment.
10. You can't tolerate them having a bad day, because their bad day means they can't meet your needs.
11. You can't tolerate your own bad day, because you immediately demand they fix it instead of staying with yourself.
12. You become unable to soothe yourself, because soothing has been outsourced to your partner.
13. The skills of self-regulation atrophy in you, because you've stopped practicing them.
14. You become more childlike over time inside the marriage, not more mature.
15. Your partner becomes parental over time, whether they want to or not.
16. The dynamic becomes inherently unequal. There's no peer relationship in a need-meeting structure.
17. S*xual desire dies in inequality. You can't fully want someone you've been treating as a parent.
18. They can't fully want you either, because they've stopped seeing you as a peer.
19. You start to feel chronically unsatisfied even when your partner is doing a lot for you, because there's always another need behind the one they just met.
20. They start to feel chronically inadequate, because no matter how much they do, it's never enough.
21. The resentment builds invisibly, on both sides.
22. You don't know it's resentment. You think it's love that's not being returned correctly.
23. They don't know it's resentment either. They think they're failing.

If the primary reason you're in your relationship is to have the other person meet your needs, you are in much deeper trouble than you know. It's the difference between a marriage that becomes more alive over time and one that quietly hollows out while looking fine on the surface.

2. Need-based relationships make your partner a service provider. Service providers can be replaced. People you're connected to can't.

3. The moment your partner stops meeting a need, you experience them as failing you, even if they're doing everything else well. Connection survives a partner not meeting a need. Need-based love doesn't.

4. You start keeping score without realizing you're keeping score.

5. You measure the relationship in transactions instead of in moments.

6. Your partner becomes an instrument of your wellbeing instead of a person whose interior life matters to you.

7. You stop being curious about who they actually are. You only care about what they can do for you.

8. The conversations between you get reduced to whether they're meeting your needs that day.

9. You experience their independent activities as a threat. Anything they do that doesn't serve your needs feels like abandonment.

10. You can't tolerate them having a bad day, because their bad day means they can't meet your needs.

11. You can't tolerate your own bad day, because you immediately demand they fix it instead of staying with yourself.

12. You become unable to soothe yourself, because soothing has been outsourced to your partner.

13. The skills of self-regulation atrophy in you, because you've stopped practicing them.

14. You become more childlike over time inside the marriage, not more mature.

15. Your partner becomes parental over time, whether they want to or not.

16. The dynamic becomes inherently unequal. There's no peer relationship in a need-meeting structure.

17. S*xual desire dies in inequality. You can't fully want someone you've been treating as a parent.

18. They can't fully want you either, because they've stopped seeing you as a peer.

19. You start to feel chronically unsatisfied even when your partner is doing a lot for you, because there's always another need behind the one they just met.

20. They start to feel chronically inadequate, because no matter how much they do, it's never enough.

21. The resentment builds invisibly, on both sides.

23. They don't know it's resentment either. They think they're failing.

24. The gap between you and them widens every year while you both think the marriage is fine.

25. Connection requires both people to bring their whole selves into the room. Need-based love requires only that one person perform a role for the other.

32. The arguments don't end with repair. They end with one person winning and the other person resenting.

35. They can't apologize either, for the same reason.

36. The marriage becomes a place where neither of you can be wrong, which means neither of you can grow.

37. Growth is impossible without the willingness to be wrong. So the relationship stays frozen at whatever level of maturity you both had on the day you committed.

The 47 Things You Focus On When You Think the Relationship Is Moving Too Fast (And the One Thing That Actually Determines the Speed)
Most people in a new or developing relationship spend an enormous amount of time worrying about whether it's moving too fast. They're watching the calendar. They're reading articles about timelines. They're asking their friends for opinions. They're consulting advice columns. They're cross-referencing how long other couples waited before doing certain things.
And the thing they're tracking has almost nothing to do with what actually determines whether a relationship is moving at the right speed.
Here are 47 things people obsess over when they think a relationship is moving too fast, almost none of which are the actual measure.
1. How soon you said I love you.
2. How soon they said it back.
3. Whether you said it first or they did.
4. Whether the I love you came before or after a milestone holiday.
5. How quickly you were introduced to their friends.
6. How quickly you were introduced to their family.
7. How quickly you met their parents.
8. How quickly you met their siblings.
9. Whether you met their kids too soon.
10. Whether you met their ex's kids too soon.
11. Whether you've been invited to family events that imply commitment.
12. Whether you've been to a wedding together.
13. Whether you've been to a funeral together.
14. How quickly you started spending most nights together.
15. Whether you stayed over more than three or four nights in a row in the early months.
16. Whether you have a drawer at their place.
17. Whether you have a toothbrush at their place.
18. Whether you have your own keys.
19. Whether you've been given a code to the alarm.
20. How quickly you've started cooking for each other.
21. How soon you booked a vacation together.
22. Whether the first vacation was a weekend or a full week.
23. Whether you've met each other's pets.
24. Whether you've watched each other's pets.
25. How quickly you discussed moving in.
26. The exact month you moved in together.
27. Whether you moved into their place or yours or got a new one together.
28. How much you each contribute to rent.
29. Whether you've combined any finances.
30. Whether you have a joint account.
31. Whether you've merged any subscriptions.
32. Whether you've merged any streaming services.
33. Whether you've added each other to phone plans.
34. Whether your name is on each other's emergency contacts.
35. How long it took before you talked about marriage.
36. How long it took before you talked about kids.
37. The age at which each of you wants to be married by.
38. The age at which each of you wants to have kids by.
39. Whether you've discussed where you'd raise the kids.
40. How quickly you've integrated into each other's social circles.
41. How quickly you've started showing up on each other's social media.
42. Whether you've made it official online before you felt ready offline.
43. Whether your relationship status is public or private to each other's networks.
44. Whether your photos together have been shared with their family group chat.
45. How quickly you've adopted each other's slang or speech patterns.
46. How quickly you've adopted each other's hobbies.
47. How quickly you've started planning futures together that involve specific years, specific places, specific outcomes.
These are all the things people track.
These are all the things friends ask about. These are all the things advice columns address. These are all the things you bring to your therapist when you're worried the relationship is moving too fast or too slow.
And the entire framework is wrong.
The speed of a relationship is not determined by any of these things.
Not one of them.
You can hit every single one of these milestones in the first three months and have a relationship that's actually crawling. You can be slow on every external marker and have a relationship that's accelerating into the deepest territory two people can reach.
The speed of a relationship is determined by exactly one thing.
The frequency at which both of you risk sharing the imperfect, vulnerable, embarrassing, hidden parts of yourselves with each other, and stay in the room together while you feel the pain of those revelations, and repair when one of you mishandles them.
That's it.
That's the only measure.
Two people can move in together after a month and still be strangers, because neither of them has risked anything real. Two people can date for two years without moving in and be deeply, irrevocably bonded, because they've been doing the actual work of revealing themselves.
The work of becoming close to another human being is the work of letting them see the parts of you that you've been hiding from everyone, including yourself, and watching them stay. It's the work of telling them, early, the things you don't like about them, before those things calcify into resentments. It's the work of telling them, early, the things you're afraid of and ashamed of, so they can start to know who they're actually with. It's the work of letting them tell you the same, and absorbing it, and not running from it.
It's the work of repair.
Because the moment one of you reveals something real, the other one is going to mishandle it at least once. They'll say the wrong thing. They'll react in a way that hurts. They'll get defensive. They'll go silent. The mishandling is inevitable. The mishandling is not the failure of the relationship. The willingness to come back and repair the mishandling is the actual relationship being built.
Most people never do this.
Most people skip the revealing. They stay in the curated version of themselves for months, sometimes years. They show their partner the polished interior. They wait until they feel safe to share the harder parts, and the safety never quite arrives, because safety isn't built by waiting. Safety is built by risking.
So the relationship hits all the external markers. They move in. They get engaged. They get married. They have kids. They build a life together. And the whole time, neither of them has been brought into the actual interior of the other person. The interior has been guarded. Hidden. Managed.
And then, ten years later, they wonder why the marriage feels hollow despite everyone having done all the right things on schedule.
The hollowness is the relationship that wasn't built.
Because the relationship doesn't get built through the milestones. The relationship gets built through the moments of revelation and repair that the milestones were supposed to mark, but couldn't actually produce on their own.
If you want to know whether your relationship is moving at the right speed, don't look at the calendar.
Look at this instead.
How many things have you told your partner, in the time you've been together, that you've never told anyone else? How many imperfections have you let them see? How many fears have you named to them out loud? How many things have you not liked about them and said something about, instead of swallowing? How many ruptures have you had together and successfully repaired?
If those numbers are high, your relationship is moving fast in the way that matters, regardless of how many of the 47 milestones you've hit.
If those numbers are low, your relationship is moving slow in the way that matters, regardless of how many of the 47 milestones you've hit.
Most relationships are moving slow in the way that matters.
That's why so many marriages, after years of moving fast on every external metric, find themselves staring at strangers across a kitchen table.
The strangers were always there.
Nobody risked enough revelation to make the strangers known.
The work of a real relationship is not the work of hitting milestones.
It's the work of being seen, and seeing, and staying through the pain of both.
If you want to move at the right speed, share something tonight that you've been holding back.
Watch what happens.
If they can stay with it, you've just moved a real step forward.
If they can't, you have important information about what kind of relationship you're actually in.
But don't measure the relationship by how quickly you booked the vacation or moved in together or said the words.
Measure it by what you've risked.
That's the only number that ever mattered.

How to Revive a Dormant Layer Without the Conversation Feeling Forced or Therapeutic
Once you've identified that a layer of love has gone dormant in your marriage, the temptation is enormous to try to fix it. To do something about it. To turn the layer into a project.
Don't.
The project kills the layer. Every time. Without exception.
Let me explain why, because it's one of the most counterintuitive things about long-term relationships, and it's the reason most couples who finally identify what's missing make the very mistake that ensures they'll never get it back.
Here's what happens when you turn a layer into a project.
You realize, let's say, that romantic love has been dormant for years. You sit with the realization. You decide you want to bring it back. So you do what feels logical. You schedule a date night. You make a reservation. You buy a card. You light candles. You put on the outfit. You announce, in some form, that this is a romantic evening. You and your partner show up to the candlelit dinner having both prepared for the romantic experience.
