The Slow Death of Curiosity in Long-Term Love
I want to ask you a question, and I want you to actually answer it before you keep reading.
When was the last time you asked your partner a question you didn't already know the answer to?
Not a logistical question. Not "what time are you home tonight." Not "did you pick up the dry cleaning." Not "do you want pasta or chicken." Those don't count. Those are operations, not questions.
A real question. About them. About what they think. About what they're afraid of. About what they want from the rest of their life. About what's been on their mind lately. About what they believe about something. About something you genuinely don't already know the answer to.
If you can't remember the last time, you're in trouble.
If you can remember it, but it was longer ago than you'd like to admit, you're in trouble.
If you've been asking versions of the same questions for years and getting the same answers and not noticing that the questions stopped producing new information a long time ago, you're in trouble.
You're in trouble because curiosity is the lifeblood of long-term love, and curiosity is one of the first things busy adults stop bringing to the people they live with. Not because they don't love them. Because they've decided, somewhere along the way, that they already know who their partner is.
That decision is wrong.
It's wrong every time.
It's wrong even when you've been with someone for thirty years.
People keep changing. The person you married is not the person you're married to now. The person you're married to now is not the person you'll be married to in five years. Every person inside a long-term relationship is in continuous quiet evolution. They're having thoughts they didn't have last year. They're afraid of things they weren't afraid of when you met them. They're hungry for things they didn't know they were hungry for. They're letting go of beliefs they used to hold without telling anyone they let them go.
If you stop being curious, you don't get to know any of that.
You don't get to know who your partner is becoming.
You stay in a relationship with the person they used to be.
Meanwhile, the person they actually are, the current one, the one in continuous becoming, is going through their evolution alone. They have no witness. The most important person in their life has decided they already know the answer to who they are, so the questions stopped getting asked, and the new self is unfolding in private.
This is one of the deepest forms of loneliness in a long-term relationship.
Being unknown by the person who claims to know you best.
Let me describe how curiosity dies, because the death is so quiet that almost nobody notices it as it's happening.
In the early years of the relationship, curiosity is automatic. You're hungry to know everything about them. You ask about their childhood. About their dreams. About the people who shaped them. About what they're afraid of. About what they hope for. You listen with full attention because every answer is new information, and the new information is thrilling. The asking and the listening is how the bond is being built.
Then time passes.
You start to feel like you have a sense of who they are. You start to feel like you've heard the major stories. You start to feel like you can predict what they'd think about most things. The hunger to ask diminishes, because the asking starts to produce information you already have.
Then life gets busier. Kids. Jobs. Mortgages. The bandwidth that used to be available for long open-ended conversations gets eaten by logistics. The questions you ask shrink to fit the available time, and the available time only fits operational questions. What time. Who's getting whom. What about Friday.
The deeper questions stop happening, not because you don't care, but because there's no room.
And here's the killer.
After a while, the absence of the deeper questions starts to feel normal. You forget you used to ask them. You forget there was a time when you wanted to know what your partner was thinking about something that wasn't on the schedule. The forgetting is total. You don't experience yourself as someone who used to be curious and stopped. You experience yourself as someone who already knows their partner. The previous version of yourself, the curious one, has been edited out of your own self-narrative.
Meanwhile, your partner is doing the same thing to you. They've stopped asking about your interior life. They've stopped wondering what you're thinking about that isn't logistics. They've stopped tracking the small evolutions in who you're becoming.
So you've become unknown to each other. Both of you. Simultaneously.
And nobody named the becoming-unknown as it was happening.
This is why so many couples in their fifties and sixties, when the kids are grown and the logistics finally have less weight, sit across from each other at the kitchen table and discover they have nothing to say.
The nothing-to-say isn't an aging problem. It isn't a dying-marriage problem. It's a curiosity-died-decades-ago problem. The conversational reservoir was supposed to be replenished by ongoing curiosity throughout the entire marriage. The replenishment stopped sometime around year five or seven or ten. The reservoir has been running on whatever curiosity stored up before then.
By the time the kids leave, the reservoir is empty.
The two people sitting at the kitchen table are looking at strangers, because they stopped being interested in each other years ago, and you can't be in a real conversation with someone you're not curious about.
I want to give you the warning signs of curiosity dying, because they're specific and concrete and almost everybody can spot them once they know what to look for.
You can predict, almost word for word, what your partner will say about most topics.
You finish their sentences in your head, sometimes out loud, sometimes accurately, sometimes not, but you've stopped waiting for them to finish.
You're surprised, occasionally, by something they say, and the surprise registers in you as wrong instead of as evidence that you don't actually know them as well as you think.
You correct them when they describe themselves in a way that doesn't match your version of them. You tell them what they actually mean. You tell them what they actually feel. You tell them who they actually are. As if your version is more authoritative than theirs.
You feel mildly annoyed when they tell a story you've heard before, instead of feeling curious about why they're telling it again, what made the story arise tonight, what part of them is reaching toward you through the retelling.
You've stopped reading what they're reading. You've stopped asking what they're learning. You've stopped engaging with their interior life as something worth visiting.
When they have a strong reaction to something, your first move is to interpret the reaction in terms of your existing model of them, instead of asking what's happening in them right now.
When they want to talk about something abstract, something philosophical, something about meaning or values or what they're worried about in the world, you redirect to logistics, or you tune out, or you give a short answer that closes the conversation.
You'd rather talk to a friend or a coworker about something interesting than your partner. Because they don't bring the same kind of curiosity.
You don't tell them what's been on your mind, because they wouldn't really know what to do with it. You experience this as their failure. It's actually the result of you having stopped asking, which trained them to stop offering, which trained you to stop telling, which closed the loop.
When you imagine your partner's interior life right now, what they might be thinking about, what they might be afraid of, what they might be quietly grieving, you have nothing. The image is blank. You don't know what's in there. You haven't asked in a long time.
If those signs are present, curiosity has died in your marriage.
Now I want to tell you what to do about it.
You start asking again.
Not all at once. Not as a project. Not as a relationship-rebuilding exercise. Just one question, on an ordinary night, that you actually want the answer to.
Try one of these, tonight, and see what happens.
What's something you've been thinking about lately that you haven't told me about?
What's something you used to believe that you don't believe anymore?
What's something you're more afraid of now than you were ten years ago?
What's something you've changed your mind about recently, and what changed it?
What's something you wish I knew about you that I don't ask about?
What's something you're proud of that nobody really knows about?
What do you think happens when we die? I'm curious how that's evolved for you.
What's something you've been hungry for in your own life that you haven't been able to name?
If you had a free Saturday, no obligations, no me, no kids, what would you actually do? Not what you'd say. What you'd actually do.
What's something you used to want that you don't want anymore?
What's something you want now that you didn't want when we got together?
Pick one. Ask it. Then sit there and listen, without interpreting, without projecting, without responding too quickly.
Watch your partner's face.
You may see something cross it that you haven't seen in years.
The look of being asked a real question by the person who's supposed to know them best.
It's a look of relief. Of being seen. Of being tracked. Of being met.
Most partners in long-term relationships have not received that look in a long time, because nobody has been asking them anything that requires them to bring their actual self to the answer.
When you ask a real question, you give your partner permission to bring their real self into the room.
And the real self, when it comes into the room, is unbelievably interesting.
You will discover things you didn't know.
You will be surprised.
You will think, somewhere in the conversation, "I had no idea they thought about that." Or, "I had no idea they were afraid of that." Or, "I had no idea they wanted that."
The not-having-known is information.
It's evidence that you've been in a relationship with a sketch of them, a sketch that hasn't been updated in years, instead of with the person they actually are.
The good news is, you can update the sketch.
You can keep updating it for the rest of your life.
The marriage that gets to do this is the marriage that stays alive, even after thirty years, even after the kids are grown, even after the logistics get quiet and the kitchen table is just two people sitting across from each other in the evening.
The marriages that don't do this are the marriages where the kitchen table becomes a place of silence. Where two people who used to know each other have become strangers without realizing they were becoming strangers.
You don't have to become strangers.
You just have to keep asking.
One question a week.
One question at a time.
The kind that requires a real answer.
The kind that says, in a single sentence, "I'm still curious about you. I haven't decided I know you. I want to keep finding out."
That sentence, asked over and over for the rest of the marriage, is the difference between two people who keep falling into deeper love over decades and two people who quietly become coworkers.
Which marriage do you want?
The choice is in the questions.
Ask one tonight.
You may rediscover the person you've been sleeping next to for fifteen years.
And they may rediscover you.

The Slow Death of Curiosity in Long-Term Love

I want to ask you a question, and I want you to actually answer it before you keep reading.

When was the last time you asked your partner a question you didn't already know the answer to?

Not a logistical question. Not "what time are you home tonight." Not "did you pick up the dry cleaning." Not "do you want pasta or chicken." Those don't count. Those are operations, not questions.

A real question. About them. About what they think. About what they're afraid of. About what they want from the rest of their life. About what's been on their mind lately. About what they believe about something. About something you genuinely don't already know the answer to.

If you can't remember the last time, you're in trouble.

If you can remember it, but it was longer ago than you'd like to admit, you're in trouble.

If you've been asking versions of the same questions for years and getting the same answers and not noticing that the questions stopped producing new information a long time ago, you're in trouble.

You're in trouble because curiosity is the lifeblood of long-term love, and curiosity is one of the first things busy adults stop bringing to the people they live with. Not because they don't love them. Because they've decided, somewhere along the way, that they already know who their partner is.

That decision is wrong.

It's wrong every time.

It's wrong even when you've been with someone for thirty years.

People keep changing. The person you married is not the person you're married to now. The person you're married to now is not the person you'll be married to in five years. Every person inside a long-term relationship is in continuous quiet evolution. They're having thoughts they didn't have last year. They're afraid of things they weren't afraid of when you met them. They're hungry for things they didn't know they were hungry for. They're letting go of beliefs they used to hold without telling anyone they let them go.

If you stop being curious, you don't get to know any of that.

You don't get to know who your partner is becoming.

You stay in a relationship with the person they used to be.

Meanwhile, the person they actually are, the current one, the one in continuous becoming, is going through their evolution alone. They have no witness. The most important person in their life has decided they already know the answer to who they are, so the questions stopped getting asked, and the new self is unfolding in private.

This is one of the deepest forms of loneliness in a long-term relationship.

Being unknown by the person who claims to know you best.

Let me describe how curiosity dies, because the death is so quiet that almost nobody notices it as it's happening.

In the early years of the relationship, curiosity is automatic. You're hungry to know everything about them. You ask about their childhood. About their dreams. About the people who shaped them. About what they're afraid of. About what they hope for. You listen with full attention because every answer is new information, and the new information is thrilling. The asking and the listening is how the bond is being built.

Then time passes.

You start to feel like you have a sense of who they are. You start to feel like you've heard the major stories. You start to feel like you can predict what they'd think about most things. The hunger to ask diminishes, because the asking starts to produce information you already have.

Then life gets busier. Kids. Jobs. Mortgages. The bandwidth that used to be available for long open-ended conversations gets eaten by logistics. The questions you ask shrink to fit the available time, and the available time only fits operational questions. What time. Who's getting whom. What about Friday.

The deeper questions stop happening, not because you don't care, but because there's no room.

And here's the killer.

After a while, the absence of the deeper questions starts to feel normal. You forget you used to ask them. You forget there was a time when you wanted to know what your partner was thinking about something that wasn't on the schedule. The forgetting is total. You don't experience yourself as someone who used to be curious and stopped. You experience yourself as someone who already knows their partner. The previous version of yourself, the curious one, has been edited out of your own self-narrative.

Meanwhile, your partner is doing the same thing to you. They've stopped asking about your interior life. They've stopped wondering what you're thinking about that isn't logistics. They've stopped tracking the small evolutions in who you're becoming.

So you've become unknown to each other. Both of you. Simultaneously.

And nobody named the becoming-unknown as it was happening.

This is why so many couples in their fifties and sixties, when the kids are grown and the logistics finally have less weight, sit across from each other at the kitchen table and discover they have nothing to say.

The nothing-to-say isn't an aging problem. It isn't a dying-marriage problem. It's a curiosity-died-decades-ago problem. The conversational reservoir was supposed to be replenished by ongoing curiosity throughout the entire marriage. The replenishment stopped sometime around year five or seven or ten. The reservoir has been running on whatever curiosity stored up before then.

By the time the kids leave, the reservoir is empty.

The two people sitting at the kitchen table are looking at strangers, because they stopped being interested in each other years ago, and you can't be in a real conversation with someone you're not curious about.

I want to give you the warning signs of curiosity dying, because they're specific and concrete and almost everybody can spot them once they know what to look for.

You can predict, almost word for word, what your partner will say about most topics.

You finish their sentences in your head, sometimes out loud, sometimes accurately, sometimes not, but you've stopped waiting for them to finish.

You're surprised, occasionally, by something they say, and the surprise registers in you as wrong instead of as evidence that you don't actually know them as well as you think.

You correct them when they describe themselves in a way that doesn't match your version of them. You tell them what they actually mean. You tell them what they actually feel. You tell them who they actually are. As if your version is more authoritative than theirs.

You feel mildly annoyed when they tell a story you've heard before, instead of feeling curious about why they're telling it again, what made the story arise tonight, what part of them is reaching toward you through the retelling.

You've stopped reading what they're reading. You've stopped asking what they're learning. You've stopped engaging with their interior life as something worth visiting.

When they have a strong reaction to something, your first move is to interpret the reaction in terms of your existing model of them, instead of asking what's happening in them right now.

When they want to talk about something abstract, something philosophical, something about meaning or values or what they're worried about in the world, you redirect to logistics, or you tune out, or you give a short answer that closes the conversation.

You'd rather talk to a friend or a coworker about something interesting than your partner. Because they don't bring the same kind of curiosity.

You don't tell them what's been on your mind, because they wouldn't really know what to do with it. You experience this as their failure. It's actually the result of you having stopped asking, which trained them to stop offering, which trained you to stop telling, which closed the loop.

When you imagine your partner's interior life right now, what they might be thinking about, what they might be afraid of, what they might be quietly grieving, you have nothing. The image is blank. You don't know what's in there. You haven't asked in a long time.

If those signs are present, curiosity has died in your marriage.

Now I want to tell you what to do about it.

You start asking again.

Not all at once. Not as a project. Not as a relationship-rebuilding exercise. Just one question, on an ordinary night, that you actually want the answer to.

Try one of these, tonight, and see what happens.

What's something you've been thinking about lately that you haven't told me about?

What's something you used to believe that you don't believe anymore?

What's something you're more afraid of now than you were ten years ago?

What's something you've changed your mind about recently, and what changed it?

What's something you wish I knew about you that I don't ask about?

What's something you're proud of that nobody really knows about?

What do you think happens when we die? I'm curious how that's evolved for you.

What's something you've been hungry for in your own life that you haven't been able to name?

If you had a free Saturday, no obligations, no me, no kids, what would you actually do? Not what you'd say. What you'd actually do.

What's something you used to want that you don't want anymore?

What's something you want now that you didn't want when we got together?

Pick one. Ask it. Then sit there and listen, without interpreting, without projecting, without responding too quickly.

Watch your partner's face.

You may see something cross it that you haven't seen in years.

The look of being asked a real question by the person who's supposed to know them best.

It's a look of relief. Of being seen. Of being tracked. Of being met.

Most partners in long-term relationships have not received that look in a long time, because nobody has been asking them anything that requires them to bring their actual self to the answer.

When you ask a real question, you give your partner permission to bring their real self into the room.

And the real self, when it comes into the room, is unbelievably interesting.

You will discover things you didn't know.

You will be surprised.

You will think, somewhere in the conversation, "I had no idea they thought about that." Or, "I had no idea they were afraid of that." Or, "I had no idea they wanted that."

The not-having-known is information.

It's evidence that you've been in a relationship with a sketch of them, a sketch that hasn't been updated in years, instead of with the person they actually are.

The good news is, you can update the sketch.

You can keep updating it for the rest of your life.

The marriage that gets to do this is the marriage that stays alive, even after thirty years, even after the kids are grown, even after the logistics get quiet and the kitchen table is just two people sitting across from each other in the evening.

The marriages that don't do this are the marriages where the kitchen table becomes a place of silence. Where two people who used to know each other have become strangers without realizing they were becoming strangers.

You don't have to become strangers.

You just have to keep asking.

One question a week.

One question at a time.

The kind that requires a real answer.

The kind that says, in a single sentence, "I'm still curious about you. I haven't decided I know you. I want to keep finding out."

That sentence, asked over and over for the rest of the marriage, is the difference between two people who keep falling into deeper love over decades and two people who quietly become coworkers.

Which marriage do you want?

The choice is in the questions.

Ask one tonight.

You may rediscover the person you've been sleeping next to for fifteen years.

And they may rediscover you.

Those were the layers that brought you together. The intellectual layer was never built because it was never there to be built. There was no intellectual chemistry to begin with, and you both got along well enough on the other layers that the absence of this one didn't seem to matter.
For years.

You've been hungry for it for years.

The wrong choice is the one most people make.
Most people, after recognizing that a layer was never there, just keep living. They don't sit with it. They don't have the conversation. They don't make a real decision. They just absorb the recognition and fold it into the structure of the marriage and keep going.
And the hunger keeps gnawing at them for the rest of their life.
Don't do that.
Sit with the recognition.
Have the conversation.
Make a real decision, with eyes open, about what you can live with for the rest of your life.
Because you're choosing your life right now.
You're choosing what you'll have in twenty years and what you'll be carrying.
If you've recognized that a layer was never there, that recognition is information about your life that deserves your attention.
Don't put it down too quickly.
Don't pretend you didn't see it.
Don't decide before you've understood what you're deciding about.
Sit with it. Watch your partner carefully over the next few weeks. Have the conversation when you're ready. And then make the choice that's right for the life you actually want to live.

That information is valuable. Painful. But valuable.

Both of those choices are valid.

And the hunger keeps gnawing at them for the rest of their life.

Don't do that.

Sit with the recognition.

Have the conversation.

Make a real decision, with eyes open, about what you can live with for the rest of your life.

Because you're choosing your life right now.

You're choosing what you'll have in twenty years and what you'll be carrying.

If you've recognized that a layer was never there, that recognition is information about your life that deserves your attention.

Don't put it down too quickly.

Don't pretend you didn't see it.

Don't decide before you've understood what you're deciding about.

Sit with it. Watch your partner carefully over the next few weeks. Have the conversation when you're ready. And then make the choice that's right for the life you actually want to live.

It deserves your full attention.

The Two-Second Gap
There's a moment that happens in long-term relationships thirty or forty times a day, and the cumulative effect of how this moment goes determines whether the marriage stays alive or slowly dies.
The moment is two seconds long.
It happens when one of you says something, and the other has to respond, and there's a gap between the speaking and the responding where both of you are doing something with your nervous systems that neither of you is fully aware of.
The two-second gap is where the entire relationship lives.
She walks into the kitchen and says, "I had a strange interaction with my sister today." She says it casually. She's not in distress. She's just bringing it. She wants him to be in the room with her for a minute about this thing.
Two seconds pass.
In those two seconds, his nervous system is doing something. He's reading her tone. He's calculating bandwidth. He's running through what he was about to do. He's deciding, without realizing he's deciding, what kind of response to offer.
Then he responds.
The response can take many forms. He can look up and say, "What happened?" with his body actually turning toward her. He can say, "Mm," without looking up. He can say, "What did she do this time?" with a slight edge that tells her he doesn't have the bandwidth. He can ask a question that opens the conversation, or one that signals he's trying to wrap it up before it starts.
Whatever he does in that two-second gap, it lands somewhere in her body.
If he turned toward her, her body relaxes. The sister story comes out. She gets to be in the room with someone who's actually in the room with her. The day's small content gets metabolized between two adults who are present with each other.
If he didn't turn toward her, something different happens. Her body registers, on a level she's not consciously processing, that she hasn't quite landed. She might tell the story anyway. She might shorten it. She might decide, in the second after his non-turning, that this isn't a story for him today. She'll tell it to her friend later. The room they're in is no longer a place where this story can be brought.
Neither of them experiences this as a significant moment.
It's two seconds.
There are forty more of them today.
Most of them go fine. Some of them go like the second version. Over a year, that's hundreds of moments where one of them tried to bring something small and the other one didn't quite turn. Over five years, it's thousands.
The thousands accumulate.
The accumulation is the marriage.
The relationship is not determined by the big things. The major conversations. The fights. The crises. The decisions about kids and houses and careers. Those things matter. They're not the relationship.
The relationship is what happens in the two-second gaps.
The two-second gap is where a thousand tiny choices get made, and every choice signals, to your partner's nervous system, what kind of room this is. Whether it's a room where they can land. Whether their interior life will be received here. Whether you're going to turn toward them.
Let me show you what the two-second gap looks like across different small moments, so you can start to see them in your own life.
He walks into the room where she is. The two-second gap is the moment when she could look up or not look up. The choice is happening in her body. She's reading the importance of what she's doing on the screen against the value of acknowledging his entrance. If she looks up, even briefly, his body registers being seen. If she doesn't, his body registers being inconsequential. He doesn't process this consciously. He just keeps walking. And his nervous system files away, one more time, that walking into rooms she's in doesn't change anything for her.
She sighs while she's washing dishes. The two-second gap is what he does with the sigh. He could pause what he's doing and ask, "You okay?" He could let it pass without comment. He could call out from the other room with something vaguely caring that doesn't require him to actually engage. Whatever he does, her body registers. The sigh was a small offering of her interior state, and how he met it tells her whether the kitchen is a place she can sigh openly or whether sighing is going to be a private matter for her from now on.
He says, "I had a weird thought today." The two-second gap is what she does with the offering. She could say, "Tell me." She could say, "Yeah?" without looking up from her phone. She could ask a follow-up question that opens the door, or one that closes it. Whatever she does, his body registers whether his weird thoughts are welcome here.
She makes a joke. The two-second gap is whether he laughs, or how he laughs, or whether he laughs reflexively at his phone instead. Her body registers whether her humor is being received. If she's not received enough times, her humor starts to live elsewhere, with people who are quicker to laugh.
He looks tired when he walks in the door. The two-second gap is whether she notices. Whether she crosses the room and puts a hand on his shoulder. Whether she says, "Long day?" Whether she keeps doing what she was doing because she didn't actually see him as he walked in. His body registers whether his physical state is something this room tracks or whether he has to perform okay-ness regardless of what's true.
She's about to leave the house. The two-second gap is whether he looks up and says, "Have a good one." Whether he comes over and kisses her. Most of the time, the two-second gap gets filled with turning toward.
That's the work.
Not big gestures. Not date nights. Not weekend retreats. The two-second gap, filled with turning, thousands of times a year, every year, for the rest of your relationship.
Couples that do this don't have a perfect marriage. They have an alive one. Their nervous systems trust each other. Their bodies relax in each other's presence. Their interior lives have a place to land. Their humor gets received. Their tired faces get noticed. Their small moments are met.
That's the same marriage as everyone else's, with one difference. The two-second gaps are filled with turning instead of with default.
You can start tonight.
The next time your partner says anything, even something small, even something you barely register, take the two-second gap as the practice.
Turn toward them.
Watch what happens.
Their face will change in a way you may not have seen in a long time. The change will be small. It will register on a level neither of you names.
But it will be there.
And if you do it again the next time, and the time after that, and the time after that, the cumulative effect over weeks and months will surprise you.
The marriage that has been quietly dying will start to come back.
Not through anything dramatic. Through the simple practice of being the one who turns when your partner reaches for you with the smallest possible offering.
The two-second gap is the entire relationship.
Start filling it.
Tonight.

There's a specific kind of silence in a marriage that's about to end.
It sounds like a normal evening.
The dishes are getting done. The kids are upstairs. Someone is folding laundry. Someone else is moving through the kitchen. The lights are on. The television is on low. There's nothing visibly wrong with the room.
But the silence is different.
It has a quality your body recognizes before your mind does. The silence isn't the comfortable kind, the kind that comes from two people being at ease in each other's presence. It isn't the tense kind either, the kind that comes after a fight. It's a third kind. The kind that sounds like two people who have stopped expecting anything from each other.
There are no small sentences being exchanged. No, "Did you see what happened at work today." No, "What time should we leave on Saturday." No, "I forgot to tell you about the thing with my mom." The small sentences are gone. They've been gone for a while. You didn't notice them disappearing because they disappeared one at a time over months.
The body in the kitchen and the body in the living room are not tracking each other.
You used to track. You used to know, without looking, when your partner crossed the room. Their footsteps registered. Their movements meant something. Now you don't know where they are in the house. You haven't known for a long time. They don't know where you are either. The two of you are operating in separate rooms inside the same house, and the rooms have been getting more separate by the month.
You're not angry.
That's the part that fools you.
You think, "We're not fighting. The marriage must be fine." But the absence of fighting in this kind of silence isn't peace. Fighting requires you to still care enough to push back. The fighting stopped when one of you, or both of you, stopped expecting that pushing back would change anything.
The silence has been there for months. Maybe a year. Maybe longer.
You'll notice it one night. You'll be standing somewhere in the house, holding a cup, and you'll suddenly hear the quality of the quiet. You'll realize you don't know what your partner is thinking about. You'll realize you haven't asked in a long time. You'll realize they haven't asked you either. You'll realize you've been doing this for a while.
You'll feel a small cold thing move through your chest.
Then you'll go back to whatever you were doing.
Because there's nothing to do with what you just noticed. There's no script for what comes next. Your partner is in the other room. The kids need to be put to bed. There's a load of laundry to switch over. The moment passes.
But it doesn't fully pass.
Something stays with you. A new piece of information you didn't have an hour ago. The information is that your marriage is in the silence that comes before the ending.
You don't tell anyone.
You don't even tell yourself, exactly.
But you know.

The two of you are operating in separate rooms inside the same house, and the rooms have been getting more separate by the month.

You're not angry.

That's the part that fools you.

You think, "We're not fighting. The marriage must be fine." But the absence of fighting in this kind of silence isn't peace. Fighting requires you to still care enough to push back. The fighting stopped when one of you, or both of you, stopped expecting that pushing back would change anything.

The silence has been there for months. Maybe a year. Maybe longer.

You'll notice it one night. You'll be standing somewhere in the house, holding a cup, and you'll suddenly hear the quality of the quiet. You'll realize you don't know what your partner is thinking about. You'll realize you haven't asked in a long time. You'll realize they haven't asked you either. You'll realize you've been doing this for a while.

You'll feel a small cold thing move through your chest.

Then you'll go back to whatever you were doing.

Because there's nothing to do with what you just noticed. There's no script for what comes next. Your partner is in the other room. The kids need to be put to bed. There's a load of laundry to switch over. The moment passes.

But it doesn't fully pass.

Something stays with you. A new piece of information you didn't have an hour ago. The information is that your marriage is in the silence that comes before the ending.

You don't tell anyone.

You don't even tell yourself, exactly.

But you know.

THE SUNDAY ACHE
A man told me he can feel Sunday evening in his chest by about 4 PM.
It isn't dread of Monday. He likes his job.
It's the slow tightening that starts when he realizes the weekend is almost over, and the week is going to start again, and the week is going to be with her.
He said it almost apologetically. Like he was embarrassed to even notice it.
I asked him how long this has been happening.
He thought about it. Then he said: "I think four years."
Four years.
Four years of his body telling him something every Sunday afternoon, and four years of him quietly disagreeing with his body. Four years of telling himself it was the season, or the kids, or the demands of work. Four years of waking up Monday morning already tired.
That's how being in the wrong relationship works.
Your body knows before your mind catches up.
Your chest tightens when their car pulls in the driveway. You exhale when they leave for the store. Sunday evening sits heavier than it should. The week is something to survive instead of something to live.
You tell yourself it's the season. You tell yourself it's the kids. You tell yourself it's the project at work. You tell yourself anything except the thing that's actually true.
And the strange part is, on paper, nothing is wrong. Nobody is cheating. Nobody is yelling. Nobody is leaving. The mortgage is paid. The kids are fed. The schedule works. By every external measure, you have a functioning life.
But there's a small voice that goes quiet when they walk into the room.
There's a Tuesday afternoon where you sit in your car in the driveway for ten extra minutes before going inside.
There's a Friday night where you find yourself disappointed that the weekend is two whole days instead of one.
There's a Sunday at 4 PM.
We're trained to ignore these signals. To override them. To call them ungrateful, immature, selfish. To assume that a real adult is supposed to be able to manage their own internal weather while staying in the marriage.
So we manage. We medicate. We get busier. We say yes to more travel for work. We schedule dinners with friends so we don't have to be alone with our partner two nights in a row. We learn the choreography of avoiding our own life.
What I want you to know is this.
Your body is not making it up.
The tightness in your chest at 4 PM on Sunday is information. It's not weakness. It's not ingratitude. It's not a character flaw. It's the part of you that is paying attention to what your conscious mind has been talked out of seeing.
The body keeps the score, as a wiser writer than me once said, and the score it keeps is more accurate than anything your mind is willing to admit yet.
The man in my office knew this, somewhere. He just needed someone to say it out loud so he could stop pretending it was the weather.
You probably know it too.
In an incompatible relationship, you don't help each other with your pain.
You harm each other with your pain. See less

35 Things That Happen in a Long Marriage That Mean More Than You Think
The pause before they answer a question you didn't think was hard.
The way they say "yeah" without looking up.
The moment they laugh at something on their phone harder than they laugh at anything you've said in a week.
The way they fold the towels exactly the way their mother did, and how that started to bother you around year seven.
The specific sigh they make when they see what's in the dishwasher.
The way you wait until they're out of the room to put the dishes in the way you actually want them.
The text you didn't send because you knew how they'd reply.
The text you sent anyway, and the reply that came back, and the way you felt about being right.
The night you both went to bed early because neither of you wanted to be in the same room awake.
The way you both pretend you didn't notice the other person went to bed early.
The specific quality of their hello when they come home, and how it's different from the way they say hello to the dog.
The way you stopped noticing what they were wearing when they left for work.
The way they stopped noticing what you were wearing too.
The conversation you had with your sister about them that you wouldn't repeat in front of them.
The conversation they had with their friend about you that you suspect happened.
The Christmas you both knew it wasn't working anymore and didn't say anything.
The vacation you took anyway after that Christmas, because the deposit was non-refundable.
The way you both perform happiness for the photos.
The way the photos are slightly worse every year, even though you've both gotten technically better at taking them.
The morning you woke up next to them and didn't recognize what you were looking at for a half-second.
The way that half-second has been getting longer, and you've never told anyone.
The friend who got divorced that you stopped seeing because you were afraid she'd be contagious.
The other friend who's still married, who you envy, until you spend time with her and realize hers is worse.
The way you started keeping money in an account they don't know about, and how you tell yourself it's just for emergencies.
The way they probably have one too, and you don't ask.
The hobby they took up that took them out of the house twice a week, and the relief you felt about it.
The hobby you took up that took you out of the house twice a week, and the relief they felt about it.
The way you don't talk about either hobby, because doing so would mean acknowledging that the relief was a real feeling.
The therapist you started seeing without telling them.
The way you've spent forty-five minutes a week, for a year, talking about your marriage to a stranger before talking about it to your spouse.
The dream you had about being single again, and the specific way the dream was not a nightmare.
The dream you had about them dying, and the specific way you felt when you woke up.
The way you can't unfeel either of those dreams now that you've felt them.
The fact that you've never told anyone about either of them.
The fact that they've probably had the same dreams, and they've never told you. See less

What Most Couples Think a Fight Is, and What a Fight Actually Is
Most couples think a fight is about whatever the fight is about.
It isn't. The surface content is the costume. The fight you're having about the dishes is not a fight about the dishes. The fight you're having about the money is not a fight about the money. The fight you're having about whether his mother stays for four days or six is not about his mother. Couples who treat the surface content as the actual content end up resolving the surface content over and over and never understanding why the same fight keeps happening in slightly different costumes for the next twenty years.
Most couples think they're fighting about the same thing.
They're not. You and your partner are almost always fighting about two different things. The fight you think you're having is not the fight your partner thinks they're having. The fight she thinks they're having is, "He doesn't see how much I do." The fight he thinks they're having is, "She doesn't appreciate what I provide." Both of those are real fights. Neither of those is the same fight. The fight ends because both people get exhausted, not because anything got resolved. The unresolved thing returns, in a different costume, on Thursday.
Most couples think the fight starts when one of them said something wrong.
It doesn't. The fight started long before the conversation. It started in the accumulated residue of every unrepaired moment in the relationship, going back years. The thing that was said wrong was just the match. The fuel was already there. Couples who treat the trigger as the cause never investigate the fuel, and the fuel keeps building.
Most couples think the goal of a fight is to be right.
It isn't. The goal of a fight, structurally, is to discharge the discomfort that has accumulated in both nervous systems. Being right is a tactic for discharging it. The discomfort wants to go somewhere, and making your partner wrong is one of the most efficient ways to get it out of your body. Couples who go in trying to be right are using the fight to manage their own internal weather, not to actually resolve anything between them.
Most couples think the loudest moment of the fight is the most important.
It isn't. The most important moment of the fight is the moment that happens an hour before, when one of you signaled something subtle and the other one missed it. The signal was small. A sigh. A shorter answer than expected. A slight pulling back. The fight that erupted later was the cost of the signal not being received. If the signal had been received, the loud moment would not have happened.
Most couples think a fight is a problem.
It isn't. A fight is information. It tells you that something between you needs attention. The fight is not the failure of the relationship. The failure would be the absence of the fight, and the absence of attention to whatever the fight is pointing at. Couples who try to eliminate fighting end up eliminating the data their relationship has been trying to give them.
Most couples think a fight is supposed to end with someone winning.
It isn't. A fight is supposed to end with both of you understanding something you didn't understand an hour earlier. About each other. About yourselves. About what's actually been happening in the relationship. If the fight ends with one of you having won, both of you have lost. Because the winning version of one of you didn't get any new information, and the losing version of the other one is now carrying additional resentment into the next fight.
Most couples think the fight is happening between two adults.
It isn't. The fight is almost always happening between two children inside two adult bodies. The child inside you, the one who didn't get something fundamental as a kid, is the one who reaches for the dish or the money or the in-law as a reason to express the larger hunger. The child inside your partner is doing the same thing. The two children are screaming at each other, and the two adults are watching from a distance, embarrassed but unable to intervene. Couples who don't see this are confused about why the fights feel so much bigger than the surface content would justify. The fights feel that big because two children are inside them.
Most couples think the fight ends when the conversation ends.
It doesn't. The fight ends when the rupture is repaired. If the conversation stops because both of you got tired, the fight is paused, not finished. The unrepaired part stays in the room. It shows up in the way you don't quite look at each other for the next two days. It shows up in the slight chill at dinner. It shows up in the way neither of you reaches for the other one at bedtime. Couples who confuse the end of the conversation with the end of the fight build up enormous reservoirs of unrepaired material that eventually become the architecture of the marriage.
Most couples think a fight is about content.
It isn't. A fight is about contact. Two people, in some form, are trying to reach each other. The reaching is happening in a distorted way, through accusation and defense, but the underlying intention is to be met. Couples who treat the fight as a debate about content never see the reaching underneath. They argue about who said what when, instead of recognizing that both of them, in their own distorted ways, are trying to be felt by the other one.
Most couples think the answer is to stop fighting.
It isn't. The answer is to learn to fight cleanly. To get under the surface content faster. To recognize when the child has taken over. To name what's actually happening before the loud moment arrives. To stay in the room long enough to repair, not just long enough to discharge. To use the information the fight is offering instead of trying to eliminate the fight that's offering it.
Most couples think a fight is something bad that happened to the relationship.
It isn't. A fight is the relationship asking to be looked at. It's the most honest moment most marriages produce in any given month. It's the place where the truth, distorted as it is, is closer to the surface than it is during the calm. Couples who treat the fight as the enemy miss that the fight is one of the most useful events the relationship will offer them, if they know how to read it.
Most couples think a fight ruined the day.
It didn't. The fight didn't ruin the day. What ruined the day was the years of small unrepaired moments that built up into the fuel that the fight ignited. The fight is a flare. The damage was done before the flare went off. The flare is just the visible part. The couples who understand this stop trying to prevent flares and start working on the moments before, where the actual damage is being done quietly.
A fight is two people, often inside the wrong nervous system state, trying to reach each other about something neither of them can fully articulate, using the closest available content as the vehicle for the actual material underneath.
That's what a fight is.
Once you can see it that way, you can stop fighting about the dishes.
And start having the conversation underneath the dishes that you've been needing to have for the last ten years. See less

Why Is Relationship Advice Almost Always Awful?
When you take the enormous risk of bringing a new romantic interest into your life, there are two very separate parts of you at work.
These two parts need to be separated out a bit, for you to understand what the heck is going on.
There's the adult part... conscious, decisive, and knows exactly what it's doing. Well, not exactly, but it knows it feels sooooo good.
And there's the inner child part... unconscious, deeply tucked away somewhere, and is mostly directing the show, and making choices that the adult is not quite aware of.
Let's focus for a second on the simpler one.
The adult part.
This part picks a partner because he's handsome, she's beautiful, she has the same hobbies as you, he dresses nice, he makes you feel special, she's a wonderful lover, she travels, he's politically aligned with you... this list is endless.
Now, back to our inner child part.
When picking a partner, you pick your mirror image.
Your inner child part is always doing pushups in the back room. It's always trying to resolve SOMETHING.
A romantic partner, whether you might like this or not, is here to show you exactly what you believe about yourself.
If your beloved is not open and real and authentic, then you might have more to learn about how to be vulnerable and take emotional risks.
If you have frustration with how your partner behaves, I'm not saying that it's your fault.
What I am saying is that:
1) If you stay with this partner, then you're giving into your inner child mirror, and your own wounded part believes that you should be treated exactly the way you're being treated.
2) You have a growth opportunity, which is to risk saying how you feel, and then observing to see if you have a partner that wishes to grow with you.
If you argue with a romantic partner, then the language of vulnerability is not working between you two.
If vulnerability is not occurring between you both, then its Wicked Witch Of The West sister is running the relationship: criticism and defensiveness.
The problem is not that your partner is a closed book emotionally.
The problem is that:
1) Your wounds believe that your partner is treating you exactly how you feel about yourself.
2) Your fight to have your partner change is filled with your own criticism and defensiveness.
3) You don't yet know the exact vulnerability language to use to unwind yourself from this struggle.
The question is whether or not you want to work with the inner child deep subconscious part and make friends with it.
It needs you.
The adult part knows clearly that your partner drinks too much, is unreliable, lies, and you've recently begun the sophisticated psychological art of calling them a narcissist.
But this information does not help you heal, does not help your partner heal.
Most relationship advice comes in at this level, talking to the adult part.
1) Why are you with him if he doesn't have a job and he sits around all day?
2) Why have you chosen her, if she is generally angry towards men, still punishing her father?
These questions are very simple at the adult level.
But answering these questions from the deeper inner child level is quite tricky.
1) I'm with him because I'm scared to leave, he does make me feel special when he's not drinking, and I feel loved by him. I love him so much. I can't imagine not having his arms around me. But I hate him. I don't get it.
2) I know she's angry, but my heart is so attached, and I don't understand why.
When you're frustrated with a romantic partner, and you want to know what's really happening, you must:
1) Look in the mirror.
2) Ask what makes you attracted to this person.
3) Cultivate a massive amount of self-love and gentleness for yourself.
4) Know that this part is so deep and so human, that you cannot possibly just figure it out intellectually.
5) Get a coach, or some book learning, about how to risk and be vulnerable, instead of attacking. Attacking keeps you bound to the person, and doesn't get you away from them.
6) Recognize when you're talking with friends, that they will usually talk to the adult part, and just ask questions and give advice to the adult part of you. The advice doesn't help. A friend who listens, and is gentle with the part of you that is deeply in love with this mess-of-a-human, is a friend to sit with.
7) Understand that this part of you is barely understandable and cannot be reasoned with. You're in love with this person who treats you like crap. There's a reason, and it's very deep. You must slow down to make contact with your inner-child-romantic-love-choice machine.
Couples that come to me in distress rarely had 17 years of bliss, and one year of difficulty.
They usually had 2 years of bliss, and 15 years of communication being a mess, and 4 years of continuous threats to leave the relationship.
This inner child part that chooses a relationship partner needs management.
It needs soothing.
It needs to be understood in small pieces by your adult part.
It has a mind of its own.
And it's okay that it makes kookoo choices. It doesn't know better.
This young part that makes romantic love choices needs you to be patient with it, to learn from it.
The path of moving from picking emotionally unavailable partners, to recognizing kindness and availability, is a slow healing journey.
Knowing the right emotional risks to take, and recognizing if your partner meets you there, for you both to heal, is one of the most important things you will ever do.
The next time you give a friend romantic advice, check in with yourself.
Are you going to talk to their adult part and just name all the reasons why the partner is bad, collude together on how this human is messing up?
Or are you going to find the most gentle, kind place in both of you, to discuss the topic of romantic love, and talk directly to the inner child temper tantrum that occurs when we're not loved the way we want to be loved?
Relationship advice often has good intentions, but misses the mark entirely. See less

And there's the inner child part... unconscious, deeply tucked away somewhere, and is mostly directing the show, and making choices that the adult is not quite aware of.

Let's focus for a second on the simpler one.

The adult part.

This part picks a partner because he's handsome, she's beautiful, she has the same hobbies as you, he dresses nice, he makes you feel special, she's a wonderful lover, she travels, he's politically aligned with you... this list is endless.

Now, back to our inner child part.

When picking a partner, you pick your mirror image.

Your inner child part is always doing pushups in the back room. It's always trying to resolve SOMETHING.

A romantic partner, whether you might like this or not, is here to show you exactly what you believe about yourself.

If your beloved is not open and real and authentic, then you might have more to learn about how to be vulnerable and take emotional risks.

If you have frustration with how your partner behaves, I'm not saying that it's your fault.

What I am saying is that:

1) If you stay with this partner, then you're giving into your inner child mirror, and your own wounded part believes that you should be treated exactly the way you're being treated.

2) You have a growth opportunity, which is to risk saying how you feel, and then observing to see if you have a partner that wishes to grow with you.

If you argue with a romantic partner, then the language of vulnerability is not working between you two.

If vulnerability is not occurring between you both, then its Wicked Witch Of The West sister is running the relationship: criticism and defensiveness.

The problem is not that your partner is a closed book emotionally.

The problem is that:

1) Your wounds believe that your partner is treating you exactly how you feel about yourself.

2) Your fight to have your partner change is filled with your own criticism and defensiveness.

3) You don't yet know the exact vulnerability language to use to unwind yourself from this struggle.

The question is whether or not you want to work with the inner child deep subconscious part and make friends with it.

It needs you.

The adult part knows clearly that your partner drinks too much, is unreliable, lies, and you've recently begun the sophisticated psychological art of calling them a narcissist.

But this information does not help you heal, does not help your partner heal.

Most relationship advice comes in at this level, talking to the adult part.

1) Why are you with him if he doesn't have a job and he sits around all day?

2) Why have you chosen her, if she is generally angry towards men, still punishing her father?

These questions are very simple at the adult level.

But answering these questions from the deeper inner child level is quite tricky.

1) I'm with him because I'm scared to leave, he does make me feel special when he's not drinking, and I feel loved by him. I love him so much. I can't imagine not having his arms around me. But I hate him. I don't get it.

2) I know she's angry, but my heart is so attached, and I don't understand why.

When you're frustrated with a romantic partner, and you want to know what's really happening, you must:

1) Look in the mirror.

2) Ask what makes you attracted to this person.

3) Cultivate a massive amount of self-love and gentleness for yourself.

4) Know that this part is so deep and so human, that you cannot possibly just figure it out intellectually.

5) Get a coach, or some book learning, about how to risk and be vulnerable, instead of attacking. Attacking keeps you bound to the person, and doesn't get you away from them.

6) Recognize when you're talking with friends, that they will usually talk to the adult part, and just ask questions and give advice to the adult part of you. The advice doesn't help. A friend who listens, and is gentle with the part of you that is deeply in love with this mess-of-a-human, is a friend to sit with.

7) Understand that this part of you is barely understandable and cannot be reasoned with. You're in love with this person who treats you like crap. There's a reason, and it's very deep. You must slow down to make contact with your inner-child-romantic-love-choice machine.

Couples that come to me in distress rarely had 17 years of bliss, and one year of difficulty.

They usually had 2 years of bliss, and 15 years of communication being a mess, and 4 years of continuous threats to leave the relationship.

This inner child part that chooses a relationship partner needs management.

It needs soothing.

It needs to be understood in small pieces by your adult part.

It has a mind of its own.

And it's okay that it makes kookoo choices. It doesn't know better.

This young part that makes romantic love choices needs you to be patient with it, to learn from it.

The path of moving from picking emotionally unavailable partners, to recognizing kindness and availability, is a slow healing journey.

Knowing the right emotional risks to take, and recognizing if your partner meets you there, for you both to heal, is one of the most important things you will ever do.

The next time you give a friend romantic advice, check in with yourself.

Are you going to talk to their adult part and just name all the reasons why the partner is bad, collude together on how this human is messing up?

Or are you going to find the most gentle, kind place in both of you, to discuss the topic of romantic love, and talk directly to the inner child temper tantrum that occurs when we're not loved the way we want to be loved?

25 Things to Say to Your Neurodivergent Partner When They're Debating You Intellectually and Showing No Emotion
1. "I'm not actually trying to win this. I'm trying to feel close to you. Can we slow down?"
2. "I know your brain is making sense of this through logic. I love that about you. I just need a little bit of feeling in the room with the logic."
3. "I'm not arguing with your reasoning. I'm telling you my reasoning isn't the thing I'm asking you to meet right now."
4. "You don't have to agree with me. I just want to know if you can see I'm hurting."
5. "I'm not asking you to abandon how your brain works. I'm asking if you can stay in the room with me while I feel something."
6. "I can tell you're thinking really hard about this. I want to know if you're feeling anything about it too."
7. "Your points are valid. I'm not contesting them. They're just not what I'm reaching for right now."
8. "I know logic feels safer than feeling. I get that. Can you take one small step toward the feeling anyway?"
9. "I love how your mind works. I don't want to change it. I just want it to make room for mine."
10. "I'm not trying to manipulate you with emotion. I'm telling you what's actually happening inside me. Both of those can be data."
11. "You don't have to fix this with the right framework. I just need you near me."
12. "I know it feels like I'm being illogical. I'm not. I'm being emotional. Those are different things."
13. "When you debate me, I feel further away. Not because you're wrong. Because I can't reach you through the argument."
14. "I'm going to slow down. Can you slow down with me? Just for a minute. We don't have to solve anything yet."
15. "I'm not asking you to perform emotion you don't feel. I'm asking if you can sit with mine."
16. "I know it feels like the answer is in figuring out who's correct. The answer I need isn't there. The answer I need is whether we're okay."
17. "I'd rather be wrong and close to you than right and far away."
18. "Tell me what you're feeling, in your own way. It doesn't have to sound like how I'd say it. I just want to know."
19. "I see you working really hard to make sense of this. Thank you. I also need you to know it's hurting me."
20. "I'm not going to keep building my case. I'm going to stop and just be here. Can you do that with me?"
21. "Your way of loving me through analysis is real. I see it. Right now I need a different kind of love too."
22. "If you need to think this through, I get it. Can you tell me when you'll come back to me with the feeling part? I can wait."
23. "I'm not asking you to be neurotypical. I'm asking you to be with me, in whatever way is possible for you."
24. "I know you love me. I'm not testing that. I'm telling you that the love isn't reaching me right now, and I want to know how to help it reach."
25. "I don't want to win this. I want to come back to you. Tell me how we do that."

The first column is honest. The second column is honest and skillful. The first column says what's true. The second column says what's true in a way the person across from you can actually receive.
The work is not to suppress what you feel.
The work is to deliver what you feel in a frequency the other nervous system can metabolize.
Most marriages don't fail because the truth wasn't there. They fail because the truth was delivered in a way the other person couldn't open the door to.
Open the door. Then walk through it. Then say the hard thing.
There are an ENORMOUS number of people with avoidant attachment that will not respond to these.

When a relationship is in distress, both people start making meaning about the other one. It's automatic. It's how the human mind survives long stretches of unmet need. You stop having access to your partner's interior life, so your mind generates one for them. You assign motives. You assign limitations. You assign character. You build a portrait of who your partner is, and the portrait becomes the person you've been married to for the last five or ten years, regardless of who is actually sitting across from you.
Some of the meaning you've made is accurate. Some of it is wildly off. Most of it is somewhere in between, and you have no way to tell which is which, because you and your partner stopped having the kind of conversation where the truth would be revealed years ago.
Here's the trap.
When you finally do try to talk, what comes out of your mouth is the accumulated meaning, not the present moment. You tell them what you've decided they are. You tell them what you've decided they do wrong. You tell them the conclusions you've reached after years of watching them through a particular lens.
And your partner, on the receiving end, hears a verdict. They don't hear an invitation to know you. They don't hear a reaching toward closeness. They hear a list of charges. And they defend. Or shut down. Or counter-attack. Or leave the room. None of which moves the relationship one inch toward repair.
This is the problem with telling your partner what you think is wrong with them, even when you're partly right.
Telling them doesn't change the relationship. The information goes in as accusation and produces defense. The defense produces more accusation. The accusation produces more defense. Years pass. The marriage erodes. Both people genuinely believe they've been trying to communicate, when what they've actually been doing is firing accumulated meaning at each other across a widening canyon.
There is a different way.
The way is to share what you actually see, but to share it as a request for partnership rather than as a verdict. To name what you've noticed, without weaponizing it. To invite your partner to look at it with you, instead of presenting them with the conclusion you've already drawn.
The lists below are an attempt at that.
The first list contains 47 things to say to your partner about where they need help to have a better relationship with you. Things that are honest. Things that go straight to the heart. Things your partner might initially disagree with, because hearing them is hard.

They presume that the marriage is worth trying to repair. They presume that you, too, are in a system that needs change, and you're naming your part of it by naming the dynamic.
The second list is what to say after, when you ask them to come into the work with you.
Both lists are gentle in tone and sharp in content. Honest does not require cruel. Loving does not require vague. You can name the real thing in a way that gives your partner a door to walk through, instead of a wall to defend against.

2. "I think you sometimes mistake going quiet for solving a problem. The problem doesn't go away when you go quiet. It just goes underground."
3. "I think you're harder on me than you realize. Not in big ways. In small daily tones I think you've stopped noticing."
4. "I think you've been operating on the assumption that I'll always be here, and I think that assumption has let you stop trying in ways that have hurt us."
5. "I think you defend yourself before you listen. Almost every time. I don't think you can hear me anymore."
6. "I think you've outsourced our connection to me. I think you've quietly decided I'll do the work of holding us together, and you've let yourself off the hook."
7. "I think you've stopped being curious about who I am, and you didn't notice when it happened."
8. "I think when you don't have words, you go away, and you've never come back to tell me what was happening for you while you were gone."
9. "I think you handle stress by withdrawing into yourself, and the withdrawal has become so automatic you don't even know you're doing it."
10. "I think you make jokes at moments when something real is being asked of you, and the jokes are how you close the door without admitting you closed it."
11. "I think you avoid my pain. Not because you don't care. Because you don't know how to be in the room with it without trying to fix it or fleeing it."
12. "I think you've stopped initiating with me. Physically. Verbally. Any of it. And I don't think you've grieved the stopping."
13. "I think you've gotten comfortable being parented by me, and I don't want to be your parent."
14. "I think you've made the marriage smaller, quietly, over the years, by reducing what you bring to it, and I've been holding the size of the marriage by myself."
15. "I think your phone has become a partner I'm competing with, and I think you don't see how much of you it's taken."
16. "I think when I bring up the hard stuff, you go into a mode that's about getting through the conversation, not about understanding what I'm saying."
17. "I think you've stopped letting me know you. You used to. Somewhere you stopped. I'd like to know why."
18. "I think your version of love is duty, and my version of love is presence, and I don't think we've ever really talked about the gap."
19. "I think you've handled difficult things by drinking, working, scrolling, or going somewhere else inside yourself, and the avoidance has cost both of us."
20. "I think you've made me carry the emotional labor of the marriage, and I think you don't even know what emotional labor is."
21. "I think you've stopped repairing after fights, and the unrepaired material has been quietly building a wall between us for years."
22. "I think your family of origin still runs more of this marriage than you realize, and you've never looked directly at how much."
23. "I think you've been waiting for me to give up so the marriage could just quietly end without you having to make a decision."
24. "I think you've assumed that if I haven't left, I must be fine, and I want you to know that's not how this works."
25. "I think you've stopped looking at me when I talk to you, and you don't know how much that does."
26. "I think you've been disrespectful in ways you don't notice, in micro-expressions and tones, and I think you'd be defensive if I named them, which is part of the problem."
27. "I think you've used your difficult childhood as a reason to never have to grow, and I think you and I both know it's a reason that's outlived its purpose."
28. "I think you've stopped pursuing me, and I think you wouldn't pursue me even if I started backing away."
29. "I think you have a story about how I'm the problem, and you've been running that story in your head for so long it feels true to you, but it isn't."
30. "I think you've made me responsible for your moods, and I think you don't see how much of my day is spent navigating yours."
31. "I think you've stopped asking how I'm doing, and the only time you ask is when you can tell I'm already upset, which is too late."
32. "I think you've kept secrets about how you're really feeling, and I don't even mean affairs. I mean inner secrets. The stuff that makes you a stranger to me."
33. "I think you go through the motions of love without actually being present for any of them, and I think you'd be hurt if I said that, but it's true."
34. "I think you've never let me see you scared, and I think you can't actually be close to me until I do."
35. "I think you've decided who I am and stopped updating the file, and you're now married to a version of me that's ten years out of date."
36. "I think you've used the word 'fine' more times in the last five years than any other word, and I think it's been hiding a lot."
37. "I think you've stopped showing up for the small daily moments, and the small daily moments are most of what a marriage actually is."
38. "I think you've assumed that providing financially is the same as showing up emotionally, and I want you to know it's not."
39. "I think you've made our s*x life a chore for both of us, and I think you don't see your role in how that happened."
40. "I think you've used my flaws as a permission slip to stop working on yours, and I want you to know I see that."
41. "I think you've stopped looking at our children with curiosity, and they've started to feel like assignments to you."
42. "I think you've allowed yourself to be moody in ways you would never tolerate from me, and you don't know that I notice the double standard."
43. "I think you've used your introversion or your stress or your work as a wall to hide behind, and I don't think the wall is really about those things anymore."
44. "I think you've forgotten how to be in awe of me, and I think when I lost that from you, I started to lose myself."
45. "I think you've been carrying something you've never told me, and the not-telling is what's keeping us at this distance."
46. "I think you've stopped imagining a future with me. You've been auto-piloting through the present, and the future has gone quiet in you."
47. "I think you've believed, somewhere deep down, that you don't deserve a real marriage, and you've made ours smaller as a way of confirming what you decided about yourself a long time ago."
