How Successful Couples Counseling Actually Works (And Why Most of It Doesn't)
Most couples counseling fails for a specific reason. The therapist, often well-meaning, often well-trained, tries to make the couple understand each other. They sit two resentful people across from each other and ask them to listen, to mirror, to validate, to see each other.
It doesn't work.
It can't work. Not because the technique is wrong, but because it's moving ten times faster than what's actually possible at the stage the couple is in.
Let me tell you what's actually happening when a couple shows up to my office.
They have crossed the line.
The line is real. There's a place in every long, painful relationship where resentment hardens into something more structural. The early hurts have been protested. The protests didn't work. The hurts have accumulated. The accumulated hurts have produced more hurts. By the time the couple finally walks through the door, they're not in early-stage distress. They're in a state where the most natural thing in the world is to weaponize the other person's words against them, to keep score, to defend, to attack, to flee, to shut down. Their nervous systems have been at war for so long that the war has become the baseline.
You cannot teach two people in this state to understand each other.
You cannot ask them to listen, to validate, to see the other one's perspective. Their bodies will not let them. Their bodies have classified the other person as the source of the threat, and asking them to drop their armor in the room with that threat is not a therapeutic intervention. It's an invitation to retraumatize.
What the couple has actually been doing, for years, is exactly what bad couples counseling asks them to do. They've been trying to understand each other. They've been trying to explain themselves. They've been trying to get the other one to see it from their angle. The trying is what's destroyed them. The trying is the pattern that has produced the resentment.
If a therapist asks them to keep trying, just better this time, the therapist is asking them to do the thing that broke them.
Successful couples counseling is something else.
The first thing that has to happen is that each partner, slowly, with help, begins to make contact with their own interior. Not with their partner's interior. With their own.
They have to feel what they've been feeling for a long, long time. They have to let it come up, in the room, in the presence of a therapist who is safe enough to be the witness. They have to let themselves know what it's been like to live inside this marriage, alone, for years.
This is the work.
The work is not understanding the partner. The work is understanding the self.
When a partner is doing this work, the only thing the other partner has to do is be in the room. Witness. Watch. Not respond. Not defend. Not interject. Not relate it to themselves. Just be there, in their seat, in the room, in the presence of what's happening across from them.
That witnessing, over time, does something more powerful than any cognitive understanding could.
When one partner watches the other partner finally make contact, in real time, with what it's been like inside them, something shifts. Not because they're now understanding their partner. Because they're seeing, in a way they couldn't see before, the actual size of what their partner has been carrying.
Then, the process switches.
The other partner takes the seat of the one making contact. The first partner takes the seat of the witness.
This is the whole structure. Not understanding each other. Each one making contact with self, while the other one watches.
The reason this works is that it bypasses the pattern that has been killing the relationship. The pattern is two people trying to be understood. The intervention is two people learning, one at a time, to understand themselves, in the presence of the other.
The presence of the other matters. It's not individual therapy. It's not two parallel solo processes. It's a specific kind of joint work where the witnessing is the bridge.
The witnessing is not the same as listening for the purpose of responding.
The witnessing is not the same as listening for the purpose of mirroring.
The witnessing is not the same as listening for the purpose of being seen as a good partner.
The witnessing is closer to what happens when you watch someone you love be in pain and you have no instinct to fix it, no instinct to explain it away, no instinct to defend yourself. You just see them. You just stay in the room. You just let your nervous system be next to theirs while the truth of their interior is finally being touched.
That kind of witnessing is what most marriages have been missing for years.
And it's what bad couples counseling skips, because the therapist is anxious to make the couple feel like progress is happening, and the fastest visible progress is when they "understand" each other. So the therapist drives toward understanding, and the couple performs understanding, and they leave the session feeling slightly better, and nothing has actually moved.
In successful couples counseling, the early sessions are slow.
They are quiet.
They have long stretches where one person is sitting with what's been alive in them, and the other person is sitting in the room, watching, and the therapist is helping the speaker stay with their own interior instead of leaping into the familiar fight.
There is no resolution in these sessions.
There is no plan in these sessions.
There is no homework, in the traditional sense, in these sessions.
What there is, is contact.
Self-contact. In the presence of the other.
This is what opens the door.
Only after enough of this has happened, sometimes weeks of it, sometimes months of it, depending on how long the couple has been at war, can the next phase of the work begin. The phase where the couple starts to actually be in something together. To repair. To rebuild. To turn toward each other.
But that phase cannot be rushed. It cannot be skipped. It cannot be substituted for. If you try to start the repair before the contact has happened, you're back in the old pattern. You're asking two people who don't know themselves to suddenly know each other. It doesn't work.
The order is everything.
Self-contact first. In the presence of the partner. With the partner as witness.
Only then does the work of repair become possible.
Only then can two people who have been at war begin to lay down their weapons, not because they've been told to, but because they're starting to remember that the person across from them is not an enemy. Is not a verdict. Is not a problem to be solved. Is a person, with their own interior, carrying their own pain, who has been alone for as long as you've been alone, who has been waiting to be witnessed for as long as you've been waiting to be witnessed.
That recognition is the start.
Not the goal.
The start.
Most couples counseling tries to deliver the start in the first session.
Successful couples counseling earns the start over many sessions, by going slowly enough that the nervous systems involved can actually metabolize what's happening.
If you've been to counseling before, and it didn't help, this might be why.
You weren't given the slow.
You were rushed into understanding, and you couldn't get there, because understanding wasn't the missing piece.
Self-contact was.
In the presence of the other.
With the therapist holding the space, slowing the speed, protecting the speaker from the partner's reactivity, helping the witness stay in their seat, helping the speaker stay with what's actually true inside them instead of veering back into the old fight.
This is what successful couples counseling looks like.
It looks like two people, slowly, with help, learning to come home to themselves in the presence of each other.
The understanding comes later.
It comes naturally, when the conditions have been created for it.
It cannot be manufactured. It cannot be forced. It cannot be the goal of the early sessions.
The goal of the early sessions is contact. Self-contact. Witnessed.
That's it.
That's the start.
Everything else is built on that foundation.
If you build without that foundation, you build on sand.
If you build with that foundation, the marriage that emerges on the other side is real, because both people, finally, after years of being alone inside the marriage, have been witnessed by the one person who matters most.
That's what the work is.
That's what it looks like when it actually works.

They are quiet.

There is no plan in these sessions.

There is no homework, in the traditional sense, in these sessions.

What there is, is contact.

Self-contact. In the presence of the other.

This is what opens the door.

The order is everything.

Self-contact first. In the presence of the partner. With the partner as witness.

Only then does the work of repair become possible.

Only then can two people who have been at war begin to lay down their weapons, not because they've been told to, but because they're starting to remember that the person across from them is not an enemy. Is not a verdict. Is not a problem to be solved. Is a person, with their own interior, carrying their own pain, who has been alone for as long as you've been alone, who has been waiting to be witnessed for as long as you've been waiting to be witnessed.

That recognition is the start.

Not the goal.

The start.

Most couples counseling tries to deliver the start in the first session.

Successful couples counseling earns the start over many sessions, by going slowly enough that the nervous systems involved can actually metabolize what's happening.

If you've been to counseling before, and it didn't help, this might be why.

You weren't given the slow.

You were rushed into understanding, and you couldn't get there, because understanding wasn't the missing piece.

Self-contact was.

In the presence of the other.

With the therapist holding the space, slowing the speed, protecting the speaker from the partner's reactivity, helping the witness stay in their seat, helping the speaker stay with what's actually true inside them instead of veering back into the old fight.

This is what successful couples counseling looks like.

It looks like two people, slowly, with help, learning to come home to themselves in the presence of each other.

The understanding comes later.

It comes naturally, when the conditions have been created for it.

It cannot be manufactured. It cannot be forced. It cannot be the goal of the early sessions.

The goal of the early sessions is contact. Self-contact. Witnessed.

That's it.

That's the start.

Everything else is built on that foundation.

If you build without that foundation, you build on sand.

If you build with that foundation, the marriage that emerges on the other side is real, because both people, finally, after years of being alone inside the marriage, have been witnessed by the one person who matters most.

That's what the work is.

That's what it looks like when it actually works.

The Three Things That Make Couples Counseling Actually Succeed
I want to tell you what almost no one will tell you about why couples counseling works, when it works.
It's not the framework. It's not the modality. It's not the certifications on the wall. It's not whether the therapist trained under one famous person or another. It's not the worksheets or the homework or the communication tools.
What makes couples counseling actually succeed is three things, in a specific order, that almost no one names directly.
I'm going to name them.
Then I'm going to explain each one.
The three things are these.
One. I have to tell each partner, separately and clearly, that nobody has helped them here. Not their mother. Not their father. Not their first marriage. Not their best friend. Not the last three therapists they tried. Not the books they read. Not the workshops they attended. Nobody has actually helped them in the specific place where they have been most alone, for the longest time, with the most pain.
Two. I have to tell each partner that I wish to help them there. That I'm not going to sit across from them and run them through a protocol. I am going to walk alongside them, into the specific place where nobody has helped them, and I'm going to stay there with them until something starts to shift.
Three. I have to teach the other partner how to help them there. So that what I do, eventually, becomes something the partner can do, in small doses, in the marriage itself, when I am no longer in the room.
Those are the three.
Most couples counseling does not include any of them.
Let me explain each one.
The First Thing. Nobody Has Helped You Here.
This is the sentence I say, in some form, to almost every partner I sit with in the first session.
I say it because it is true.
And I say it because if I don't say it, the partner has no way to understand why they are in such pain, after so many years of trying so hard, with so many people who claimed they were going to help.
When someone has been in distress for a long time, they often blame themselves for not being better at receiving help. They have read the books. They have done the therapy. They have meditated, journaled, retreated, processed. They have followed every reasonable recommendation. And they still feel alone inside their lives, inside their marriages, inside themselves.
They conclude there must be something wrong with them.
There isn't.
What's wrong is that the help they were given was the wrong shape.
The help addressed the wrong layer.
The help moved at the wrong speed.
The help asked them to do something that they could not, in fact, do, given the state they were in.
And so the help didn't help. It often made things worse. Because each time someone tries to help and fails, the partner concludes more deeply that they are unhelpable. That their pain is too much. That nobody can reach them. That they are condemned to carry what they're carrying alone.
When I tell a partner, in the first session, that nobody has helped them here, I am not insulting all the people who tried. I am simply telling the truth.
The truth is that most help, including most therapy, addresses the surface of what's happening. It addresses behavior, communication, conflict-resolution strategies, attachment categories. These are real things. They are not the things that are most broken in the partner I am sitting with.
What is most broken is the experience of being a person, alone, with their own interior, for years, with no one inside it with them.
The partner has been alone in their interior since childhood, in many cases. The partner has been alone in their interior since the early years of the marriage, in other cases. The partner has been alone in their interior since the last major loss in their life, in still other cases. The aloneness has different start dates for different people.
But the aloneness is the wound.
And the aloneness is the thing no help has actually addressed.
Because no help has actually gone there. No help has actually sat down inside the aloneness with the partner. No help has actually said, "I'm in here with you now. We're going to be in here together until something changes."
When I name this, the partner often cries. Not because I have said something dramatic. Because, finally, someone has named the thing they have been carrying. And the naming, by itself, is the first piece of help they have received in a very long time.
The naming is not the help. The naming is the beginning of the help.
The actual help is what comes next.
But the naming has to happen first, because without it, the partner cannot trust that what comes next is going to be different from everything they have already tried.
The Second Thing. I Wish to Help You Here.
The second sentence I say is that I wish to help them. There. In the place no one has been.
This is not the same as saying I am qualified to help them. This is not the same as saying I have a method that will help them. This is something else.
I am saying that I am willing to go to the place. I am willing to sit in the place. I am willing to be in the place with them, slowly, without trying to get them out of it, without trying to make it less painful prematurely, without trying to convert it into a problem I can solve.
This is the second piece of help.
The willingness to go to the place.
Most therapists, even very skilled ones, do not go to the place. They stay at the perimeter of the place. They give the partner tools to deal with the place. They give the partner frameworks to understand the place. They give the partner exercises to manage the place.
They do not go in.
The reason they do not go in is that going in is hard. Going in requires the therapist to be willing to sit, for long periods, in a kind of emotional intimacy with the partner that most therapists are not trained to tolerate.
Going in requires the therapist to feel what the partner is feeling, in their own body, without becoming the partner.
Going in requires the therapist to be unhurried, when most of clinical training is about producing visible progress.
Going in requires the therapist to be okay with sessions that don't have neat endings, that don't produce takeaways, that leave the partner shaking, or quiet, or in a state that doesn't look like therapeutic success on the outside.
Most therapy doesn't go in.
When I tell a partner that I wish to help them, I am telling them that I am willing to go in.
This is what I am offering.
I am not offering a method. I am offering my presence in the place no one has been with them.
This is the second piece of help.
It is enormous.
It is also rare.
Most people, even most therapists, do not actually have the bandwidth, or the willingness, or the training, to go to the place. They mean well. They try. They cannot stay.
The partner has experienced this many times. They have brought someone toward the place, and watched the person fail to enter it. They have learned, over the years, not to expect anyone to go in with them.
When I say I wish to help them, what they hear is not a generic offer of therapy. What they hear is the possibility that someone might, finally, come with them into the part of themselves they have been carrying alone.
This is the second piece.
The willingness.
The willingness produces a quality of relationship between the therapist and the partner that most therapy does not produce. It is not friendship. It is not romance. It is something more like a particular kind of professional intimacy, in which the therapist has agreed to be in the partner's interior with them for as long as it takes.
The partner can feel whether this is real or performed. The partner has been performed at, for years. The partner can tell the difference.
When the willingness is real, the partner begins, slowly, to allow the therapist into the place.
This is the work of the first many sessions. Not solving anything. Not teaching anything. Just the slow building of trust that the willingness is real, that the therapist is not going to leave, that the therapist is not going to flinch when the place is finally revealed.
When the partner allows the therapist in, the actual work can begin.
The actual work is the partner, finally, with someone alongside them, beginning to feel what they have been feeling for years.
Not analyzing it. Feeling it.
The feeling is the work.
The therapist is there to help the partner stay with the feeling, instead of fleeing into the surface again. To help the partner believe that the feeling is bearable. To help the partner discover that the feeling, when it is fully felt, in the presence of another person, begins to move.
Pain that has been carried alone for years is frozen pain. It does not move. It does not metabolize. It just sits, in the interior, doing the slow damage of long-held grief.
Pain that is felt in the presence of another person begins to move.
This is the second piece of help.
The presence.
The willingness to go to the place.
The staying once you are there.
The Third Thing. I Teach Your Partner How to Help You Here.
This is the piece almost no couples counseling includes.
It is the piece that makes everything different.
I do not just help each partner in the place no one has been. I teach the other partner, slowly, over many sessions, how to be in the place too.
Not as a therapist.
As a partner.
This is a different thing. It is smaller. It is more intimate. It is also more sustainable, because the marriage continues long after the therapy ends, and the partner needs to know how to be in the place with their partner in real life.
Here's how I teach this.
When one partner is doing the work of being in the place, the other partner is in the witness chair. I have already described, in earlier posts, what the witness chair requires.
What I haven't fully described is that the witness chair is also a training. The witness is, slowly, learning a skill they did not have before. The skill is the ability to be in the room with their partner's interior, without doing any of the things they used to do.
The witness is learning to stay in their seat. To keep their eyes open. To breathe. To not interject. To not defend. To not interpret. To not fix.
This is harder than it sounds. The witness has been doing the opposite of all of these things for years. The opposite is what produced the distress. To stop doing the opposite is to learn an entirely new way of being in the marriage.
The training happens in the witness chair, over many sessions. The witness, over time, develops the capacity to be in the room with their partner's interior without collapsing into the old patterns. They develop the muscle. They develop the bandwidth. They develop the ability to hold themselves steady while their partner is doing the work.
This is the training.
But the training is not complete in the therapy room. The training has to be brought into the marriage.
The way I do this is by, slowly, asking the witness to start doing, in real life, what they are learning to do in the room.
I send them home with one small practice at a time.
"This week, when your partner says something interior, just stay in the room. You don't have to respond. Just stay."
"This week, when your partner is having a hard day, sit next to them for ten minutes. You don't have to say anything. Just be there."
"This week, when your partner cries, put your hand on their back. Don't speak. Don't fix. Just keep your hand there."
These small practices, brought into the home, begin to do something. They begin to change the marriage outside the therapy room.
The partner who has been doing the work, who has been making contact with their interior, begins to discover that their interior is being met, not just by the therapist, but by their partner. In small doses. Imperfectly. But really.
When this starts happening, the marriage begins to repair itself, between sessions, without me in the room.
This is the goal.
The goal is not to make couples dependent on the therapy. The goal is to give the couple the skill, slowly, of being in each other's interior together, so that the marriage becomes the place where the work happens, not the therapy room.
When this transition is complete, the couple no longer needs me as often. They might come back for tune-ups, for hard moments, for new challenges. But the daily work has moved into the marriage itself.
This is what couples counseling is for.
Not for the couple to learn to communicate better. Not for the couple to resolve their fights. Not for the couple to understand their attachment patterns.
For the couple to become, finally, two people who can be in each other's interior, who can witness each other, who can help each other in the places no one has ever helped them before.
When this happens, the marriage is something new.
It is not the marriage they had before the distress.
It is not the marriage they imagined when they were falling in love.
It is something they built together, with help, by going to the place neither of them had ever been with anyone, and learning to be there with each other.
This is the marriage that lasts.
This is the marriage that holds.
This is the marriage that, on the other side of the work, is more than what they hoped for, because it is real, and because both of them know what it cost to build, and because both of them know what the alternative would have been if they had not done the work.
The three things, again.
Nobody has helped you here.
I wish to help you here.
I will teach your partner how to help you here.
If your couples counseling does not include all three, ask why.
If you are looking for couples counseling, look for someone who can offer all three.
The three together is what makes the work succeed.
The three together is what saves the marriage that everyone else, including the partners themselves, thought could not be saved.
The three together is what allows two people who have been alone inside their lives for years to finally, slowly, find their way home to themselves, and to each other.
That is what this work is for.
That is what it does, when it works. See less

What It Feels Like Inside the Partner Who Is Finally Making Contact
There's a particular experience that happens inside a partner when they finally make contact with their own interior, after years of having been disconnected from it.
It's not what most people expect.
Most people, when they imagine finally getting to say the things they've been holding inside for years, imagine relief. They imagine catharsis. They imagine the unburdening that comes with finally getting heard.
What actually happens, in the early sessions, is much closer to disorientation than relief.
I want to walk you through it, because if you understand what's happening inside the speaker, you'll understand why the work cannot be rushed, and why what looks like progress often isn't, and why what looks like a difficult session is often the most important one.
The first thing that happens, when a partner begins to make contact with their interior, is that they cannot find it.
They've been disconnected from it for so long that the interior they're being asked to access doesn't immediately respond to the asking. The therapist might say, "What's happening for you right now?" And the partner will produce a thought. Or a story about the marriage. Or a complaint about their partner. Or a piece of analysis about the pattern they've been in.
None of these are contact with the interior.
These are surface productions. They are what the speaker has been generating, for years, in place of actual interior contact. They are what's available when interior contact is not available.
The therapist's job, in this moment, is not to accept the surface production as the answer. The therapist's job is to gently, repeatedly, slow the speaker down until the surface production stops, and the speaker is left with the actual experience of not knowing what's inside them.
This not-knowing is the doorway.
The speaker, sitting in this not-knowing, often experiences it as failure. They think they should be able to answer the question. They think the not-knowing means they're doing the work wrong. They become slightly panicked. They want to produce another surface answer, to relieve the discomfort of not having one.
The therapist holds them in the not-knowing.
"Stay with the not-knowing. There's no rush. There's nothing you have to say. Just stay."

What the Anxious Partner Is Actually Asking, Underneath All the Fighting
There is a question at the bottom of every anxious partner's soul, and almost none of them have ever spoken it out loud.
The question is this.
Am I worthy of love, care, and protection?
That is the whole question. That is the question that has been running, underneath everything, since long before this marriage existed.
The anxious partner does not present this question to their partner. They cannot. The question is too tender to say out loud. The question is too embarrassing. The question feels too much like a confession of something the anxious partner is supposed to have figured out by now.
So the question goes underground.
It does not stay quiet, though.
It produces behavior.
The behavior is what we call anxious attachment. The pursuing. The protesting. The checking. The needing reassurance. The reading of every micro-expression. The hypervigilance to any sign that they might be about to be left, dismissed, forgotten, abandoned.
All of it, every behavior, every protest, every spiral, every fight, is the underground question trying to get an answer.
Am I worthy of love, care, and protection?
The anxious partner is not asking their current partner. The anxious partner is asking their mother. Their father. The original caregivers who failed, in some specific way, to give the anxious partner a clear, embodied, lived experience of being worthy.
The failure may have been catastrophic. The failure may have been subtle. Either way, the original caregivers did not give the anxious partner the foundational answer.
The anxious partner left childhood with the question unanswered.
The anxious partner entered adulthood with the question running.
The anxious partner now seeks, through romantic relationship, to finally get the answer.
This is where the trap begins.
Because the anxious partner does not pick someone who can easily give them the answer.
The anxious partner picks an avoidant.
Of course they do.
The avoidant is the perfect match for the underground question, because the avoidant is constitutionally unable to give an easy yes. The avoidant is going to be partial, qualified, withdrawn, ambivalent. The avoidant is going to produce, in the anxious partner, exactly the conditions that the original caregivers produced.
The avoidant is going to almost give the answer, and then withhold it.
The avoidant is going to seem to give the answer, and then take it back.
The avoidant is going to give the answer in a way the anxious partner cannot fully receive.
This is not a flaw of the anxious partner's selection process. This is the selection process working exactly the way the underground question designed it to work.
The underground question is not looking for a clear yes. The underground question is looking for the original conditions, recreated, with the hope that this time, the conditions will produce a different outcome.
The conditions are recreated.
The outcome is the same.
The anxious partner experiences, over and over, the partial love, the withheld love, the love that almost arrives and then doesn't. The anxious partner protests. The anxious partner pursues. The anxious partner cries, fights, withdraws in their own way, comes back, tries harder, lowers their expectations, raises their expectations, leaves, returns, and through all of it, the underground question is still running.
Am I worthy of love, care, and protection?
The avoidant, meanwhile, has their own underground question, which I will write about another time. For now I am staying with the anxious one, because the anxious one's question is so completely missed by both partners in the fight.
The fight obscures the question.
The fight is full of attachment language. Anxious. Avoidant. Triggered. Activated. Deactivating. Protest behavior. Dismissive. Preoccupied.
The two partners hurl these words at each other.
The words feel sophisticated. The words feel diagnostic. The words feel like progress.
The words are noise.
The words are noise because the words describe the surface, and the surface is not where the wound lives.
The wound lives in the underground question.
And the underground question is not being asked.
Instead, the anxious partner is asking, "Why don't you respond to my texts?"
The anxious partner is asking, "Why did you turn away from me last night?"
The anxious partner is asking, "Why don't you ever initiate anymore?"
The anxious partner is asking, "Why are you so distant?"
These are not the real questions.
The real question, underneath all of them, is the underground one.
Am I worthy of love, care, and protection?
The avoidant partner cannot answer this question, because the question is not being asked. The avoidant partner is being asked about texts, and turning away, and initiating, and distance. The avoidant partner responds with their own surface answers. They were busy. They were tired. They didn't mean anything by it. They're just like this.
The two partners have a fight about the surface.
The underground question stays buried.
Both partners go to bed hurt.
Nothing has been resolved, because the actual question was never on the table.
This happens, in the average distressed marriage with this dynamic, thousands of times. Year after year. Fight after fight. The same surface conversation. The same underground question, never asked, never answered.
What makes it worse is the shame.
The anxious partner is not just carrying the underground question. The anxious partner is carrying the shame of having the question.
The anxious partner has been told, in many ways, throughout their life, that they should have figured this out by now. That they should not need so much. That they are too much. That their pursuing is exhausting. That their need for reassurance is a flaw.
The anxious partner has internalized all of this.
So the anxious partner does not want to admit that the underground question is still running. The anxious partner does not want to say, "I am asking you, every day, in a hundred different ways, whether I am worthy of love, care, and protection."
The anxious partner would be too humiliated to say this.
So the anxious partner converts the question into something else.
The anxious partner converts the question into anger. Into accusation. Into protest. Into the language of injustice, of fairness, of behavior, of what the partner did or didn't do.
The conversion protects the anxious partner from the embarrassment of having to admit the underground question.
The conversion also makes the underground question impossible to address.
You cannot address a question that has been converted into a protest. The protest has its own logic. The protest produces its own counter-arguments. The protest leads to fights about the surface.
The question stays underground.
The shame keeps it underground.
The shame is the lock on the door.
This is what is actually happening in most distressed marriages with an anxious partner.
The anxious partner is asking, every day, in a thousand disguised ways, whether they are worthy of love, care, and protection.
The avoidant partner is hearing only the protests, and responding to the protests, and not knowing that there is a question underneath the protests.
The fight continues.
The years pass.
The marriage erodes.
And the anxious partner, exhausted, begins to hate the avoidant for not answering a question the avoidant did not know was being asked.
The anxious partner becomes bitter. The anxious partner becomes vengeful. The anxious partner becomes the version of themselves they swore they would never become.
This is not because the anxious partner is bad.
This is because the underground question has been running, unanswered, for so many years that the anxious partner has lost faith in the possibility of an answer.
When you lose faith in the possibility of being worthy of love, care, and protection, you begin to hate the person who has failed to convince you.
The hatred is not really at the partner.
The hatred is at the original wound.
But the partner is the one in the room.
So the partner becomes the target.
If the marriage is going to survive, the underground question has to come out from underground.
The anxious partner has to be able to say, eventually, with help, in a safe enough room, with a therapist or a guide or a moment of grace, the actual sentence.
"I am asking, all the time, whether I am worthy of being loved. I never got the answer to that question when I was small. I have been trying to get the answer from you. I am exhausted. I am ashamed. I do not know how to stop asking."
That sentence, said out loud, changes everything.
Because the avoidant partner, who has not been able to respond to the protests, often can respond to the underground question. The underground question is not a protest. The underground question is not an attack. The underground question is a confession of need, made by a person who has been carrying it for their whole life.
The avoidant partner, when they hear the actual question, often softens. The softening is not because they have suddenly become a different person. The softening is because they have, finally, been told the truth.
The truth is what the avoidant has been waiting for, even though they did not know they were waiting for it.
When the truth arrives, the avoidant has a chance to do something they could never do with the protests. They can offer something. Not perfection. Not a complete answer. But a piece of presence. A piece of recognition. A piece of the embodied yes that the anxious partner has been waiting for since childhood.
The anxious partner has to be able to receive this.
That is its own work.
The anxious partner has spent years not receiving the answer, because the answer has been arriving in a form that does not match what they think the answer should look like. The answer is always partial. The answer is never as big as the original wound requires. The answer is, almost always, smaller than the question.
The anxious partner has to learn to receive the smaller answer.
Because the smaller answer, received and metabolized, slowly fills in what the original caregivers did not give.
This is the work.
The work is not for the anxious partner to stop being anxious.
The work is for the anxious partner to surface the underground question, and for the avoidant partner to begin, in their own way, to answer it, and for both of them to slowly metabolize what has been missing for both of their entire lives.
Most couples never get to this work.
Most couples stay in the fight about the surface, and the underground question stays underground, and the marriage erodes, and the anxious partner becomes bitter, and the avoidant partner becomes withdrawn, and both of them end up far from each other and far from themselves.
You don't have to stay there.
If you are the anxious partner, you can begin, in private, to ask yourself the underground question.
Am I worthy of love, care, and protection?
You can sit with the question. You can feel the shame around having the question. You can grieve, for the small version of yourself that did not get the answer.
This is the beginning of the work.
The work is yours to start.
The avoidant partner cannot start it for you.
But once you have started it, you can bring the question into the marriage, slowly, with help, in a way that gives your partner the chance to answer it.
The marriage you have right now is the one that grew on top of the buried question.
The marriage you could have is the one where the question has been spoken.
The difference between the two is the whole arc of the work.

The anxious partner cries, fights, withdraws in their own way, comes back, tries harder, lowers their expectations, raises their expectations, leaves, returns, and through all of it, the underground question is still running.

Am I worthy of love, care, and protection?

The avoidant, meanwhile, has their own underground question, which I will write about another time. For now I am staying with the anxious one, because the anxious one's question is so completely missed by both partners in the fight.

The fight obscures the question.

The fight is full of attachment language. Anxious. Avoidant. Triggered. Activated. Deactivating. Protest behavior. Dismissive. Preoccupied.

The two partners hurl these words at each other.

The words feel sophisticated. The words feel diagnostic. The words feel like progress.

The words are noise.

The words are noise because the words describe the surface, and the surface is not where the wound lives.

The wound lives in the underground question.

And the underground question is not being asked.

Instead, the anxious partner is asking, "Why don't you respond to my texts?"

The anxious partner is asking, "Why did you turn away from me last night?"

The anxious partner is asking, "Why don't you ever initiate anymore?"

The anxious partner is asking, "Why are you so distant?"

These are not the real questions.

The real question, underneath all of them, is the underground one.

Am I worthy of love, care, and protection?

The avoidant partner cannot answer this question, because the question is not being asked. The avoidant partner is being asked about texts, and turning away, and initiating, and distance. The avoidant partner responds with their own surface answers. They were busy. They were tired. They didn't mean anything by it. They're just like this.

The two partners have a fight about the surface.

The underground question stays buried.

Both partners go to bed hurt.

Nothing has been resolved, because the actual question was never on the table.

This happens, in the average distressed marriage with this dynamic, thousands of times. Year after year. Fight after fight. The same surface conversation. The same underground question, never asked, never answered.

What makes it worse is the shame.

The anxious partner is not just carrying the underground question. The anxious partner is carrying the shame of having the question.

The anxious partner has been told, in many ways, throughout their life, that they should have figured this out by now. That they should not need so much. That they are too much. That their pursuing is exhausting. That their need for reassurance is a flaw.

The anxious partner has internalized all of this.

So the anxious partner does not want to admit that the underground question is still running. The anxious partner does not want to say, "I am asking you, every day, in a hundred different ways, whether I am worthy of love, care, and protection."

The anxious partner would be too humiliated to say this.

So the anxious partner converts the question into something else.

The anxious partner converts the question into anger. Into accusation. Into protest. Into the language of injustice, of fairness, of behavior, of what the partner did or didn't do.

The conversion protects the anxious partner from the embarrassment of having to admit the underground question.

The conversion also makes the underground question impossible to address.

You cannot address a question that has been converted into a protest. The protest has its own logic. The protest produces its own counter-arguments. The protest leads to fights about the surface.

The question stays underground.

The shame keeps it underground.

The shame is the lock on the door.

This is what is actually happening in most distressed marriages with an anxious partner.

The anxious partner is asking, every day, in a thousand disguised ways, whether they are worthy of love, care, and protection.

The avoidant partner is hearing only the protests, and responding to the protests, and not knowing that there is a question underneath the protests.

The fight continues.

The years pass.

The marriage erodes.

And the anxious partner, exhausted, begins to hate the avoidant for not answering a question the avoidant did not know was being asked.

The anxious partner becomes bitter. The anxious partner becomes vengeful. The anxious partner becomes the version of themselves they swore they would never become.

This is not because the anxious partner is bad.

This is because the underground question has been running, unanswered, for so many years that the anxious partner has lost faith in the possibility of an answer.

When you lose faith in the possibility of being worthy of love, care, and protection, you begin to hate the person who has failed to convince you.

The hatred is not really at the partner.

The hatred is at the original wound.

But the partner is the one in the room.

So the partner becomes the target.

If the marriage is going to survive, the underground question has to come out from underground.

The anxious partner has to be able to say, eventually, with help, in a safe enough room, with a therapist or a guide or a moment of grace, the actual sentence.

"I am asking, all the time, whether I am worthy of being loved. I never got the answer to that question when I was small. I have been trying to get the answer from you. I am exhausted. I am ashamed. I do not know how to stop asking."

That sentence, said out loud, changes everything.

Because the avoidant partner, who has not been able to respond to the protests, often can respond to the underground question. The underground question is not a protest. The underground question is not an attack. The underground question is a confession of need, made by a person who has been carrying it for their whole life.

The avoidant partner, when they hear the actual question, often softens. The softening is not because they have suddenly become a different person. The softening is because they have, finally, been told the truth.

The truth is what the avoidant has been waiting for, even though they did not know they were waiting for it.

When the truth arrives, the avoidant has a chance to do something they could never do with the protests. They can offer something. Not perfection. Not a complete answer. But a piece of presence. A piece of recognition. A piece of the embodied yes that the anxious partner has been waiting for since childhood.

The anxious partner has to be able to receive this.

That is its own work.

The anxious partner has spent years not receiving the answer, because the answer has been arriving in a form that does not match what they think the answer should look like. The answer is always partial. The answer is never as big as the original wound requires. The answer is, almost always, smaller than the question.

The anxious partner has to learn to receive the smaller answer.

Because the smaller answer, received and metabolized, slowly fills in what the original caregivers did not give.

This is the work.

The work is not for the anxious partner to stop being anxious.

The work is for the anxious partner to surface the underground question, and for the avoidant partner to begin, in their own way, to answer it, and for both of them to slowly metabolize what has been missing for both of their entire lives.

Most couples never get to this work.

Most couples stay in the fight about the surface, and the underground question stays underground, and the marriage erodes, and the anxious partner becomes bitter, and the avoidant partner becomes withdrawn, and both of them end up far from each other and far from themselves.

You don't have to stay there.

If you are the anxious partner, you can begin, in private, to ask yourself the underground question.

Am I worthy of love, care, and protection?

You can sit with the question. You can feel the shame around having the question. You can grieve, for the small version of yourself that did not get the answer.

This is the beginning of the work.

The work is yours to start.

The avoidant partner cannot start it for you.

But once you have started it, you can bring the question into the marriage, slowly, with help, in a way that gives your partner the chance to answer it.

The marriage you have right now is the one that grew on top of the buried question.

The marriage you could have is the one where the question has been spoken.

The difference between the two is the whole arc of the work.

What the Witnessing Actually Looks Like in the Room
The hardest part of successful couples counseling is the witness chair.
When one partner is finally making contact with their own interior, the other partner is asked to do something almost no one in a distressed marriage knows how to do. They are asked to sit in the room, in their body, watching their partner have an experience, without doing any of the things they have been doing for years.
They cannot defend themselves.
They cannot relate the speaker's experience to their own experience.
They cannot interject with corrections, even small ones.
They cannot offer comfort designed to redirect what's happening.
They cannot frown, sigh, look down, or send micro-signals of disagreement.
They cannot fix.
They cannot prepare their counter-argument while their partner is still speaking.
They can do one thing.
They can watch.
This sounds simple. It is not simple. For a partner who has been in a war for years, sitting still in the room while the other one finally accesses something interior is one of the hardest things a nervous system can be asked to do.
Let me describe what's actually happening in the witness's body while the speaker is doing the work.
The witness's nervous system is on high alert. The speaker is, in their experience, the source of years of pain. The speaker's mouth is now opening, and out of that mouth is coming language about the marriage, about feeling alone, about hurt, about disappointment. The witness's body, trained by years of conflict, is preparing to defend before the speaker has even finished the sentence.
The witness's mind has already started rebutting. Already started rephrasing what the speaker said into something more accurate. Already started cataloguing the moments where what the speaker is saying isn't quite right. Already started building the case that the speaker is missing important context.
This is automatic. This is not a character flaw of the witness. This is what every distressed nervous system does in the presence of a partner who has been categorized as a threat.
The therapist's job, in this moment, is to hold the witness in their seat without shaming them for the activation.
This is delicate work.
If the therapist treats the witness like a problem, the witness will collapse into more defense. If the therapist treats the witness like they have to perform good listening, the witness will fake it, and the speaker will feel the fakeness, and the work will not move.
What the therapist has to do, instead, is help the witness understand that their only job, in this moment, is to keep their body in the chair and let their eyes stay on their partner.
That's it.
They don't have to feel anything specific.
They don't have to look like a good witness.
They don't have to perform connection.
They just have to stay.
The staying is the entire intervention.
Because what's happening for the speaker, while the speaker is making contact with their own interior, is not a transaction with the witness. The speaker is not speaking to the witness. The speaker is speaking from inside themselves, with the therapist as the safe holder, with the witness as the steady presence in the room.
When the witness can stay, even without doing anything else, the speaker can go deeper.
When the witness cannot stay, when they sigh, when they look away, when they start to argue, when they collapse into their own defense, the speaker loses access to the interior they were just touching. The work collapses. The session goes backwards.
So the therapist watches the witness as closely as the therapist watches the speaker.
The therapist is reading the witness's face for the moment when the activation is about to take them out of their chair. The therapist is reading the witness's body for the rising defense. The therapist is ready to intervene with the witness, gently, when needed.
The interventions sound like this.
"Stay with me. Keep your eyes on your partner. You don't have to agree with anything. Just stay."
"I see you wanting to respond. We'll get to your turn. Right now, your only job is to be here."
"Take a breath. You're safe. Your partner isn't attacking you. They're touching something inside themselves. Let them have it."
"I know what you're hearing isn't the whole truth from your side. That's okay. The whole truth isn't what we're after right now. We're after the part that's been living alone in your partner for a long time."
"Stay in your seat. Even if you don't agree. Even if it doesn't match your memory. Stay."
The therapist may have to say versions of these sentences many times in a single session. The therapist may have to slow the session down to nearly a halt while the witness regulates. The therapist may have to spend more time on the witness, in some moments, than on the speaker, because if the witness leaves the seat, the speaker can't keep working.
This is what the holding of the space looks like.
It's not glamorous. It's not the dramatic confrontations of bad couples counseling. It's not the rapid breakthroughs you see in movies.
It's slow. It's quiet. It's a therapist watching two nervous systems, helping each one stay in the role they're in at that moment, refusing to let the old pattern reassert itself.
Now I want to tell you what the witnessing actually looks like, in the witness's body, when it's working.
When the witness can stay, something shifts inside them.
The first thing that shifts is the noise stops. The internal rebuttal quiets down. The catalog of counter-evidence falls away. The argument the witness has been preparing dissolves, because there's nothing to argue with. The speaker isn't accusing them. The speaker is sitting with what's been alive in them for years.
The witness begins to actually see their partner.
Not the partner they've been at war with for years. Not the partner they've been categorizing as the problem. The actual person, sitting across from them, with their own interior, with their own pain, with their own years of accumulated grief.
This seeing is not cognitive. It's not the witness deciding to see their partner differently. It's something more like the witness's nervous system, finally given a moment of safety, recognizing the person across from them as another nervous system, also in pain, also alone, also waiting to be witnessed.
The witness might cry. The witness might not. The witness might reach out, or sit very still. There's no required reaction.
What's happening, in the witness, is a kind of slow, almost imperceptible softening. The armor is coming off one molecule at a time.
The therapist, watching this, doesn't comment on it. The therapist doesn't say, "I see you opening." The therapist doesn't celebrate the moment. Because pointing at the softening would interrupt it. The softening has to happen without being witnessed by language. It has to happen in the body, in the quiet, in the staying.
Sometimes, after the speaker has finished their turn, the witness will say something small. "I didn't know it had been that bad for you." "I'm sorry you've been alone in this." "I haven't been listening for a long time."
These small sentences are not the goal of the session. They are sometimes a byproduct of the witnessing. When they come, they come naturally. When they don't, that's also fine. The session is not measured by what the witness says afterward. It's measured by whether the witness stayed.
In the same session, or in a later session, the roles will switch. The witness becomes the speaker. The speaker becomes the witness.
The speaker, who has just spent an hour or more in contact with their own interior, often has more capacity to be a witness than they ever have before. Because they have just been witnessed. Their nervous system has just experienced what it feels like to be safely held in their own interior, in the presence of their partner, with a therapist protecting the space.
The new witness, having received that experience, often has more bandwidth to give it back.
This is how the structure works. Not by teaching the couple skills. By giving them, slowly, week after week, the actual experience of being witnessed and being a witness, until the witnessing becomes something that can happen between them, sometimes, even when the therapist isn't in the room.
That is the long arc of the work.
The witnessing is the practice.
The therapist is the temporary scaffolding.
The eventual outcome is two people who have learned, in their bodies, what it feels like to stay in the room with each other's interiors, without defending, without collapsing, without fleeing, without fixing.
That is the foundation everything else is built on.
If you've never been in a counseling session like this, what I'm describing might sound strange. Most counseling does not look like this. Most counseling is full of structured exercises, communication tools, homework assignments. There's nothing wrong with those things in their place. But they don't work for couples who have crossed the line into accumulated resentment. For those couples, the work has to start in the witness chair.
And the witness chair, more than anything else, is what determines whether the counseling succeeds.
The therapist, the speaker, and the witness. Three people in a room. The therapist's job is to make the chair safe enough that the witness can actually stay in it.
When the witness stays, the work works.
When the witness leaves the chair, even subtly, even just in their face, the work stops.
That's why most couples counseling fails. Not because the therapist is bad. Because the therapist hasn't been trained to watch the witness as closely as they watch the speaker. Because the therapist hasn't been trained to slow the session down enough to make the chair survivable. Because the therapist hasn't been trained to understand that the witness is doing the harder job, and needs the more careful protection.
When a therapist learns to watch the witness, the whole structure of the work changes.
That's what successful couples counseling looks like in the room, moment by moment.
It is the slow, careful, deliberate protection of the witness, while the speaker does the work of coming home to themselves.

25 Things Your Avoidant Partner Does That Look Like Love but Are Actually Distance
1. They handle every logistical thing in your life so well, you stop noticing they haven't asked you a real question in months.
2. They buy you the gift. The thoughtful one. The right one. And they hand it to you without making eye contact, because the gift was easier than the looking.
3. They tell you they love you, every night, in the same three words, said the same way, and the sameness is what's keeping the rest of the conversation from ever happening.
4. They do the dishes, take out the trash, fix the leak, manage the bills, and they have, somehow, replaced their interior life with the to-do list.
5. They text you back quickly. Always. With a thumbs-up emoji, or a heart, or a "love you," and the speed of the response is meant to substitute for what the response is missing.
6. They show up on time. They never miss a commitment. They are the most reliable person you've ever met. And reliability has become their entire offering.
7. They cook for you. They make the coffee. They bring you the snack. The acts of service are real, and they have become a wall between you, because they look like love and feel, increasingly, like a transaction.
8. They make you laugh. Often. With the same kind of joke they've been making for years. The humor is real, and it is also the most consistent way they have of changing the subject.
9. They compliment your work. Your project. Your accomplishment. They are proud of you in public. They have not asked, in private, what it actually felt like to do the thing.
10. They plan the vacation. The dinner. The weekend. The logistics are immaculate. The presence, once you arrive, has gone somewhere else.
11. They tell you they're proud of you. The words come easily. The pride does not include any specific knowledge of who you've become in the last few years.
12. They show up to the family event. They are charming. They are warm with your parents. They drive home in silence, and you have no idea what they thought of any of it.
13. They sleep next to you. Every night. The bodies are in the bed. The presence in the bodies has migrated somewhere else.
14. They tell you "of course" when you ask if they love you. The "of course" is so fast, it has the quality of a door closing.
15. They reassure you when you express worry. The reassurance is well-practiced. It does not include them actually being curious about why you were worried.
16. They protect you from their stress. They don't tell you about the hard day at work. They don't tell you what their boss said. They have decided that not burdening you is the same as loving you, and the decision has slowly turned them into a stranger.
17. They never raise their voice. They never escalate. The peace in the house is so intact that you have started to wonder if the peace is what's keeping you both from being honest.
18. They are physically affectionate in specific, repeatable ways. The hand on your back as they pass you in the kitchen. The kiss on the head. The same touch, in the same spot, for years. The repetition has stopped meaning what it used to mean.
19. They know your coffee order. Your favorite snack. Your routine. The data is encyclopedic. The interior of you has not been visited in a long time.
20. They make a fuss on your birthday. They send the flowers on the anniversary. They remember the dates. The dates have become the only time they perform the role of partner, and the performance is leaking the truth between performances.
21. They tell other people how lucky they are to have you. The telling happens at parties. In emails to their family. In passing comments to friends. The thing they tell other people is something you've stopped hearing them say directly to you.
22. They take care of you when you're sick. They make the soup. They bring the medicine. They are exquisite in the role of caregiver. They cannot be the same person when you're well.
23. They tell you "you can talk to me about anything." They have said this many times. You have, slowly, stopped trying.
24. They never complain about you. To you, or to anyone else. The not-complaining is meant as evidence of their devotion. The not-complaining is actually the muting of any real engagement with who you are and how you affect them.
25. They stay. Year after year. Through everything. And the staying, which used to feel like commitment, has started to feel like the most polite form of absence you've ever experienced.

25 Things Your Avoidant Partner Does That Look Like Distance but Are Actually Love
1. They go quiet when something matters to them. The silence is not avoidance. The silence is them trying to find the words for something they've never had words for before.
2. They walk out of the room in the middle of a hard conversation. They come back twenty minutes later, sometimes an hour later, and they sit down. The coming back is the love. It cost them something you can't see.
3. They don't say "I love you" first. They wait until you say it. Then they say it back, with a slight roughness in their voice. The slight roughness is the love. The fact that they couldn't initiate isn't proof they don't feel it.
4. They sit in the same room as you, on the other side of the couch, doing their own thing. The proximity is intentional. They could be anywhere. They chose to be near you. The choice is the love.

25 Things Your Avoidant Partner Does That Look Like Love but Are Actually Distance

1. They handle every logistical thing in your life so well, you stop noticing they haven't asked you a real question in months.

2. They buy you the gift. The thoughtful one. The right one. And they hand it to you without making eye contact, because the gift was easier than the looking.

3. They tell you they love you, every night, in the same three words, said the same way, and the sameness is what's keeping the rest of the conversation from ever happening.

4. They do the dishes, take out the trash, fix the leak, manage the bills, and they have, somehow, replaced their interior life with the to-do list.

5. They text you back quickly. Always. With a thumbs-up emoji, or a heart, or a "love you," and the speed of the response is meant to substitute for what the response is missing.

6. They show up on time. They never miss a commitment. They are the most reliable person you've ever met. And reliability has become their entire offering.

7. They cook for you. They make the coffee. They bring you the snack. The acts of service are real, and they have become a wall between you, because they look like love and feel, increasingly, like a transaction.

8. They make you laugh. Often. With the same kind of joke they've been making for years. The humor is real, and it is also the most consistent way they have of changing the subject.

9. They compliment your work. Your project. Your accomplishment. They are proud of you in public. They have not asked, in private, what it actually felt like to do the thing.

10. They plan the vacation. The dinner. The weekend. The logistics are immaculate. The presence, once you arrive, has gone somewhere else.

11. They tell you they're proud of you. The words come easily. The pride does not include any specific knowledge of who you've become in the last few years.

12. They show up to the family event. They are charming. They are warm with your parents. They drive home in silence, and you have no idea what they thought of any of it.

13. They sleep next to you. Every night. The bodies are in the bed. The presence in the bodies has migrated somewhere else.

14. They tell you "of course" when you ask if they love you. The "of course" is so fast, it has the quality of a door closing.

15. They reassure you when you express worry. The reassurance is well-practiced. It does not include them actually being curious about why you were worried.

16. They protect you from their stress. They don't tell you about the hard day at work. They don't tell you what their boss said. They have decided that not burdening you is the same as loving you, and the decision has slowly turned them into a stranger.

17. They never raise their voice. They never escalate. The peace in the house is so intact that you have started to wonder if the peace is what's keeping you both from being honest.

18. They are physically affectionate in specific, repeatable ways. The hand on your back as they pass you in the kitchen. The kiss on the head. The same touch, in the same spot, for years. The repetition has stopped meaning what it used to mean.

19. They know your coffee order. Your favorite snack. Your routine. The data is encyclopedic. The interior of you has not been visited in a long time.

20. They make a fuss on your birthday. They send the flowers on the anniversary. They remember the dates. The dates have become the only time they perform the role of partner, and the performance is leaking the truth between performances.

21. They tell other people how lucky they are to have you. The telling happens at parties. In emails to their family. In passing comments to friends. The thing they tell other people is something you've stopped hearing them say directly to you.

22. They take care of you when you're sick. They make the soup. They bring the medicine. They are exquisite in the role of caregiver. They cannot be the same person when you're well.

23. They tell you "you can talk to me about anything." They have said this many times. You have, slowly, stopped trying.

24. They never complain about you. To you, or to anyone else. The not-complaining is meant as evidence of their devotion. The not-complaining is actually the muting of any real engagement with who you are and how you affect them.

25. They stay. Year after year. Through everything. And the staying, which used to feel like commitment, has started to feel like the most polite form of absence you've ever experienced.

I have been given the gift to help others heal
And I need you to know
I stand where you stand.
I'm pretty good at it because
My heart has been hemorrhaging from my very first breath
When my mother abandoned me for the first 3 weeks of my life.
Tonight, I lay down this weight I've been carrying
this bewilderment at how something so necessary
can be so impossibly hard.
I came here to love and be loved.
Such a simple assignment.
Yet here I am again,
watching love slip through my fingers
like water I'm trying too hard to hold.
I see it now
how my mother's fears became my fears,
how my father's walls became my walls,
how the child who learned to hide
still hides inside the adult who claims to be brave.
Every time I reach for connection,
my history reaches faster.
Every time I try to stay soft,
my armor assembles itself without permission.
I fight the very thing I'm starving for.
Oh God, Universe, Spirit of Love itself
I'm so tired of pushing away
what my heart breaks open to receive.
Tired of turning my beloved into my enemy
when all I wanted was to turn them into home.
Grant me the mercy to forgive myself
for all the times I chose being right over being close.
For all the times I protected myself
straight into loneliness.
Tomorrow, let me wake one second slower.
Let me pause before the first defensive word.
Let me remember that the person across from me
is just another broken-hearted human
trying to love with a heart that's been taught to fear.
I know you made us for each other.
I know this longing is holy.
I know there's a reason my skin still hopes
to be touched with tenderness,
why my arms ache to hold and be held.
So here's my prayer:
Soften me where I've gone rigid.
Open me where I've shut down.
Teach me to stay when everything in me wants to run.
Show me to run when staying means disappearing.
Let me learn the difference between
the past and the present,
between danger and discomfort,
between them and the ghosts I'm actually fighting.
And please, when I forget all of this tomorrow,
when I'm back in the ring boxing shadows,
send me one small reminder:
That love is still possible.
That I'm still capable.
That somewhere inside this defended heart
lives someone who knows how to surrender.
Tonight I release the old way.
Tonight I grieve what didn't work.
Tonight I make space for the love
that's been waiting all along
for me to stop fighting long enough
to let it in.
This is my prayer.
This is my promise.
This is my hope returning.
My mother did the best she could
And she royally fucked up
And if blame was any kind of material that could help
It would have helped by now.
So I don't blame,
I put all in its authentic place.
The truth is that
She died inside too because I would not love her back
And even if she deserved to be abandoned by me
That won't help either
Because I did the same thing that her mom did to her.
In her coffin laid pictures of me up and down her body
Because the family knew I was her greatest loss.
In this moment I wish she hadn't died by her own hand
Because it took me five decades to realize
She might have held
The keys to the biggest risk I could have ever taken,
Loving the one back who nearly destroyed my soul. See less

Why Most Couples Have Spent Years Rehearsing Their Pain Instead Of Revealing It
There is a difference between rehearsed pain and revealed pain.
Most couples have never been taught the difference, and so they spend years doing one while believing they are doing the other. They think they are being vulnerable. They think they are being honest. They think they are opening up. They think they are sharing what is really going on.
They are not.
They are running a script.
Rehearsed pain is the pain you have already explained to yourself. It is the pain that has been turned into a story. It is the pain that has been polished. It is the pain you can deliver in complete sentences without your voice cracking. It is the pain that comes with a plot, a sequence, a beginning and middle and end. It is the pain that has been workshopped in your own head for months or years before it ever comes out of your mouth.
Revealed pain is something else entirely.
Revealed pain is the pain that arrives before you have figured out what it is. It is the pain that surprises you while you are trying to speak it. It is the pain that breaks your sentence in the middle. It is the pain that makes your face do something you did not plan for it to do. It is the pain that is still hot, still messy, still finding its shape as it leaves your body.
The first kind of pain creates distance.
The second kind of pain creates closeness.
And almost everybody is doing the first kind while thinking they are doing the second.
This is one of the great unspoken tragedies of long relationships. Two people, both trying so hard, both telling each other what hurts, both believing they are being open, and neither of them actually reaching the other, because both of them are delivering pain that has already been rehearsed into a shape their partner's nervous system reads as performance.
Performance is not vulnerability.
Performance is the costume vulnerability wears when the body underneath is not actually willing to be seen.
Your partner's body knows the difference. Your partner's body has always known the difference. Your partner cannot tell you why your honest, heartfelt explanation of your pain still felt like an attack, but their body knows. Their body knows because the pain you brought into the room had already been turned into a case. The pain had a structure. The pain had a thesis. The pain was being argued.
And the thing about argued pain is that it requires a defendant.
The moment your pain is argued, your partner becomes the defendant.
It does not matter what words you use. It does not matter how soft you tried to make your tone. It does not matter that you used I-statements. It does not matter that you started with appreciation. It does not matter that you said you were not trying to attack them. If your pain is rehearsed, the rehearsal itself puts them on trial.
Their body responds the way any body responds when it is on trial.
It defends.
It explains.
It denies.
It withdraws.
It counterattacks.
And then you walk away from the conversation thinking, why does my partner always get defensive when I try to be vulnerable. Why can't they just hear me. Why is it so hard for them to receive my feelings.
It is not hard for them to receive your feelings.
It is impossible for them to receive your prosecution.
And the prosecution is what you have been bringing into the room without knowing it.
Here is how rehearsed pain sounds.
"I feel like you don't prioritize me. I feel like I'm always last on your list. I feel like I have to fight for your attention. I feel like everything else matters more than I do. I feel like you don't even see me anymore. I feel like I've been telling you this for years and nothing changes."
Notice what is happening in those sentences.
They sound like feelings. They start with the words I feel. They use the language of vulnerability. They appear to be a person sharing their inner world.
They are not.
They are a case.
Each sentence is a charge. Each charge is an indictment. The cumulative effect is a verdict that has already been reached before the trial begins. The partner hearing this is not being invited into the speaker's inner world. They are being told, with the costume of vulnerability, that they have failed.
Their body knows.
Their body braces.
The conversation is over before it began.
Here is how revealed pain sounds.
"There is something in my chest right now that I have been trying to put words around for a long time, and I do not have it figured out yet, but I am going to try. Sometimes when I am sitting next to you, I feel a kind of loneliness I do not understand. I do not know if it is about you. I do not know if it is about me. I just know my body has been carrying it and I do not want to carry it alone anymore."
Notice what is happening here.
There is no charge. There is no thesis. There is no case being argued. The speaker is not telling their partner what their partner has done wrong. The speaker is letting their partner see something inside them that they themselves do not yet fully understand. They are opening a door, not delivering a verdict.
This is the move almost nobody has been taught.
Revealed pain does not have a target.
Rehearsed pain always does.

Am I about to say something I have rehearsed, or am I about to say something I am discovering as I say it.
If you have rehearsed it, your nervous system is already in defense, and your partner's nervous system will respond to your defense, and the conversation will collapse the way it has collapsed a thousand times before.
If you are discovering it as you say it, your nervous system is open, and your partner's nervous system will respond to your openness, and something different might happen.

The conversation you have been planning all day, the one you have been mentally rehearsing in the car, the one you have been drafting in your head while folding laundry, is almost certainly going to fail. Not because the content is wrong. Because by the time it comes out of your mouth, it has been workshopped into a case.
The conversations that change relationships are almost never the ones you planned.
They are the ones that happen at the kitchen sink when one of you reaches for a glass and your hand stops moving and you look up and say something you did not know you were going to say.
That is the body finally getting through.
That is the place where revelation lives.

When you bring rehearsed pain to your partner, you are not actually asking them to meet you. You are asking them to validate the case you have already built. You are asking them to agree with your conclusion. You are asking them to confess to the charges.

This is the part of you they fell in love with.
This is the part of you they have been missing for years.
This is the part of you that, if you can let it back into the room, can change everything.

You cannot get to it through better preparation.
You cannot get to it through more articulate sentences.

It only does one thing.
It lets your partner finally see you.

Their body will soften.
Their words will come slower.
They will reach.
Not because they are following a script of their own. Because something in their nervous system recognizes that the person in front of them is not arguing anymore. The person in front of them is showing themselves. The person in front of them has put the case down.

This is what most couples do not know.
Their failure to repair is not a failure of effort.
It is a failure of register.
They have been speaking the language of prosecution while believing they were speaking the language of intimacy. They have been bringing the case they built into the very room where they were hoping to be met. And the case, no matter how true, no matter how justified, no matter how patient the delivery, will always end the same way.
Defense. Withdrawal. Repeat.
The way out is not to argue better.
The way out is to stop arguing.
The way out is to put down everything you have prepared and find out what is underneath it. The way out is to sit with the person you love and let your own body show you a truth your mind has not finished editing. The way out is to let your sentence break in the middle, because the breaking is the part that finally gets through.
Your partner has been waiting, maybe for years, to meet the version of you that does not have a case.
You have been waiting, maybe for years, to meet the version of yourself that does not need one.
The waiting is over the moment one of you stops rehearsing and starts revealing.
That is the whole shift.
That is the only shift that has ever changed a relationship.
